THRE _ A maiden waits for the postman's call, Her heart is light and her eye is bright, As she listens for his faint footfall, And thrills with joy when he comes in sight; For she knows he brings her a message sweet From her love, who dwells in yonder town. Now eagerly she runs to meet The mail that brings the message down. • As the maiden reads the glowing lines Her face with a tender love-light shines. t-7. A young wife waits for the mail to come, And she sings the while an old love song; ; As she thinks of him, now far from home, For her heart is true and her trust is strong. She sighs that she has so lowg to wait, For time goes slow, though her heart beats fast. But now the postman is at the gate, And the longed-for letter arrives at last. She smiles as she reads the message dear, ; And feels that her absent one is near. A widow waits for the postman's ring, Her eye is dial and her cheek is pale, , She hopes the mail will tidings brim,'' Of her boy who years ago set sail For a foreign port, and ne'er returned. For a sight of the young lad's face once more All these years her heart has yearned. And now the postman is at the door; • But the letter tells, in a stranger's hand, That her toy has died in a distant land. MAY IN SURREY. BY WILLIAM SHARP. The cuckoo's thrilling voice is in the air; • Thrush calls to thrush with piercing notes of song, Like flute strains haply wandering everywhere; The yellowhammer's cry is borne along The gorse-clad heath, whose gold Is wave-like far outrolled ; A lark—a hundred larks are in the sky; A myriad birds an undersinging make; And, hush! where the long shadowy grasses lie, . The harsh voice of the crake. Likewind-swept snows the blossoms from the pear, The quince and cherry, all are blown away; But still the rose-flushed apple-bloom hangs fair About the rough-gnarled boughs with lichen grey. The wasp, and banded bee, And grey gnat drowsily , Hum i' the air, or yield to honey-spells: , Where the sweet-scented flowers usurp the grass, Tale azure o'er the hyacinth bells, The tiny blue moths pass. ;Down by yon slope there lies a magic glade (Its Dale-green shimmer through the hop-poles bare (~ can scarce be seen), where wondrously is laid A carpet such as never human care Wrought from the looms of old In Ty-rian purple bold; . Of delicatest blue it is—mayhao The glad sky dropt a furtive kiss on earth, A kiss here caught, and treasured in her lap Till this divine rebirth. sweet this soul-felt beauty of the spring, This stirring of the leaves and flowers long furled In sappy sheaths! This joy the birds outsin7— The Joy of all the gladsome, glorious world— How sweet, how sweet it is! And how serene the bliss That floods with golden glow this afternoon, In azure lying on the distant hills Whereover hangs the white disc of the moon The dayshine fills. Thus may it be (ah, hush! thou dubious thought That dost recall the waning of the year— The bleak drear, wintry death) when, all forgot; The soul awakens in some newer sphere, And sees a new light fall Divinely over all, While far away behind, even as the pale Moon-disc in heaven, the fading earth at last Seems, like a dream long dreamt, of no avail— The shadow of the past. —Good Words.

"See there !" exclaimed a returned Irish soldier to a gaping crowd, as he exhibited with some pride, his tall hat with a bullet hole in it. "Look at that hole, will you? You see that if it had been a low-crowned hat, I 'Should have been killed outright." A lawyer in an eastern State, whose reputation in the community was not very high,-met an old gentleman one day, and said to him, "Do you know, Mr. H., that I am a direct descendant from Miles Standish?" "Is it pos- sible ?" was the reply; "what a descent r That was a delicate compliment a seven-year-old boy paid his mother the other evening. The family ;were discussing at the supper table the qualities which go to make the good wife. Nobody thought the little fellow had been listening, or could understand the talk, until he leaned over the table, kissed his mother, and said, "Mamma, when I get big enough, I'm going to marry a lady just like you." Lord Norbury-, when once charging a jury in a breach of promise case, noticed that the letters of the faithless defendant had been so long in the plaintiff's pocket, or so often shown to her sympathising friends that they were greatly frayed at the folds and almost in tatters. "Gen- tlemen," said Lord Norbury,-carefully, folding up one of the fragmentary epistles to the gaze of the jury, "It's easy to see that these are• love4etters, because they are so exceedingly tender." At a church in Scotland, where there was a popular call for a minister, as- it was termed, two candidates offered to preach, whose names were Adam and Low. • The latter preached in the morning, and took for his text, "Adam, where art thou?" He made a very excel- lent discourse, and the congregation were much edified. In the afternoon Mr. Adam preached upon these words: "Lo, here am I." The impromptu and the sermon gained him the appointment. Lever tells a story of his once dining at a boarding- house by the invitation of a friend who resided there. At his elbow stood a decanter of sherry bearing a paper label, "Robert M'Grotty ;" and Lever, in ignorance that this betokened private property, helped himself freely to the wine. Presently, his friend, who was seated some -way off, inquired what he would drink. "Thanks," re- sponded Lever, "I'm doing very well; I'll stick to my friend here, 'Bob M'Grotty'"—imagining the name on the bottle to be some jocular title given to the wine. To his horror an indignant voice by his side spoke out, "And ye may weel stick to it, sir, and hae all the bottle now, for it's little of his sin wine .that Bob M'Grotty, as ye call him, has tasted this day." THE COMING MEN.—Discipline at home will prevent the necessity of punishment at school, and a mother's gentleness, combined with firmness, goes very far to counteract the natural waywardness of the average boy, A boy who truly loves his mother will rarely e 6Tieve her if he is brought up right, and boys generally cling more to their mother than to their father ; therefore it the mother who has the blessed privilege of bending the . boy's mind in the line of duty, which should remain a • perfect line -all his life. The blessing of having good sons is better than ()Teat riches, to which fact I happily 'testify. My mother heart aches as I pass along the streets and se* the poor untrained urchins, some amok- hg, some swearing, and all of wham think that the louder they swear and the more slang they use the more like men they will be, and all for want of a mother's guidance and training. What a fearful ;responsibility iteS upon parenta who, forgetful of the-tender souls en- trusted to their care, leave them to get on as they can without check or hindrance. Let them think of these . always (as you English say) a word and a blow, and the blow fist.' Fe had fought so many duels that the :soldiers used to call him Sudden Death,' and to say That the best way to end the war would be for him to challenge the enemy's whole army, man by man. Well, •aie day this lieutenant had committed some 'fault, for which the 'Colonel gave him such a scolding that the young fellow's hot blood couldn't bear it any longer. -Quick as lightning he whipped out a pistol and fired right at St. Hilaire's face, so close that the muzzle almost touched him. But the pistol missed fire, and the colonel said, quite coolly, 'Forty-eight hours' arrest for not keeping your arms in proper order.'" "And was that all that the -lieutenant got?" asked a dozen voices at once, ;in undisguised amazement. "That was all; and I can tell you that he thouglA it was7quite enough. Ha! General, good evening; I was just telling these gentle- men how you once put use under arrest for not having my pistols in working order."—Harper's .z7fagazine. -things, remembering that by early neglect the welfare of the coming men is.at stake.—Silver Pen. THE COOLEST MAN IN THE ARMY.—" The coolest man I Aver knew was old 'Victor de St. Hilaire, the colonel of an infantry regiment that saw some service in Algeria," said Colonel Henri Dubois, one of a party of French -officers who, having halted to take a look at Siam on their way home from-We Tonquin war, had come to dine with us on board of a Eritish gunboat which had some- how found its way up the Mei-Nem river. "I've known men," he continued, "who managed to put on a great show of coolness in time of danger; though they were really very much excited; but these was no putting-on with Se Hilaire—it-came as natural to him as eating his liner. All his hairbreadth escapes (and he bad so many that he could hardly count them hiniaelfl had left him as , cool as before, and it really seemed as if dangers passed him by because he would not condescerki to notice that they were there at all. Once his men mutinied, and two of them clapped their bayonets to his breast as if to run bina through; but the Cailonel only smiled, and said, as quietly as ever, Be careful, nay lads; you might hurt me! Now, it happened that in Colonel St. Hilaire's regiment there was a peppery young sab-lieutenant who was as hot as the Colonel was cool. Don't argue with a fool, or listeners will say there are i two of you. - One to-day is worth two to-morrows.—By the street of By-and-by we arrive at the house of Never.—To-morrow is the fool's holiday. The images with which the mind holds converse may uplift or degrade as truly as companions in bodily form. A thought may scar the soul as a weapon leaves its mark on the flesh. Husband and wife should study the weak parts of each otheez character, for the same purpose that a skater keeps a lookout for weak spots in the ice—to keep away from them. A country rector, going up to preach at Oxford in his turn, complained to Dr. Routh, the venerable Principal of Maudlin, that the remuneration was very inadequate, considering the travelling expenses and the labour neces- sary for the composition of the discourse. "How much did they give you?" inquired Dr. Routh. "Only five pounds," was the reply. "Only five pounds !" repeated the doctor. "Why, I would not have preached that aermon for fifty." .

_ TO-MORROW. To-morrow you will live, you always cry. In what far country does this morrow lie, That 'tis so mighty long-cre it arrive? Beyond the Indies does This morrow live? 7717 'Tis so far-stretched, thismorrow, that I fear "Twill be both very old and very dear. " To-merrow I will live," the fool doth say; To-day itself, too late; the wise lived yesterday. Among the visitors to a fine art exhibition were two old ladies fresh from the country. They were engaged in examining, with great interest, a statue of a young Greek, underneath which were the words "Executed in terra-cotta." "Where is Terra-cotta ?" asked the elder of the two, turning to her companion. "1 havn't the least idea," replied the other," "I never heard of the place before." " Ali, well," observed the first speaker, "it doesn't much signify. The poor man who was exe- cuted there is not the less to be pitied wherever it may be.' ADAM AND EVE AND THAT APPLE.—At the repeated request of many correspondents, we repeat the following :—How many apples did Adam and Eve eat? Some say Eve 8 and Adam 2—a total of 10 only. Now we figure the thing out differently. Eve 8 and Adam 8 also. Totall6. —Boston Journal. We think the above figures entirely wrong. If Eve 8, and Adam 82, certainly the total will be 90. Scientific men, however, on the strength of the theory that the antediluvians were a race of giants rea- son something like this—Eve 81 and Adam 82—tota1163. —Gloucester Advertiser. Wrong again; what could be clearer than if Eve 81 and Adam 812, the total was 89311—Lawrence American. If Eve 811 st and Adam 812, would not the total be 1,623 P—Boston Journal. I believe the following to be the true solution :—Eve 814 Adam 8124 Eve—total 9338. Veritas. Still another cal- culation is as follows: If Eve 814 Adam, Adam 81242 oblige Eve—total, 82,056. We think this, however, not to be a sufficient quantity. For though we admit that Eve 814 Adam, Adam if he 8081242 keep Eve company— total 1,082,056.—New York: Mail. All wrong. al Eve, when she 81812 many, and probably felt sorry for it, but her companion, in order to relieve her grief, 812. There- fore Adam if he 818142401 y Eve's depressed spirits. Hence both ate 81,896,864.—R055t0n, in Quincy Wkly. LIVING ACCORDING TO RllLE.—Physicians know that they must live by rule when attending cases during a pestilence. The body must be kept up toyithe health standard. In times of epidemic let everyone see to him- self, attend to every rule of health, live regularly, and keep the stomach most carefully in order, and 'be ab- stinent. There is no other way of defending the Fortress of Life against invisible foes. " This living according to rule," said my friend, musingly, "is a terribly hard thing to have to add. At least, I am sure most people find it so." "Few people," I replied, ' think of doing I anything of the sort, until actual danger to life stares I them in -the face. Someone else, I believe, has made a Iremark similar to this before now, but it is worthy of being repeated." " And it is true," added Horton, "I have been thinking a good deal lately--" "Most peo- ple who are laid low do think," I said. "I have been thinking," said my friend,'" most of us err by eating; more than is necessary." "How very true that is, Hor- ton! Why, in careful regulation of diet—a diet that should incline to the abstemious—we have one of the best defences against inviAble foes of all kinds. This is one of our posts, and should be held at all risks, if we care for life at all—and not for life only, but comfort while we do exist. It is a fact which all should bear in mind, that over-eating not only corrupts the blood, but destroys nervous energy."—Cassell's Family Magazine. i DANTE's DESCRIPTION OF HELL. —lf anything were t wanted to prove the demoralising effect on any human being of setting himself up in the position of the Almighty as the eternal judge of 'other individual and contemporary men's sins, it would be found in the crescendo movement in Dante's personal cruelty in the descriptions of the "Inferno "—from the most ignoble and ghastly gambols in the "new sport" with the Male- branche, the episode of Vanni Fucci and the serpents,— "From that time forth the serpents were my friends,"— the cowardly attack on Bocca, degli Albati, pulling shocks of his hair out—to the culminating point where our Christian poet shows himself at once cruel and a traitor in his treatment of the shade of Friar Alberigo, who says in his frozen helplessness— But hitherward stretch out thy hand forthwith. , Open mine eyes-, and open them I did not, , And to be rude to him was courtesy. And this after having made a sclemn compact with the shade—

If thou wouldst have me help thee, Say who thou wast ; and if I free thee not, May I go to the bottom of the ice. There can be no comment on this passage—except, per- haps, to admit that with a widening psychology we are forced to the conclusion that the greatest minds, the most noble spirits, often carry within themselves vol- canic intensity of passion for evil as well as for good. It may be supposed that on re-reading these lines, and leaving them to stand fer all time, Dante had the same feeling towards them that lie must have had to the pas- sionate passage in the " Convito." where he says that to arguments against the immortality of the soul, "one would wish to reply not with words, but with a knife." This, though intense, is not really so malignant, because the eyes of the contemporary, who did not take precisely Da,nte's view of the most knotty of all problems, not be- ing frozen, he might have had the chance of defending himself. These expressions must of course be taken figuratively.—From "Dante for the General," in Black- wood's Magazine for May, 1886. CHINESE OFFICIALS OF RAILWAYS.—Europo expects great things at present from the immediate development of a system of railways in China, and the consequent opening to trade influences of a vast and densely popu- lated empire. Never was the airy superstructure of hope built upon foundations more slender! In the first place, the sums of money required would be too enormous to be raised by the Imperial Exchequer, and would be too large even to be accomplished by foreign loans, unless guarantees were forthcoming, which are not possible. It must not be forgotten that China is not so much an empire as a collection of eighteea kingdoms, all doing vassalage to a common emperor. The huge distances of China, aud the absence of roads, practically cause the viceroys of her eighteen provinces to exercise kingly functions. These rulers and other high officials are ap- pointed to their posts by the Central Government of Pekin; but as their pay is nominal, and as they are left to collect and administer the revenues of their provinces, it will easily be understcodthat their power is great, as also their facilities for becoming wealthy. In the same manner all official appointments, from the highest to the lowest, are filled. The lower officials bleed the people under their control, taking care that their superiors have their share of the 'squeeze," and so on up to the Vice- roy. If anyone shows unusual greed, he is denounced, and is immediately pounced on and sucked dry. In the course of a term of years a high official usually accumu- lates very large sums. He is generally then invited to Pekin to give an account of his stewardship; if he is a wise man, he takes with him half to two-thirds of his gains, and after a few months at the capital, having dis- posed of all this, he obtains leave to retire, or, perhaps, is appointed to some other post. The corruption of a system of government such azthis—for it is a system per- fectly organised on the recognised basis that an appoint- ment is given to a man to make what he can out of it, always provided that he is not found out—is widespread in its effects. It cramps the trading instincts of the most in- genious and commercial nation in the East; it crushes the lower orders, making their life one bitter struggle for existence: and it both corrodes and fossilises the:official classes, making them blind to reason and to pity, deaf to the call of patriotism and of duty. From whichfit will be seen that, while the governing classes have their in- ht ietsi et ss ba oh ud nd actualities Up na soyfspteomwewr hanicdh wgeaiveltshthwei i c hp they is se could not enjoy under a less decentralised government, so long will they oppose such progress, as great lines of railway would not fail to effect in binding; together the country under a powerful and well-informed central government with wideltretching arms. The iron horse would break the; spell, and the officials whose :districts are situated at present several months' journey from Pekin would be brought under the immediate:sway of the high authorities. Add to the above the fact that, amongst the official classes and the Chinese of tile in- terior, the old hostility to and contempt of the foreigner still exists. They recognise his existence at the seaward settlements, but they fear as well as dislike his influence and interference. The railway, they largely believe, is a device of the foreigner such as the wooden horse pre- sented to the Trojans, ard they foresee in it an insidious effort to penetrate the recesses of their vast country in order to rob it of its wealth; and they are afraid foreign influence may become as powerful in the interior as it is on the coast-line. They dread lest their empire should slip from them. The feeling of " Timeo Ds.naos et dona ferentes" is strong with the Chinese, and even were waysrail- th erh tt oo br rest s tmi and foreign 0, rt ehi ge they whoaunldds,noatnsdr werithtohuet wsoomrkeinsgucohf guarantee as this, European capßalists would hardly care to operate, as previously stated. China is essentially a country where it is the unexpected that takes place, and it would cause no surprise were the Imperial assent to railways issued to-morrow; but the opinion of the well- informed is that railways on any scale, if at all, are not likely to be made at present. A cow dealer, of Maryport, Cumberland, has been fined 305., with the alternative of 30 days' imprisonment, the other day, for having ill-treated a cow by allowing her • udder to be painfully distended with milk while in the cattle market. Tnis is the fourth case of the kind which has come before the Court recently. , A reference under the Agricultural Holdings Act has just been settled in the parish of Kilmaurs, Ayrshire. The parties were the proprietor and tenant of the farm of Fergushill. £2OO was claimed by the tenant. The arbiters have awarded him £l3 us. Bd., each party to pay his own expenses and half the cost of reference. An agricultural college, for the training of young gentlemen farmers, is about to be opened at Indian Head, 312 miles west of Winnipeg, on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The college, which is in- tended to accommodate fifty pupils, will, it is stated, be opened by July 1 next, and will be under the direction of Professor Tanner, Director of Education, under the Insti- tute of Agriculture, South Kensington, London. LAMBS EATING WOOL.—A " Shepherd " writes in the Field :—" That balls of wool are often found in the stomachs of lambs is a well known fact. They are gene- rally supposed to owe their origin to wool taken in by the lambs in their efforts to suck, and we see directions given in shepherds' manuals for clearing away the wool from the udders of ewes previous to lambing time, lest this should happen; but my belief on the subject got a shock recently. I have a small flock of Border Leicester steep, which have a covered yard for shelter at night or in bad weather. It was a snowy day when, happening to look in at them, my atfention was attracted by a lamb of about a month old, which was chewing some wool. I watched till it swallowed it, when, to my sur- prise, it pulled a fresh lock off its mother's hind leg, and went on with the masticating process as before. The lamb is in perfect health and very thriving, the mother having abundance of milk." ENSILAGE EXPERIMENTS.—At a Council meeting of the Bath and West of England Society, held a few days ago at Bristol, Mr. Dyke, as chairman of the Ensilage Com- mittee, applied for a grant of space in the showyard for the exhibition of specimens of ensilage from the silos erected by the society at Bower Ashton, and also for per- mission to circulate printed particulars of such experi- ments in the showyard. Both of these requests were unanimously complied with by the Council. Mr. Alder- man Wm. Smith, an active member of the Bristol Local Committee, who has taken much interest and trouble with regard to these experiments, and at whose sugges- tion they were undertaken' was then introduced to the meeting by Mr. Dyke, and at the request of the Council gave some details of the course which had been pursued. He stated that the experiments, which had been con- ducted under the supervision of the most eminent ex- perts on a very carefully prepared scheme, as approved by Sir J. B. Lawes and Dr. Voelcker, had been most care- fully carried out, no hitch whatever haying occurred, nor anything that could interfere with an exact and re- liable result being obtained. The ensilage, which is both sour and sweet, is in six wooden silos. The special ob- ject the society has in view is to ascertain the loss or gain of nutritive qualities incurred in the process of ensiling crops as compared with hay made from the same herbage. SEPARATOR TERSITS CRITRN.—" More Anon," writing to the Agricultural Gazette, refers to a communication from Mr. Toulmin in the previous issue as to the separator versus the churn. Ho says :—The communication from Mr. Toulmin is most interesting. As ascertained by tests constantly being carried on under my supervision, it is found that the yield of butter from churning ripened milk (" lappered," as the Scotch people say), and which is always more or less acidified, varies from one to two ounces more butter per gallon than in the case of the separator, according to the season. But in my own opinion this loss is more than compensated for by the superior quality of the butter made from cream, and the higher price obtainable for separated milk as compared with buttermilk, 6d. a gallon being a low retail price, which ought to net 4d. per gallon to the producer, who is located within reasonable distance of any centre of population where the consump- tion is considerable. And happily for the dairy interest, its use for the purposes of a beverage and for baking; purposes is on the increase, and everywhere its more ex- tended use is a matter of education and cultivation. Even if fed to animals, it is questionable if skim-milk would be less valuable than buttermilk produced by the churning of the milk, from which the fat has been almost entirely extracted. Although Mr. Toulmin's result of 1 lb. butter from 20•5 lb. of milk is a very satisfactory one (sweet milk being churned, presumably), still better results would be obtained by allowing the milk to be- come ripened by standing; at a temperature of 70 degrees for a time before churning, without any deterioration in the quality of the butter. Whilst the difference in cost between churn and separator is considerable, as stated by Mr. Toulmin, it is probable that, in most cases this difference would be more than compensated for by the more profitable sale of skim-milk as compared with but- termilk of the quality referred to. - -

FEEDING OF COWS' AND CATTLE.—In the management of dairy cattle two systems are pursued. First, that of pasturing. Secondly, that of housing or soiling, in which the cows are kept under cover all the year round, being fed, groomed, littered, and kept warm and clean as horses, and only allowed sufficient daily exercise for health's sake, say about two or three hours per diem. Under the former system the cows are kept out in the pasture all day, and sometimes all night, during the summer; but in winter, when cold and there is neces- sarily little pasture, it would be folly to subject such animals to a like exposure, which not only lessens the flow of milk, but causes the cows to fall off in condition. However, when the winter is mild and there is some herbage to crop, there can be no objection to pAsturing them for a few hours during the warmest part of the day.. With this exception, mulch cows should be stall-fed in winter, if it is desired to turn the " keep" to the most advantage in the shape of milk and flesh. Cold, and especially cold and wet, it is well known, lessens the secretion of milk, and in hot summer weather animals ' are often teased and worried by insects, which keep them in a perpetual state of feverish agitation and irrita- tion, which, equally with cold, lessens the yield of milk. Therefore, it is equally necessary that cattle should be artificially protected from the heat of summer and its incidents as the cold of winter by sheds, trees, or hang- ing hedges. Then, again, cattle, whether fattening or dairy stock, should not have their food suddenly changed, but the change should be made gradually from a poorer to a richer dietary, especially such as to turnips, or to a riCh herbage, or from dry to green forage, as they are apt to scour, get hove, or become feverish, all of which circumstances derange the system and check milk pro- duction. Therefore, in carrying out this system of pas- turing, all these points must be kept strictly and dili- gently in view in grazing cows or cattle, so as not to expose them to these injurious casualties.

REPORT OF THE ENSILAGE COMMISSION. The efinal report of the Ensilage Commissioners has just been printed by order of the House of Commons. The following is a quotation with respect to the advan- tages claimed for the ensilage process "The advantages which are claimed for the process of ensilage may be classed under three heads: I. In render- ing the farmer independent of weather in saving his crops. 2. In increasing the productive capabilities of I farms: (a) In greater weight of forage saved, (b) In greater available variety and rotation of crops, (c) In

div.head: EXAMINER SkTURDA_Y, MAY 29, 1886
div.p: THE EXAMINER SkTURDA_Y, MAY 29, 1886

Increased 'facility for storage. S. In connection with feeding: (a) Dairy stock, (b) Breeding stock, (c) Store stock, (d) Patting stock, (e) Farm horses. "1.. INDEPENDENCE OF WEATHER IN SAVING. CROPS.— In this respect it has been abundantly proved to us that ensilage is of great economic value. In Scotland, in Ireland, and in the north and west of England, few sea- sons occur in which more or lees difficulty is not expe- rienced in reducing green fodder crops ti a sufficiently dry condition for stacking in the ordinary way. This is especially, the case with second crops of clover and after- math. the loss occurring through ineffectual attempts to dry such crops, or through their inferior condition when carried, is often very considerable, and it is -ob- vious that any system which enables a farmer to store these in good condition for future use must be a great saving of expense and anxiety. "2. ADVANTAGES IN INCREASING THE PRODUCTITH CAPA- BILITIES OF FARMS.— (a) In greater weight of forage saved. Itis obvious that unless the forage in a weighty condition be of more feeding value per acre than when saved in a less 'weighty form there can be no gain to the farmer. It has been contended that the loss of weight in the process of drying is simply loss of water by evaporation, and that by avoiding this nothing is saved. If such were truly the case, dry forage should give the same feeding results per acre as green forage. No prac- tical farmer would contend that it does so, and the dif- ference is especially noticeable in the case of dairy stock. So far as we have been able to ascertain the opinion of competent men on this subject, we estimate the value of green forage well preserved In a silo at somewhat more than one-third, weight for weight, of the value of the same material made into hay under favourable condi- tions. The very wide difference of value between good and bad silage cannot be too strongly insisted upon. It is found that grass well preserved in a silo, after deduc- tion for loss, will yield approximately five times the weight of the same grass made into hay. We have, therefore, say, five tons of silage, which, taken at one- third the value of hay per ton, yields a profit of over 60 per cent, as compared with one ton of hay. If we take it at one-fourth, it still leaves a profit of 25 per cent. Any waste that may occur to reduce the weight of nu- tritious forage, whether by evaporation or by excess of chemical change, must necessarily affect this calculation, which is based upon the highest degree of perfect pre- servation so far known to be attainable. "(b) IN AVAILABLE VARIETY AND ROTATION OF CROPS. —By the process of ensilage many crops can be pre- served which would not otherwise be found profitable if used in the form of green forage. Rye, oats, millet, maize, barley, and even wheat, if cut about the time of attaining their full development, but before the seed be- gins to harden, have been successfully used as food for cattle through the medium of the silo. Such of these crops as are found to reach the required condition before the middle pf June, if cut before that time, will leave the land free for a second sowing, and thus increase its capabilities of annual production, while maintaining the fertility of the soil. Where land is well treated, maize, buckwheat, or, in some parts of England, also turnips, can be sown after green rye or oats are cut and carried, and thus a second crop may be secured for preservation in the silo, or for consumption by sheep on the land. "(c) IN INCREASED FACILITY FOR STORAGE.—This ad- vantage has been forcibly impressed upon us. It enables farmers to guard themselves against emergencies, such as frequently arise in our climate through prolonged cold in February, March, and April, causing great scarcity of food for cattle and sheep, where the supply of roots is inadequate. "3. ADVANTAGES CONNECTED WITH FEEDING.--(a) DAIRY STOCK.—We have received the strongest evidence of the undoubted advantage of the system for the feeding of dairy stock. The effect of dry winter food given to such stock has always been to reduce in quantity and to deteriorate in quality milk, cream, and butter, as com- pared with the same products resulting from green sum- mer food. Although the degree of perfection attainable in summer has not been reached, it has been at least much more nearly approached by ensilage than by the use of hay and other dry foods, while at the same time the ob- jections inseparable from the employment of roots for Otis purpose have been overcome. A sensible improve- ment in the colour of butter has been especially noticed. "(b) BREEDING STOCK.—Green fodder preserved by ensilage has been successfully employed in feeding sheep and cattle at the time of breeding, and as it has been shown to increase the flow of milk, it will undoubtedly be found useful for this purpose, although the propor- tion of its admixture with other kinds of food must al- ways require care and judgment. (c) STORE STOCK.—It forms a complete and whole- some food for store stock. "(d) FATTING STOCK.—The value of this process for the purpose of forming flesh and fat has not yet perhaps been so widely demonstrated as in the case of dairy produce. At the same time, the results attained show that it compares favourably, with the use of roots, and, if given in proper propertions with other food, it affords a cheap substitute for the same bulk, which would other- wise be required in some different form. The advantage of its use is most apparent in the degree to which it en- ables a farmer profitably to consume straw chaff, rough hay chaff, and other dry materials, which, without ad- mixture with some kind of moist food, would not be palatable or advantageous to the growth of stock. (e) FARM HORSES.—Strong as the evidence has been of the advantage of ensilage for keeping all stock in healthy condition, farm horses have by no means been excepted. We have received highly satisfactory ac- counts from several quarters of the health of working teams when given a limited proportion of silage mixed with other food. "As in the case of all important innovations, it is not surprising that the introduction of the system of en- silage into this country has been met by a considerable amount of prejudice and incredulity. During the pro- gress of our inquiry, we have endeavoured amply to discount all exaggerated estimates of its merits. After summing up the mass of evidence which has reached us, we can without hesitation affirm that it has been abun- dantly and conclusively proved to our satisfaction that this system of preserving green fodder crops promises great advantages to the practical farmer, and if carried out with a reasonable amount of care and efficiency, should not only provide him with the means of insuring himself to a great extent against unfavourable seasons, and of materially improving the quantity and quality of his dairy produce, but should also enable him to increase appreciably the number of live stock that can be profit- ably kept upon any given acreage, whether of pasture or arable land, and proportionately the amount of manure available to fertilise it." All those who are interested in the subject would do well to obtain the full report, and read the evidence upon which the opinions of the Commissioners are based. The report may be obtained from Messrs. Hansard, Great Queen-street, Lincoln's Inn-fields, or of any of the dealers in Parliamentary papers.

August, and( those sown at the present time would pro- duce good flowering plants next spring. Slugs are most destructive to them when in the seedling state, and ' when we have anything choice of this nature we sow in a box or pan, and stand it on inverted pots, and these twain in garden saucers, which always contain water, which the slug must obviously pass through before it can get to the seedlings. The same course is frequently followed when the seedlings are pricked out before they are sufficiently largo to be trusted in the open ground. Seeds of common kinds are risked on a warm border, and when large enough to handle are pricked out in a bed well manured with decayed dung, about four to six inches distant, where they will require no attention beyond a watering or two if the weather is dry at plant- ing time, and passing the hoe occasionally between them to destroy weeds. TEE WiNnovr.—The Arum Lily is a plant that might be safely turned outside after this date, and in order to prevent its being blown over by the wind a stake should be driven into the ground and the plant tied to it; or if the pots are stood near a wall, and a string attached to a nail driven into the latter, the plant can be secured in that way. The flowers and foliage of this plant are sub- ject to be infested with green fly, which may be destroyed in the following manner :—To every quart of pain water add the juice of a quarter of an ounce of tobacco and a piece of soft soap the size of a walnut, and if the water is made hot enough it will soon dissolve the soap and extract the juice from the tobacco, and for convenience this should be put in a piece of muslin or rag. When ! cool it. may be applied with a syringe, or the plant held ! over a vessel and the liquid poured over it.;

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

Vegetation has been checked during the past week by biting winds and cold pelting rain, sleet, snow, and hail. Happily we have Laot experienced any frost, though many things look as though they were bitten, especially seedlings that had the protection removed from them when the weather became summer-like the week before. Plants of Spring Cabbage have been twisted about by the wind to such an extent that each plant has a circular cavity round its base, which is strong evidence of the struggle they have had. Each plant should be examined, and where necessary the soil pressed well up Lo it with the hands, and if they are not further disturbed they may root into it; but whether or not it is highly im- portant that the soil should be packed firmly round them.

BEETROOT.—We are not particular to a week or two when we sow this delicious vegetable, being guided more by the season and state of the soil than date. We have sown as early as April 24th on one occasion, but this year left it till this week. The bed had been ready for some time, but the wind blowing the seeds in all ',direc- tions checked us one time and the rain the other, com- pelled us to put sowing off to such a late date. The Beet succeeds best in moderately light soil that isi in good heart from manure applied to a previous crop. As a rule it is best to tread the soil or press it with the back of the spade, then draw drills 2in. deep and not less than 10in. distant. Some allow as much as 15in. between the rows, and in that case the plants are thinned out 6in. or 7in. apart, whilst those at 10in. would be left corre- spondingly thinner. The ground must be free from slugs or there will be no Beetroot, for they will be destroyed before the sower is able to see them. It is a good plan to sow the ground over with fresh slacked lime, the first still moist morning either before or after the seeds are sown. Another excellent plan to destroy these marau- ders is to place a few handfulls of the Kales when pulled up on the surface of the seed beds to entice the slugs, and if these are examined occasionally the slugs will be found congregated underneath them, when they may be destroyed either by sprinkling lime or salt over them. The greens must be placed in a fresh spot or they may be destroyed, and fresh ones introduced. Other decaying green veffetables or weeds will form A harbour for slugs if left in heaps for two or three days, and if their re- moval is followed up the garden would soon be free from these pests. French or Dwarf Beans should be sown in drills simi- lar to those made for Broad Beans, and about 18in. dis- tant; and 24in. should be allowed for Canadian Wonder on good soil. The seeds are sown in single rows 4in. distant, a space that they soon fill if the soil is good and favourable to their growth. The plants bear for a long time if the pods are not left on too long to form seeds, which has such an exhaustive action that the plant's growth is suddenly stopped. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Polyanthus and Primroses: Any of these that may have done flowering should be divided, if the clumps have become large, and the pieces planted in rich soil. When left too long in the same spot they extract all nourishment out of the soil, the foliage be- comes small and starved looking, the flowers poor and weakly, and the plants are more apt to die off than when occasionally diAded. The weather is so favour- able for the operation at the present time that even plants which may not have done flowering would come to no harm if taken up and replanted. Pieces may also be cut from the parent plant without further disturbing it, and inserted where permanently required, or in a border in the vegetable garden, and transferred to the front garden in the autumn or early in spring. ro raise new varieties seeds must be sown now or in July or

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.

ANNUAL MEE TING. The annual meeting of the Runcorn Foothall Club was held on Tueeday night in the large room of Wilson's Hotel. The president, Mr. J. R. Frith, occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance, amongst those present being Dr. Mitnean, Messrs. S. Pope, T. D. Timmins, and R. Gorst, S. Orme, W. R. Was, P. Wright, W. Brookes, J. M. Frith, I H. llughes, J. Gatley, F. Joule, W. Wright, 'H. Wright, J. D. Widders, W. Hughes, J. B. Clarke, John Clarke, J. Lunt, W. G. Ward, W. Carroll, G. Booth, R. Hughes. tte. Mr. J. E. Lategshaw, secretary, reed the report as fellows: ' —First team results: matches played 32, of which 21 were won, 5 drawn, and 6 lost. The team scored 40 goals, 57 tries, and 112 minor points against their opponents 13 goals. 20 tries, and 54 minor points. The tries were obtained: By a. alugnes, 13; H. Andrews, 10; H. Speakman, 10; W, 1 Hughes, 9; G. Wainwright, 8: T. Johnson, 6; W. Wright, 5 ; E. Lunt, 5 ; J. Gatley, 5; W. Cox, 3; I'. Davies, 3; J. Holland, 2; J. Barns, 3; J. Lewis, 2; W. Broady, I 2; J. Dean, 2; and J. Winstanley, W. Riley, cad F. Joule one each. H. Speekman was successful in dropping eix goals from the field. The goal-kicking analysis was as follows :—J. Lewis out of 57 attempts converted 21 into goals; T. Woods, 21 attempts, 10 goals; W. Hughes, 9 attempts, 2 goals ; W. Faulkner, 3 attempts, 1 goal.; J. Gatley, 1 attempt, nil; total, 91 attempts, 34 goals. The second teem had played 20 matches, won 16, i lost 2, drawn 2. They had scored 13 goals, 21 tries, 66 minor points, against their opponents 4 tries, 15 minor points. The tries were scored by W. Faulkner, 4 ; G. Whitby, 4; E. Orme, 3 ; H. Cawley, 3 ; E. Andrews, 2.; E. Lunt, 2; G. Wainwright, 2; T. Davies, 2; W. Riley, 2; W. Antrobus, 2; and W. Dunbavand, Cox, J. G hams, and A. Raffu one each. E. Lunt dropped two goals and Wainwright and Davies one each.— Mr. C. Pownall, the treasurer, read the financial statement. It appeared that the club commenced the season with a balance ot £73 193 9d, including which sum the receipts amounted to £444 lie 101. The honorary members sub- scriptions amounted to £l7 5s 6d, ordinary members £l3, season tickets £4, gate receipts £320 8s 61, and the profit of sports £7 161. The expenditure included the following items :—Gatekeepers £l5 14s 6.1, half gate receipts to eight clubs £42 Is 11d, three piasters' rent £l5, field expenses £36 141 9d, Unsworth Brothers (jerseys) £2O 83, printing, stationery, and postage £4O Os 7d; expenses of players and secretarf £124 6s Bd, refrestements £4O 2s sd, and referees £ll. Other small items brought the expenditure to £397 113 sd. There was a balance in band of 47 Os 5d —After several inquiries had been satisfactorily answered the report and financial statement were adopted unanimously.—The Chairman said it afforded him much plea,sure to be present that evening. The secretary's report was very gratifying, and he must congratulate the players for what had been achieved by both the first and second teams. (Applause.) a success not the result of luck but of diligent, careful, and steady play. (Hear, hear.) He bad also to congratulate the players upon their steady conduct in the fiejd. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to find that most of the players were still teetotallers—(hear, hear)—and he only hoped that they might continue so; and then he felt sure that the success that had carried them through so far would follow them for years to come. It was gratifying to him to find so good a result this year, following upon the achieve- ments of last year. He had been disappointed in some of the matches played. He had thought, and he knew many others who held a similar opinion, that the Runcorn team had not had on several occasions that fair play which it was the duty of everyone to give. (Hear, hear.) Some of the matches had not been won simply because the referees had not thoroeghly understood the game as it was played in these parts. He was certainly very much disappointed with the result of the match with Warrington at Widnes. He considered that match almost thrown away. He did not think justice was at all done, and it was only due to the player who was sent off the field to say that he (the speaker) fully believed that the player was net in fault at all. (Loud applause.) Although the player might be of a hasty tem- perament, he was not to blame on that occasion—(bear, hear)—and he (Mr. Frith) considered that the entire blame rested on the man from Warrington, who was turned off the field. (Hear, hear.) If that match had been fought out he believed Runcorn would have won it. They drew first blood, and that was an augury for a good result. How- ever, they lost the cup, and he was not sorry they had, be- cause, in his opinion, the matches they had played in con- nection with the Union did them no good. (Hear, hear.) He hoped and trusted that last season was the last year that they would play those matches. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) He believed justice was not done to the club by the Union or by the Union officials—(hear, hear)—and therefore he trusted the club would at once throw them overboard. He dared say it would be said by their oppo- nents that they were afraid, but never mind that. They would do better playing their ordinary club matches, be- cause he believed the excitement of the cap matches tended to no real good, but to a very great amount of harm. (Haar, hear.) after again congratulating the players, the president concluded, amid loud applause, by wish- ing them greater success in future. On the motion of Mr. T. Booth, seconded by Mr. W. Pownall, jour., Mr. Frith was heartily thanked for his services during the past year, and was unanimously re- elected president.—The following gentlemen were added to the list of vice-presidents :—Messrs. J. T. Brunner, M.P., W. H. Verdin, J.P., F. Fairhurst, T. Harris, W. R. Wass, and J. T. Waterworth.—Mr. W. Brookes, moved, and Mr. J. D. Widders seconded the re-election of Mr. J. E. Langsbaw as secretary, a motion which was unanimously agreed to.— Mr. Langshaw returned thanks for his appointment, and sad he would do his best for the club in the future as he had in the past. A very good list of fixtures had been arranged for next season, and he hoped the first team would pull themselves together, put in as regular an appearance as they did lest season, and be able to carry all the matches to a victorious issue. (Applause).—Mr. C. Pownall was un- animously re-appointed treasurer on the motion of Mr. J. Lunt, seconded by Mr. J. Stubbs.—Mr. A. Riley was ap- pointed assistant secretary.—The Chairman, referring to the services of Mr. Hughes as captain during the past sea- son, said he had shown a forbearance and an amount of skill which was to him wonderful.—Mr. F. Joule, as one of the oldest members of the club, proposed that their grate- ful thanks be tendered to Mr. Hughes for the way in which he had capteined the first team during the last season. He was sure there was no member who had played in the team but felt it to be a great pleasure to act under so skilfull a captain and one who understood the game so thoroughly Mr. Joule also moved Mr. Hughes' re-appoint- ment.—Mr. W. Jones seconded the motien.—As Mr. W. Wright was also proposed for the position of captain by Mr. J. B. Clark, seconded by Mr. Lunt, the vote of thanks was heartily accorded to the retiring captain, who re- marked that it had been a great pleasure to hold the posi- tion, as they had all worked well together.—The voting for the captaincy was taken by the ballot with the result : H. Hughes 71 votes. W. Wright 16. The declaration was received with loud applause.—Mr. Hughes thanked them for the confidence they had again placed in him, and also for the enthusiasm with which they had received his elec- tion. He could only say that he would do his hest for the club in the future as he had in the past, and he hoped they would have every success next season. (APPlause.)—mr. S. Orme made some highly eulogistic remarks with refer- ence to Mr. H. Hughes and Mr. W. Wright, and nomina- ted the latter gentleman for the sulacaptaincy.—Mr. w. Riley seconded the motion.—There were also nominated several other players. The ballott was as follows :—W. Wright 30. H. C. Speakman 21, J. Gatley 13, H. Andrews 12, F. Joule 12.—W. Dunbavand was appointed captain of I he second team by 41 votes, J. Gittens receiving 33, and W. Riley 16 votes. J. Gittens was appointed vice-captain with 45 votes, Whitby receiving 19 and W. Riley 24 votes.—Mr. H. Wright was elected umpire of the first team. He received 54 votes, against Mr. R. Hughes' 39 votes. Mr. J. Stubbs was appointed umpire of the second team. Much interest was centred in the appointment of committee, and a proposition was made and seconded that no players should be nominated. Mr. Widders proposed that four players should be selected, but this motion was not seconded. Upon the vote being taken it was decided by 51 to 41 that players be not eligible to serve upon the com- mittee, and considerable feeling was shown upon the an- nouncement of the numbers. Mr. H. Hughes declared that the decision was unfair to the players, (Hear, hear.) He had heard several prominent players say that the committee must play the matches' and he (Mr. Hughes) certainly thought they would have to do. (Loud applause.) —Eventually the proposal was cancelled, and that of Mr. Widders submitted, viz., that players form one-third of net committee. The players were first elected on the com- mittee as follows :—W. Hughes 80, H. Andrews 62, J. Galley 56, F. Joule 42, J. Clark 31, W. Riley 28, H. C. Speakman 24, G. Whit bv 18. The first four were elected. The remainder of the committee was decided as follows : R. Gorst, unanimously; J. B. Clarke 66, W. Riley 60, .R.

Hughes 57, J. Lunt 53, T. Booth 53, T. Moores 47, 3. Wit" son 40. The unsuccessful nominations were W. Page 38, W. Janes 36, W. Brookes 30, W. CArroll 28, W B. Brim- elow 24, G. H. Kerkham 21, W. Pownall, junr., 13, and G. Ward 10. There were several other important matters to be decided, and the meeting was adjourned until Monday next.

THE HOME RULE CRISIS. PROBABLE DISSOLUTION OF PARLIAMENT. It is stated that the writs are being prepared for a general election, and one writer says that it is almost certain that if Mr. Gladstone is defeated, he will, on the day following, obtain the Queen's consent to an immediate dissolution.

The Exford Liberal Three Hundred on Saturday I night passed a resolution, with only five dissentients, approving of the Home Rule Bill. Mr. Gaskell, M.P., in a letter to the Committee of the Morley Liberal Association, says that in voting for the second reading of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill he recognises only the assertion of a principlo of some form of self-government for Ireland. Dr. Walsh, Roman Catholic Archbishop of Dublin, has been in London endeavouring to influence Mr. Parnell and his party to consent to the proposed re- tention of Irish members at Westminster, alarm be- ing felt at the prospect of the Imperial Parliament being deprived, if Mr. Gladstone's scheme of Home Rule should be carried in its present form, of the Roman Catholic Nationalist members. One of the most prominent and enlightened of the advanced section of the Liberal party in Ulster writes :—Feeling here was at first intensely fierce against Home Rule. In my opinion Mr. Gladstone's manifesto and his last speech have caused many to veer round to his views—l mean of the Liberal party here. I notice this by the conversation when one meets the intelligent members of our body. Only for the fear of religious ascendancy all parties would be agreed upon the: subject. It is asserted that the treasurers of the committee by which the Orange manifesto was issued declare that money is pouring in to them so fast that they do not know what to do with it. They assert that at the present rate they will have £lOO,OOO for the ' Orange crusade in less than a month. . An open-air meeting of working-men was held on : Saturday night at Newcastle, upwards of 2,000 be- ing present. A resolution expressing the emphatic adherence of the meeting to the fundamental prin- ciple of the Government of Ireland Bill was enthu- siastically carried. Ten voted only for an amend- ment.

A letter has been received from Mr. Rylands ex- ! pressing a desire to meet the Burnley Liberal Coun- cil, as he should like to hear from the requisitionists calling the meeting why they have changed their opinion on the Irish question, adding that he had not changed his. The feeling in Burnley becomes intenser every day, and ward meetings are being called to press upon the Executive Committee the necessity of taking steps to select another candi- date immediately. A Cabinet Council was held at noon on Tuesday at the Prime Minister's official residence. The de- liberations were of an important character, the Lord Chancellor being summoned at half-past twelve from a law case to attend. All the Ministers were present except Mr. Mundella, who has recently been ! suffering from a slight indisposition. The Cabinet rose at I-20 p.m. Immediately after the Council I broke up, Mr. Gladstone drove to Paddington and took train for Windsor, where he had an audience with the Queen lasting 20 minutes. The Central News says :—The Cabinet Council which met on Tuesday was summoned for the pur- pose of discussing, firstly, the desirability of aban- doning or of further modifying clause 24 of the Irish Government Bill, which provides for the with- drawal of the Irish members from Westminster; and secondly, the advisability of dissolving Parlia- ment in the event of failure to carry the second reading of the bill. In regard to the first point, we have reason to believe that there was some diff- erence of opinion amongst Ministers, blAt in the end the urgent necessity of making a last effort to meet the views of the dissentient Liberals was recog- nised, and it was decided to make certain modifica- tions which will, it is to be hoped, ensure the second reading of the bill. In regard, however, to the wis- dom of appealing to the constituencies' against a ! possible hostile vote of the House of Commons, the Premier's opinion in favour of such a course was unanimously endorsed by his colleagues. On Monday night, a meeting of the Executive ! Council representing the Liberal party in the Lley- wood Division was held at Bury, in view of the threatened dissolution. A resolution was adopted recommending Mr. lbyle, M.P., as the Liberal can- didate at the next election. The Conservative party have not yet chosen their candidate, who, it is ' thought, will be a local man.

The "Standard" says :—There is reason to be- lieve that the Government have not merely decided on advising a dissolution in certain contingencies, but that preparations are already being made in view of an early appeal to the country. It is ru- moured that in case a dissolution takes place the writs will be issued on the 22nd of June.

div.head: LIBERAL UNIONIST COMMITTEE.
div.p: LIBERAL UNIONIST COMMITTEE.

A largely attended meeting of the members of the Liberal Union was held at the Westminster Palace Hotel, London, on Satarday at noon. The president, Lord Hartington, oc- cupied the chair. Among those eresent were the Duke of Argyle, Sir R. Blennerbaccett, Bart., Lord E. Cavendish, M.P., Mr. H. F. C. Cavendish, M.P., Lord Derby, Duke of Grafton, Mr. Goschen, M.P., and Mr. Peter Ry- lands, M.P.

Lord Hartington, ,who was received with loud cheers, pointed out that the meeting was called not for the purpose of discussing the Irish policy of the Government, but for purposes of organisation. It was necessary that a counter Liberal association should be established in order to give definite shape, strength, and efficiency to the opinion of that large section of the Liberal party which was opposed to the establishment of a separate Parliament in Ireland. They were not going to be content with a barren protest, but they were determined to carry on the contest with the same vigour and the same resolution in the country as they had shown within the walls of Parliament. Mr. Goschen, who proposed the resolutien which defined the constitution of the association, pointed out the way in which Liberal unionists could assist in the work of organi- sation. He emphasised the imoortence of raising at once a large fund so as to enable them to run as many candi- dates as possible, and resist with success in the coun- try, as in the House of Commons, the dictation of local caucuses. Mr. Rylands said what was going on in the House of Commons should make them more determined than ever to resist the crushing of indepeodent opinion. He urged that the Government were adopting means for prolonging the debate, not in the hope of altering opinion, but for the purpose of blinging pressure to bear upon individual members. The Duke of Argyll, in moving the appointment of the general committee. condemned the character of the scheme wbich the Prime Miois er had produced. He trusted that a proposal so insidious and so dangerous would not survive tie opposition that had been so courageously raised and so ably conducted. Mr. Cropper, late member for Kendal, seconded the ap- pointment of the committee; and the resolution was carried unanimously. The Earl of Derby proposed a vote of thanks to Lord Hartington for his independent action in this matter. He Considered that the crisis was the gravest and most danger- ous which had occurred within his time. The difficulties were not of their seeking. They had been forced upon them by the Government. They had to defend themselves, and he cordially approved of the steps which had been taken by the association to meet the crisis. Every man who wished to preserve the integrity of the Empire and the supremacy of Parliament would, he was sure, be prepareel either by his influence, or by his speaking, or with or by money to assist in the enterprise in which they were en- gaged. Mr. H. R. Grenfell seconded the vote of thanks, which was carried amid the warmest enthusiasm, the whole meeting rising from their places and heartily cheering Lord Hartington. Lord Harltngton replied, and the meeting,which through- out its proceedings had been most enthusiastic, separated. The General Committee remained behind to appoint the executive and to consult as to future arrangements. The following are the General Committee :—Duke of Argyll, Mr. Ashley, Sir R. Anstruther, M.P.; Sir T. Brocklebenk, Sir R. Blennerhassett, Mr. Biddalph, M.P. • Mr. Blackhouse, R. Bickersteth, M.P.; Duke of Bedford. Rey. J. Bond, Mr. flutter, H. Brand, M.P.; Mr. Bruce, Mr. Brodie, Dean of Gloucester, Earl of Camperdown, Sir E. Colebrooke, Mr. Craig Sellar, Mr. Caetwrieht, Mr. Dent, Earl Derby, A. Elliot, M.P.; Mr. Foljarnbe, Lord Fife, Sir A. Fairbairn, Mr. Finlay, M.P.; Mr. Foy, Mr. Gell, Mr. Goschen, Mr. A. Grey, Mr. Hornby, Mr. W. Hoeg, H. Hobbouse, M.P.; Mr. Heneage, Lord Hartington, Mr. Hallett, Sir J. Lubbock, M.P.; E. A. Leathern, Mr. A. Milner, Mr. Morrison, Lord Monteagle, Mr. Maude, Earl Northbrook, Mr. Noel, M.P.; Mr. Pease, Mr. T. W. Russell, Mr. Rylands, M.P.; Lord Revelstoke, Lord Rothchild, Duke of St. Alkane, Duke of Westminster, Lord Stallbridge, Mr. Wodehouse, M.P. ; Mr. Watson, Sir W. Thomson, Mr. A. Dicey, Sir R. Cunliffe, A. M. Thompson, Baron F. Rothchild.

Adams and indemnifying the owners. PORTLAND (MAINE), MONDAY.—The fishing schooner Sisters, of Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, has been seized here, having, ne manifest. DESTRUCTIVE TORNADO IN GERMANY. CAssz, TIIESDAY.—A tornado, causing great devastation swept over the Wetzlar district last evening. The railway station was destroyed, seven houses were unroofed, and some factory chimneys blown down. SPAIN. FATAL DYNAMITE EXPLOSION. MADRID, WEDNESDA.Y.—A. dynamite manufactory near Valencia was destroyed yesterday by an explosion of nitro- glycerine. The accounts received up to the present state that at least 12 people perished, and it is feared that there are other victims. THE CZAR AT MOSCOW. MOSCOW, TIIHSDAY.—At the Imperial reception held at the Kremlin to-day the Mayor, in presenting to the Em- peror the customary bread and salt, addressed his Majesty as follows :—" The representatives of the old capital of the Empire most humbly request you, Autocrat and Einperor, to accept our bread and salt and the expression of our love, and to be assured of our joy in seeing you, the Czarina, and the Czerewitch. You come to us from that blest south, where yon have restored life to the Black Sea. Oar hope gains wings, and strength is imparted to our belief that the Cross of Christ will shine upon St. Sophia. So thinks Moe- cow. and in this hope remains steadfast." The Emperor, in reply, said that he loved Moscow, and rejoiced to find him- self within its walls on the anniversary of his coronation—a period in his life which would always be to him full of the haphiest reminiscences. STRIKE RIOT AT TORONTO. TORONTO, TuBsDAY.—A strike has broken out here among the men employed by the Tramway Company. Forty cars have been wrecked by the mob. IRISH HOME RULE MEETING AT CHICAGO. °incite°, TUESDA.Y.—A large meeting in favour of Horse Rule, attended by about 10,00(i persons—the Governor of Iliinoie in the chair—was held here this evening, at which resolutions were passed pledging the continued support of thoee present to the movement for the establishment of an Irtah Perliament. THE ERUPTION OF MOUNT ETNA. Boicr, THURSDAY—The lava streams from Mount Etna are advancing towards Nicoloei at the rate of forty metres an hour, and have now reached within one kilometre of the town. The surrounding country is seriously menaced. PROPOSED EXCULSION OF THE ORLEANS PRINCES. PARIS, THURSDAY.—At the Cabinet Council held this morning the text of the bill in regard to the Orleans Prin- ces was drawn up. The measure contains two articles. The first gives the Minister of the Interior the right of pro- hibiting the stay on French territory to members of former French reigning families. The second decrees the penalties to be imposed by the Correctional Tribunal in the event of the prohibition being infringed, the maximum to be five years' imprisonment. The prohibition will be notified by the decree of the Minister of the Interior.

THE PRELTYR MURDER. CONFESSION OF BROOKS. Sr. LOUIS, MONDAY.—In the course of to-day's proceed- ings in the trial of Maxwell for the murder of Mr. Preller, a detective gave evidence to the effect that he was confined, ostensibly as a prisoner, in the cell next to that occupied by Maxwell, while the latter was awaiting his trial, and that Maxwell had confessed to him that he had murdered Mr. Preller with chloroform. In a telegram dated Tuesday. the New York correspon- dent of the _Daily Yews says :—A decided sensation has been produced by the Brooks trial at St. Louis. Yesterday a detective was examined as a witness. He made a state- ment that he had committed e pretended forgery in Fek- raary last, had been arrested and lodged in jail with Brooks for the purpose of gaining his confidence and securing his true confession. The plan worked perfectly. About ten days after arriving in the jail, Brooks told him the whole story. They were frequently thrown together, and the de- tective gained his confidence by pretending to be an expert forgor. Brooks began by saying that if he could secure two witnesses to testify right, he would be able to escape. He wanted them to testify that they had seen him have in Bos- ton before going to St. Louis $7OO or $BOO. 'net would account for the money he had after the murder. The detec- tive promised to get two of his gang of forgers to testify to this. lie then asked Brooks to tell the whole story of the murder. This be did as follows:—"I first met Preller in Liverpool, and afterwards on the steamer Wand for Boston. We pissed same weeks together in Bos- ton, and subsequently we both arrived at St. Louis. There we had a talk about going to Auckland. I wes anxious to accompany Preller. and desired him to pay the expenses. Preller said he had only enough money to pay his own. I then determined to fix him because of his meanness. He occasionally had pains in the stomach. One Sunday after- noon we went to my more., and he was attacked by a pain in the abdomen. I told him I had a remedy, and asked him to try it He asked what it was. and I told him it was hypo- dermic injections of morphia. He said I will try it if it will do me good.' I took a syringe and gave him a good dose in the arm. He went to sleep. Then I got chloroform and held it under his nose until all was gone. He was still breathing, so I went out and got some more chloroform, and held a saturated cloth under his nose until he was dead. I got 700 dollars from him, threw my things out of my trunk, and put the body in. Next morning I bought two trunk, packed my things, and skipped." Brooks also gave a full account of his subsequent movements until be was arrested. The detective's evidence made a profound im• twession. It is believed that it will secure a conviction. Whet' Brooks !Lew the detective appear in the witness box he started from his seat, his face blanched with terror. He then sank, cowed and trembling, into his chair, but soon re- covered himself.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF

• GUARDIA.NS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman). and Messrs. Balbarry, Brown, Greening, Jones, Gibson, Blackburst, Jolley, Brown, Voisey, Heaton, Har- rison, Isherwood, Clark, Woods, Ratcliffe, Bonnell, Owen, Grange, J. Houghton:VV. Houghton, Strange, Pennington, Eckersley, Wright. Broadbent (sx-officio), Si'shall, Swinton, Hibbert, Forster, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (deputy clerk.) 00T-DOOR RELIEF. In answer to Mr. Harrison it was stated by the Creaa that theincrease in out-door relief throughout tbe union amounted to £2O for the past fortnight as compared with the corresponding fortnight last year. THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. The committee reported that new dietary tables had been submitted by the doctor for the committee's appraval. and were approved with the exception of some meciffications with regard to oatmeal. The committee had ordered the euperintendent of the schools to secure samples of hats and caps for the children from Warrington tradesmen. The committee thanked Mr. Heaton for the present of six hens and a cock for the schools.—The CLERK remarked that he was afraid the Local Government Board would not approve of cocks and heas being at the schools. There was an ob- jection to poultry being kept at institutions of this kind.— The CHAIRMAN said they would run the risk, and moved the confirmation of the minutes. In answer to Mr. Jolley with regard to the death of a child at the schools, the Chairman said that was the first death that had occurred at the schools since the children were taken there.—Mr. GREENING said the c'eild whose death was referred to was in a very feeble state of health when it went to the schools. —The minutes were than confirmed. SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE. This committee reported that it had allowed school fees in 97 cases, 79 of them being old and 18 new cases.—Mr. BLACKHURST moved the adoption of the minutes, and re- marked that there was very little change in regard to the number of cases. There was no material increase.—Mr. GREENING seconded the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to. MORE SURCHARGES. The minutes of the House Committee referred to a commu- nication from the Local Government Board asking for the comments of the Board as to surcharges of the workhouse master (Mr. Mackey) by the dis'rict auditor. One of the surcharges amounted to t?, Os 61 for whet was termed an excessive consumption of 27ibe. of tea in the workhouse, and the other was in regard to a sum of 53 31 for what was likewise termed an excessive consumption of 45 pints of beer. The committee reported that after hearing Mr. Mackey's explanation they considered it satisfactory. In the course of some discussion on this matter it was ex- plained that a ceanparatively small quantity of beer was used in the workhouse, and owing to its being kept some time a quantitr of it at the bottom of the barrel had be- come unfit to be served to inyalias ; hence the surcharge on this account. With reference to the tea, it Was stated that the extra consumption was due to their having been short of milk for a certain period, when tea was served out instead. In the end, however, the raatter was referred hack to the committee for further inquiry. THE NUMBER OF OFFICERS. Mr. BROWN moved and Mr. HEATON seconded," That a person be appointed to take all inmates whe have to attend religious services out of the Workheuse, and who will be responsible for their attendance at the church (Raman Catholic) and due return."—Mr. PENNINGTON thought that, as they kad managed all these years without anything very serious happening, they ought not is these hard times to go in for increasing the number of their officers. When he looked around at their present number of officers and compared them with what they had 10 or 15 years ago the increase seemed very feilrious. Besides the Roman Catholic Place of worship was not so far away from St. Paul's, to which the other inmates went.—Mr. BALHARRY supported Mr. Pennington's renarks, and on Mr. Brown's motion being Out to the meeting it WAS negatived by a considerable ma- jority.

PROPOSED TRIP. Mr. WM. HOUGHTON suggested that the children's trip, which had been discontinued for some years, should be re- vived.—Mr. HEATON having supported this proposal, a small committee was appointed for the purpose of making arrangements. The ',lief cane were then proceeded with.
