div.head: TPE EXAMINTR. SATURDAY, MAY 29, 1886:
div.p: TPE EXAMINTR. SATURDAY, MAY 29, 1886:

a good many years in the other House, maintained that the Sunday Closing Act had proved very successful in the principality.—Lordon Noracne, though he voted against the second reading, intended to vote for the third reading, as it appeared to be ti,e popular wish in the county of Dur- ham that the Bill should aes.—The Marquis of FALISBURY accepted the suggestion that the main and practical ques- tion they had to decide was whether there was sufficient evidence that the people of Durham really desired the mea- sure, and lipon that point he thought there was considerable doubt.—Earl GISANYILLM said the noble Marquis had ex- pressed doubt as to whether it was the general wish of the people of Durham that the public-houses should be closed on Sundays, but on that point the case made by the promoters of the bill appeared to him to be un- answerable. Out of 16 members for the county, 15 voted for the bill in accordance with the pledge upon which they were returned at the last election.—Their Lordships divided, and the numbers were—For the third reading, 70; against, 9T ; majority, 27. The bill was therefore thrown out. Their Lordships rose at 6-55. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIJESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 40. TAB DERBY DAY.—Mr. LAIIOI7CHBRE, in moving that the House at its rising do adjourn to Thursday, said the tendency of the age was to reduce the hours of labour. (Laughter,) With that object bank holidays had been in- stituted, and after fulfilling their duty to their constituents they owed a duty to theruselves—(laughter)—a duty that the Procedure Committee had clearly in view in their minds. When most sacred institutions were manacled they must hold fast to something, and a man who would tamper with their holidays must be a bad man, a crochety man, or a Scotchman. (Laughter.) He moved that the House at it, rising adjourn to Thursday.—Mr. Isakcs seconded and Sir G. CAISPB3LL opposed the motion. He had no objection to the holiday, and he bad no objection to people going te see the Derby, but he had strong objection to the great gambling saturnalia which always marked this particular occasion. (Cries of "Oh " and " hear, bear.")—The House then divided, and the numbers were—For the mo- tion, 251; againet, 150; majority, 101. The announce- ment of the numbers was received with cheers. THE HOME RULE DEBATE. The adjourned debate on the second reading of the Go- vernment of Ireland Bill was resumed. Lord LvetteiceroN said the House had been asked to ac- cept the bill because it was a measure to provide for Ireland in autonomy. For his part be failed to see any principle in the bill to which the House ought to give its Resent. Not- withstanding the threat of dissolution with which members who opposed it were met, for his part he would rather not re- tain his seat in that House at the price of the acceptance of this measure.

The ATTORNIY. GENERAL, who followed, on behalf of the Government, said the cardinal principle of the bill was to establish a legislative body in Ireland which should have administrative as well as legislative functions, and to which the Irish Executive should be responsible. (Hear, hear.) The Government, ef course, could expect nothiog from those who objected to this principle. But the Government might fairly claim the votes of those who were in favour of grant- ing legislative power to a legislative assembly in Ireland, even though their support in the later stages of the bill Eight depend on the adequacy of certain safeguards and conditions. The position of the Conservative opposition to the bill was sufficiently clear to be intelligible, bat he found a difficulty in drawing a line of demarcation between the position assumed by Lord Hartington and that occupied by hon. members opposite. In the case of Mr. Chamberlain, a scheme of federation existed and in reference to that ques- tion he (the Attorney-General) contended that if this bill were carried it woeld in reality be no bar but rather an aid to forward the process of federation if Parliament should determine en such a course. To satisfy the Marquis of Hartington and Mr. Goschen would involve the abandon- ment and destruction of the cardinal principles of the bill. tle controverted the contention of Sir Henry James that the establishment of a separate Parliament in Ireland would destroy the unity of the kingdom, and asserted that not one of the reasons given by Mr. Pitt for the necessity of the Act of Union was at all touched by anything contained in this measure. The arguments and protests urged on behalf of the Ulster Protestants he regarded as mainly bunkum and bluster. The Government had been called disunionists, hut they were not so. What they sought was to substitute a real for an unreal union. (Cheers.) Moreover, the promo- ters of the bill belonged to a party, and were led by a Iltnieter who had &me the most that had yet been achieved to give a voice to the people of the empire and to make the blessings of that the free inheritance of all. (Loud cheers.) Mr. WESTLAKE criticised the bill, and urged objections to some of its proposals. Mr. J. C. FLYNN cordially supported the bill, which was a generous recognition of the demand of the Irish people for self-goverment. Mr. TREVELYAN spoke after Mr. Fenwick, and announced himself as one of that hon member's constituents who was not in agreement with his member. The objections urged against the bill had never in his opinion been satisfactorily anserered from the Treasury bench. The" financial aspects af the questiom were unsatisfactory to him, and the Land Purchase Bill he viewed as a confession that the Ministry dare not trust the Irish Parliament to carry out their land Policy of 1881. " Why cannot the Government alter this hill."' he asked, "so as to remove what appears to some of their most devoted and loyal supporters to he most grave defects ? " He himself, he said, only asked that the , Government should retain such a bold on law and order in Ireland as would enable the House to dispense with the necessity of baying out the landlords. Mr. T. HEALY answered Mr. Trevelyan in his sarcastic fashion, and in the course of a long oration asked in con- temptuous tones what puny whipster could hope to settle this question if Mr. Gladstone, with his vast experience could not. On the motion of Mr. RIGBY the debate was adjourned till Thursday:, MISCELLANEOUE.—CoIoneI Hughes introduaed a bill to amend the law relating to the expenses of the Metropolitan Fire Brigade, which was raid a first time.—The House re- sumed Committee on the Public Health Acts (Improve- ment Expenses) Bill, and continued sitting nntil a late hour. Clanoes four to 17 were added to the bill.—Tbe bill passed through Committee. Tile House adjourned at half-past two o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIIIRSDA.Y. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. THE PAYMENT OP INTISRAST Otlt OW CAiirtit.--The Low) CHANCELLOR rneed to substitute for standing order No. 128 the new stencling eider suggested by the Lords' Select Committee, so as to nilort of the payment of interest out of capital, and not out of earnings during the construc- tion of railway and other works, upon clear and distinct notice being given of what was being done. His lordship stated that the committee were unanimous in the conclusion at which they arrived, that a provision of the sort proposed should be recommended, as it would give a substantial feeling of security ! against any injustice or wrong being done. The Committee I Mad satisfied themselves that unless in some cases provi- sions of this sort were permitted undertakings perfectly substantial in character would not and could net be carried out, because the money which would be subscribed with such a provision weuld not be subscribed without it.—The Earl of SBLEORNII would not oppose the motion, having regard to the desirability of having unanimity between the two Houses, but he continued to think that the stan4ing order they were departing from was the better of the tlvo.—The motion was then agreed to. Tisi Caofrnoe BlLL.—Their lordships then went into committee on the Crofters Bill.—On Clause 1, Lord ABINGER proposed to add to the conditions which weiuld cause a crofter to be ejected from his bolding or prevent him assigning it "felon', theft, or the receipt of parechiel relief."—After some discussion, the amendment was nega- tived.—On the motion of the Duke of ARGYLL, an amend- ment was inserted declaring that a crofter should not per- sistently yiolate a written condition signed by him which was approved by the Land Commissioner.—On Clause 6 an amendment, moved by the Duke of RICHMOND and GORDON, providing that no improvement should be compensated for unless it was suitable to the holding was agreed to.
Their Lotdships adjourned at ten minutes to nine o'clock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TAURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QumTioNs.—Mr. BRYCE stated that the reorganisation of

the consular service on the West Coast of Africa. which was now under the consideration of the Government, would include the appointment of a consul on the Congo.—Mr. STANSVELD informed Mr. Jasper More that the Government had under eonsideration a measure dealing with the regis- tration of voters which they hoped shortly to introduce.— Sir JULTAVI GOLDSMID asked if the Prime Minister would consider the desirability of issuing a new Treasury warrant to divert the etatetable payment of £lO,OOO now made to the Patronage Secretary, and said to be used for political party purposes, from the Patroeage Secretary to the &ere- Cary of State.—Mr. GLADSTONZ replied that the point men- tioned was certainly included in the engagement given to the House the other night. THE dams BILL.—On the motion for going into Com- mittee on the Arms (Ireland) Rill, Mr. T. M. HEALY moved as an amendment that no measures dealing with the dis- armament of Orange districts would be satisfactory or im- partially administered which required to be put in force by a proclamation of the Irish Privy Council, composed almost entirely of member; of, or sympathisers with, the Orange organisation. He remarked that as it was probable now that the Home Rule Bill would be postponed till the autumn there would likely be lively times with the Orange- men in the meanwhile, and he Suggested that the bill should be passed for only one year, as an experiment, to let them see how it would be worked, and, further, that there should be a large accession of Liberals to the Irish Privy Council at an early date.—The amendment was seconded by Mr. Dtrazer, who suggested that the power of enforc- ing the Act should be vested in the Lord Lietetenant alone, or else that the Act should be extended to the whole of Ireland.—Mr. IVIORLEY Pointed out that this was only a continuance bill, and said the Act was not at all necessary to enable the Irish executive to deal with ordinary violence and disorder. There was some misapprehension with regard to the composition of the Irish Privy Council, for there were twenty Liberals in it, and there was no reason for say- ing that it was almost entirely composed of members of the Orange organisation. As to the question of the extension of the Act to the exempted districts, if the Government saw the slightest necessity for doing so they would do it promptly. The deb Ito was continued by Mr. W. Redmond, Mr. M. henry, Mr. W. O'Brien, Sir Julian Goldsrnid, Mr. Holmes,Mr J. O'Doherty, Mr. M. Healy, Mr. Handel Coss- ham, and Sir T. Esmond& 'Upon a division the amend,.

me.nt was rejected by 180 to 104, and the House went into Committee fat the bill. The bill having passed through Coramittee, progress was reported. A SIIDDIIN AI.LIOURNMENT.-011 the order for the adjourned debate or. the Government of Ireland Bill, Lord R. CHURCHILL spoke of the poisonous atmosphere that had ta be breathed, and moved the adjournment of the House to mark its sense of disapprobration of the inertia of the authorities of the House in regard to the matter.—Sir W. Eleacouirr was happy to find himself in entire sympathy with the noble lord, and spoke of the disgrace to the House to have each arrangements as those from which it had suf- fered that night. He assented to the motion, which was pat and agreed to amid laughter. The House adjourned at 12-25.
TFIEBRITISFI ASSOCIATION OF INSPEC-
TORS OF WEIGHTS AND MEASURES.

The annual meeting of the members of this associa- tion has this year been held in Warrington. On Mon- day morning the meeting opened by a gathering in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall, and was pre- sided over by Alderman Chandley, of Warrington, the president of the association. The following gentle- men were also present—Messrs. T. H. Merritt (Man- chester), S. Denison (Leeds), W. Grime (Wigan), Jas. Farrell (Blackburn), J: McGrath (Londan), William Linney (Stockport), John Parkin (Sheffield), W. H. M. Blews (Birmingham), W. 11. Hopkins (Manches- ter), Elijah Place (Warrrington), J. Thompeon (Man- chester), W. Shaw (Edinburgh), Hugh Richmond (Glasgow), Thomos Jones (Liverpool), J. Johnson (Salford), Henry Jackson (Macclesfield), tTdmes Rigby (Warrington), 'Thomas Bennett (Bolton), Edward Horton (Derby), Samuel Massey (Mancheoter), J. W. Robinson (Stockport), Wm. Hutton (York), and Wil- liamson (Manchester). THE CHAIRMAN'S ADDRESS.

The CHAIRIGIN, in opening the proceedings, said he could ensure them a hearty welcome to Warrington. "fitere were, of course, many towns that at these annual meetings they might visit possessing objects of greater in- terest, and with architectural surroundings infinitely more beautiful, but still in Warrington they had some pretensiu.ns to excellence in some departments. They considered their educational appliances very advanced, and their means for the eleyatiou and refinement of the people eminently satis- factory. They had also a very advanced state of machin- ery for the destruction of dirt and disease, and he thought he might say that their poor were well cared for. They had an extensive market, offering ample accommodation for both the be and the cheapest goods and for the choicest and freshest foods. Their streets were clean, and, without troubling them too much, he would sum up by saying their hearts were warm. (Applause.) That Associatin of Inspectors of Weights and Measures sought to oppress none. They had a broad platform and had no political in- fluences there. lbey meted out justice to the rich and to the poor, and to the buyer and seller all in the same spirit. Their great motto was that tbe stricttst impartial- ity should be meted out to every individual ; in fact "To do unto others as ye would they should de unto you." He thought these the grand objects of their association. (Hear, bear, and applause).

div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIA.MF,NT.

—„ HOUSE OF LORDS.—MUNDAY. The House met at 415. MARRIAG2 WITH A DECSABIID WIFE'S SISTBR.—The Duke of St. ALBANS, in moving the second reading of the Marriage with a Deceased Wile's Sister Bill, said it only proposed a return to what was the ancient law, and stated that when Lord Lyndhnrst brought in this bill to limit the right to then existing and previous marriages it was held that such marriages had hitherto been voidable but not void. The noble duke pointed oat that these marriages were legal in our colonies, and pat it to the House that what had been assented to in her Majesty's far-off possessions ought net to be illegal in the British Islands. He reminded their lerdehips that not only had the bill passed the other House seven times, but had been brought before their lordships time after time with narrow and decreasing majorities against it, while in 1883 it had actually been read a second time in that Chamber, though it was afterwards rejected on the third reading by a resort to a very unusual expedient.— The Duke of. ARGYLL. in mevint the rejection of the bill, appealed to the Hebrew and Roman law as furnishing authority against it. He also cited the action of the French Republic in the early part of this century, when tbe mar- riage of brothers and sisters-in-law was forbidden, on the ground that experience had shown the deleterious results preduced by such alliances. Another point was that the bill if carried would withdraw from the wife one of the degrees of incestuous adultery which at present enabled her to obtain a divorce from her busband.—Lord Betamwnt.r. supported the measure, as a means of getting rid of a most cruel and mischievous law, that was without the least jai- tification.—The Archbishop of CANTZBEITRY argued that the passage of this meesure would be a breaking in upon the sanctity of the family. which in civilised life was the basis of the community. Such a marriage as was contemplated by this bill was without precedent in the Christian Church, and was, moreover, ranknown to the Hebrew and Roman law. The most reverend Primete further contended that if the bill was carried, while it might cause rejoicing among those who had broken the law, it would cause, on the other band, the withdrawal from innumerable hotseholds of females who would otherwise remain to take care of the children of their dead sisters. The HOMO divided, and the numbers were—

Contents Non-contents 149-22 The announcement of the numbers was received with cheers. BILLS ADVANCED.—The Oxford University (Justices) Bill was read a second time. The reports of amendments to the Bankruptcy (Agricultural Labourers' Wages) Bill and the Durham Sundae, Closing Bill were brought up and reed. The West Indian Encumbered Estates Bill, the British North American Bill, and the Companies Acts Amendment Bill were lead a third time. The House adjourned at 7-40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4.0 SEGIIET SERVICE MONEY.—Ni R. H. Fovrann stated, in reply to Mr. A. Grey, that £10,060 was handed ever an- nually to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Treasury in accordance with the provisions of the Act lit Vie, chap. 2. That sum was granted for secret service, and the expen- diture, of it was not subjected to the scrutiny of the Con- troller and Auditor General. The Financial Secretary to the Treasury had no information as to the objects to which it was applied. (Laughter from the Opposition.) MR. Fatreeet said the minute he had quoted bad been in exis- tence six weeks or two months. The warrant had been in force since Mr. Burke got an Act passed in 1782 tinder which the money had always been paid to the Secretary to the Treasury.—Met. H. HENRY gave notice of his inten- tion to move a resolution declaring that it would be an abuse and _contrary to public policy that any money raised by taxation should be expoich=d by the Government of the day for eleclon purposes. (Laughter and cheers). Tan SALE Oic Carnet BY WEIGHT.—In answer to Mr. Seton-Karr, Mr. ACLAND said be was net aware that up to the present time there had been any general demand for weighing houses or mechines for weighing live cattle. Although by law provision was made by the local authori- ties regulating markets for weighing goods sold therein, it did not rest with her Majesty's Government to enforce the provision as to weighing machines for live steck as dis- tinguished from dead meat. THE HOMH RULE DEBATE.—Mr. RICHARD drew Mr. Gladetone's attention to the statement attributed to Lord Harrington at the meeting of the Loyalist Union Commit- tee too Saturday. that the debate on the Government of Ireland Bill is being prolonged .deliberately, and that the time gained is being used for the intimidation of members. —Mr. T. P. O'Cotewon asked whether the Prime Minister would use his influence to procure the right hon. member for West Birmingham the earliest opportunity of laying be- fore the House his alternative proposals. (Laughter.)—Mr. GLADSTONE had no doubt the member for West Birmingham would have ample means of taking part in the debate. On Friday he undertook to put himself into a condition to form some judgment as to the probable duration of the debate. He was waiting for the result of those inquiries when he saw published a statement attributed to the Marquis of Her- at gton. He was made to assert that that pressure, of which he (Mr. Gladstone) did not know anything—(Op position laughter and counter cheers)—was beisg exercised on members+ by party associations, and that with a view to facilitating the exercise of that pressure a determination had been come to that that the debate should be inde- finitely prolonged. As a personal attack had been made on ' Lord Kilcoursie, he must state what actually happened. tiefere the debate began he did enconrage his noble friend. The Liberal party had been turned entirely out of the Irish representation, and Irish Liberals were rather precious. (Laughter.) Considering that his noble friend belonged to a family which for three centuries had been connected with Ireland, he did not expect that his intervention in the de- bate would have been made the subject of invidious remark. ' (Ministerial cheers.) That letter, and what else had hap- pened, disabled him from being of use in the matter. He thanked the member for West Birmingham for fulfilling his part of the engagement, because he wrote on Saturday morning to say he thought that some members with whom he had been in communication were of the same mind as those refered to by the member for Rossendale. (Laughter.) The ind-finite prolongation of debates .of this kind was a great addition to the burden of public affairs. He hoped to get rid of the Committee on the Arms Bill that night. He hoped gentlemen would claim their own just liberty in proportion to the importance of the subject under debate, but that they would avoid retaliation. The opeechee for the bill at the time the charge was made were 23, and the speeches against were 24. (Ministerial and Irish cheers.) When the Protectionist party were opposing Sir Robert Peel in 1346 the debate extended over twelve nights. He hoped it might not be neceeeary to extend that debate so much, but under existing circureetanoes he could not do more than express his earnest hope that no gentleman would give any real colour to the charge which, by the hon. alder- man, had been brought against them.—Lord HARTINGToN said that he thought it was possible be might have referred at the meeting to an apparently indefinite ppolongation of the debate, and also to the rumours that pressure Wag being put on individual members, but as the meeting was private and no reporters were present, he declined to admit until he seen the report gusted from that he had joined the two to gether in a manner to give offence. ISECEFT SERVICE MONEY AND PAELIAMEETARY ELECTIONS. The House then went into Committee ef Supply. On a vote of £2,266,400 an account of the Civil Service and Reveeue Departments, Mr. RYLANDS moved to omit an item of £5,000 for secret service money. He said they were entitled to some guaran- tee that this money was not devoted to purposes repugnant to the feeling of the House. He maintained that it was not always properly applied, and referred to the rumours that the Patronage Secretary of successive Governments had been in the habit of applying the balance to electioneering purposes—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said he could only speak as to the money voted by Parliament, and though when he was Secretary of State he should have declined to give any information as to how it was spent, be was certain it had never been spent for political pur- posea—Mr. Labonchere, Mr. Bradlangh, Mr. Dillon, aed others spoke; and Sir H. Semiseeho condemned the alleged use made of the £lO,OOO as contrary to the spirit of the Corrupt Practices Act, suggested that further inquiry should be made into the sebject —Mr. GrAnsrorrn, in reply to an appeal from Lord R. Churchill, said, as Prime Minis- ter, he knew nothing whatever of the expenditure of secret servies money, but he promised to consider whether the ex- penditure of the sum from the Consolidated Fund could not he broight under the same conditions as the vote.—Sir M. Hicks-Beach thought this satisfactory •, and Mr. Rylands offered to withdraw his motion; but Sir J. M'Kenna, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, and other Irish members objecting, it was nezotived by 319 to 44. Among other subjects mentioned were the Scotch Fishery Board, the constitution of which was commented upon by Scotch members, and various Irish items upon which most of the Irish members spoke at considerable length and with much iteration. Subsequently Dr. CAMERON called attention to the dis- closure of telegrams in the Islands of Scotland by officials of the Post Office, and moved a reduction ef the vote.—A. division was taken and the amendment was negatived by. 116 to 54. At 2 o'clock the vote on account was agreed to. A vote in the Army Estimates of £3.243,000 for forage, and a vote in the Navy Estimates of £207,600 for Coast- guard service, Royal Naval Reserve, dm., Were also agreed to; and £113,200 for the Scientific Department of the Navy. and £812,900 for halfpay and served and retired pay of officers of the Navy and the Marines were also agreed to. —Progress Was then repotted. The Committee on the Arms (Ireland) Bill was postponed till Thursday, and, after other business The House adjourned at 2-25. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Terrsnev.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 30. The Infants' Bill passed through oornmittee, and the 1 Bankruptcy (Agricultural Labourers' Wages) Bill was read a third time and passed. Tux DIJRNAM SUNDAY CLOSING Mrs.—The Bogor of DURHAM moved the third reading of the Sale of Intoxica- ting Liquors on Sunday (Durham) Bill, and observed that the noble lord who bad given notice to move its rejection knew very little of the sturdy and independent people of Durham if he supposed that they had been influenced in the demand for Sunday closing by anything like episcopal or ecclesiastical dictation.—The Earl of WILMS moved that the Bill be read a third time that day six months. He objected to the measure en account of its exceptional character, and on the general principle it invelved.—Lord _ Korsixotox, having repteeenled a Welsh constituency for

The TZHASURER (Mr. W. H. Hopkins) stated that the balance in hand that time last year was £354s 2d. They had received during the year £62 19s 11, and there was a balance in hand of £2O is 71. But owing to £l3 or £l4 of laa year's subscliptions having been received, they would practically be a trifl, better off than they were at the com- mencement of the year.—The Hon. Sec. ( pro. tem.), Mr. John W. Robinson, read the Committee's annual report, which stated that during the year several members had joined the association and several died, leaving the numbers about the some as last year, namely, 60. The Committee had nothing of importance to report, as nothing bad been done by the legiblature in the direction required by their as- sociation, and would therefore urge upon every member the necessity of redoubled efforts to obtain an Act of Par- liament which would create uniformity of returns through- out the United Kingdom.—The report and balance sheet were adopted.

div.head: PLACE OF MEETING.
div.p: PLACE OF MEETING.

York, Derby, Bristol, and Blackburn were suggested as places to meet next year, and after some debate York was selected. In this ancient city, it was said, the weights and measures are dealt with in a very primitive fashion. It was, according to one member, four or five hundred years behind the age, the York inspector being in the habit of going round with tools to put right any defective weights he migLt discover. APPOINT %SENT OF OFFI.DERS. Mr. Alderman Chandley was restlected president of the association ; Mr. W. H. Hopkins, treasurer; and Mr. J. W. Robinson and Mr. S. B. Massey, secretary and assistant scretary respectively. SUGGESTIONS.

On the suggestion of Mr. W. H. HOPKINS it was agreed to urge upon the Board of Trade, in the event of an amend- ment of the Weights and Measures Act, to abolish the clause under which coutta lc-et have power to appoint in- spectors, who are practically beyond control.— The desir- ability of a uniform scale of fees for the whole country was urged by Wr. W. HUTTON (York).—Mr. W. H. M. BLEWS (Birmingham) said the scale of fees in Manchester was higher than in most other places, but there was no doubt that in general the scale wal too low.—Mr. J. PARKIN' (Sheffield) said p,3ch a scale should be imposed as woutd guarantee local adtkorities from any loss ha connection with the inspection of weights and measures. ADDRESS BY THE MAYOR. .

In the afternoon the MASOR (Alderman Harrison) pre- sided, and in opeuing the proceedings said that he ought perhaps to blush to say that until he was invited to take the chair he did not know of the existence of an as.sociation of that kind. However, he had since been quite satisfi,d that that was a most valuable association and one that ought to receive the support of the public. For instance, while he had been in the,other room he had seen an ingenious instru- ment which be was told when in proper order would weigh within the 500th part of a grain. That association evi- dently recognised the importance of strict accnra,cy in these sort of thinggi and Pne ientieriP tvid hlin that he had it on wry high autherity inai many lives were lost in the I coursa. ef the twelve months. in conseciance of the inac- curacy of the weights and measures used tot the chemists. (Hear, hear.) It was a matter of great consequence that there should be a tribunal to see that people were not swindled in the purchases they were obliged to make, and he looked up3n an inspector of weights and measures as-9. sort of minister of justice who was entrusted with very great powers. It was indeed highly desirable that be should be discreet in the exercise of those powers, and that he should not allow the power be was invested with to de- generate into anything like tyranny. (Hear, hear.) His experience of the weights and measures inspector of War- rington gave him the highest opinion of his integrity and of his desire to act fairly, conscientiously, reasonably, and properly. (Hear, hear, and applause.)
"PROSECUTIONS UNDER THE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT"

Mr. J. PARKIN (Sheffield) read a paper on "Prosecutions under the Weights and Measures Act." He said the Act was on the whole a highly penal one. There were 25 different offences, with penalties varying from 403 to £5O. As to what was an unjust weight, he said that a much greater margin should be allowed in respect of weights and measures in use in rough pr heavy trades. The inepector would. AR a rule, divide weights and measures into three categories—correct, requiring Adjustment, and unjust. The litter he would seize with a view to further proceedings. But no hard and fast line could be drawn. A Ilb weight a dram light gave as great a gain by its deficiency if used, say, in the sale of tobacco as a 11b. weight an ounce light used by a greengrocer, or a 581 b. weight a pound light need an the sale of coal. A certain amount of discretion should therefore be exercised in the seizure of weights, especially if they had been duly stamped and the deficiency seemed to be due to fair wear. He took it that flour scales an ounce against the buyer, butchers' or provision dealers' retail ecalee half an ounce, tea dealers' or tobacconists' retail scales one or two drams, were to all intents and purposes unjust acelee, and as a ride such cases should go before the magis- trates. It certainly would not be right to tolerate even less deficiencies than those indicated to continue from time to time. Habitual repetitions of such minor offences would abundantly jus'ify legal proceedings. The section relating to fraud•should be as strictly enforced as the difficulties of proof in such cases admitted of, and he thought there should be an connection with every important local authority an officer with authority to advise in all difficult cases, not only of weights and measures, but in all cases where "moral culpability or trading dishonesty " was implied in the charge. Such an officer should have the authority to decide whether prosecutions should be commenced and to conduct the prosecutions in cases of difficulty.— Some discussion teok place on the paper, in the course of which the use of china weights was referred to by Mr. Hare (Burnl-v). S veral speakers condemned these weights, b' canoe they absorbed meisture, which made them heavier.— Mr. GILLMAN (Leeds) said as a scale maker he objected to sell china wrigl ts He thought inspectors should have powers to enter the shop of rale makers to test scales, dm., before they were sel,l.—Mr. RICHMOND (Glasgow) said he now had instructions from the magistrates not to stamp china weights —At the close of the discussion a vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Parkin for his paper., MEDIC AL WEIGHTS. Mr. W. H. M. BLEWS (Birmingham) read a paper on "The necessity of correctness in medical weights.'' He de- sired that all inspectors should have such balances and in- struments as would enable them confidently to test all gram or apothecaries' weights presented to them for trial, and he hoped to awaken the authorities of cities and towns to the vital importance of providing their officers with such balances and instruments as would enable them to correctly discharge their responsible duties. In October, 1882, Mr. Wirnhurst, the father of the association, presented to the Manchester Corporation a tabular statement of scales, weights, and measures examined in that city from 1873 to 1882. 1r.11873 no less than 27,950 shops and warehouses were visited ; 57,848 scales were sul,jected to examination, and 171,869 weights. Of these weiahts 30,618 required readjusting. I Was it peesible to overestimate the services discharged by weights and measures inspectors? And was it not a wretched economy which neglected to provide those men with the hest and most perfect of instruments? The mul- tiple of 30,01 G i Incorrect weights might represent n the course of one year millions of oasts of dishonest sales. To prove the necessity of accurate balances for testing grain weights, some months ago he had two gross of sets of gri!in weights examined and stamped by a duly authorised an-
I •

nectar. He forwarded some of them to tbree eminent Lon- don firms, also to the S.andards Office. Westminster, and to their late friend Mr. Wimhurst, then chief inspector of weights at Manchester. The result of Mr Wiinhurst's care- ful examination of 84 weights showed six to be correct, 78 incorrect. Of 42 weights sent to one firm four were erred, 38 incorrect. Another of the firms found every weight in- correct. Mr. Chaney. the head of the Standards Depart- ment, had 84 weights tested, with the result that only two werecorrect. The general result was only 4 per cent. correct.i He need not remark what serious, if not fatal, consequences might result from medical prescriptions in which drugs of intense potency were used if such inaccurate weights were permitted. Lie believed the defects mainly arose from the use of inadequate balances by the inspectors. He did not blame the inspectors, bat he conld not free local authorities who failed to provide the requisite instruments to enable their officers to carry out the onerous and responsible duties entrusted to them.—A brief discussion followed, in which surprise was expressed that so much looseness was possible in regard to the fine weights used by apothe- caries.—A vote of thanks was given to Mr. 'flews for his paper.

div.head: DINNER.
div.p: THE DINNER.

In the evening the annual dinner of the association was held at the Lion Hotel, The Mayor occupied the chair, and he was supported by Alderman Chandley, chairman of the association, and Mr. Hare, vice-chairman. A glee party consist:llg of Messrs. F. J. Dell, R. Grounds, H. Atkinson, and G. Monks was present and sang several selections. TUESDAY'S BUSINESS. _

On Tuesday morning the meeting was resumed in the Town Hall, Alderman Chandley presiding. The business consisted otatbe reading of a paper on "The Oscillating Counter Machine and the Swan Neck Beam" by Mr. 8 B. Massey, of Msnchester, to whom a vote of thanks was given after a discussion on the paper. Votes of thanks were also passed to the Mayor for allowing the use of the Town Hall ; to Mr. Place for the assistance he had given the as- sociation; and to Alderman Chandley for presiding. In the afternoon the members of the association paid a visit to the Liverpool Exhibition.

EXTRA.ORDINARY DAMAGE TO PRO-
PERTY AT 6T, BELENS. TWENTY-ONE MUSES CARRIED AWAY.

An extraordinary case came h2fore the magistrates at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Thursday. Within the last year or two no fewer than 21 houses, situate on Greenbank—the lowest part of St. Helens—have gradually disappeared in a most extraordinary way. The value of the property in the neighbourhood has been reduced to a minimum in conse- quence of the depredations of the people living thereabouts, who have profitably employed themselves in pulling down untenanted houses and cal ting awey and selling the mate- rial. The stolen property belongs principally to Mr. John Kitchen, Messrs. Giver and Co., and Mrs. Wolfenden. It is stated some of the houses were reduced to such a state of , dilapidation that when put up fer sale by auction they only I fetched the sum of £ll 10e. It would seem that the pur- i chaser did not strike a very profitable bargain, for since the sale what remained of the five houses has disappeared. With a view of putting a stop to the practice Mr. Kitchen has instituted proceedings against three men for stealing a portion of his property, and at the St. Helens Police Court on Thursday, before Alderman Harrison, the three men whose names are John Masterson, 71, Bold-street; Michael Callaghan, 51, Bold-street, and Patrick Keerahan, 54. Bold- street, were cbarged. the two first-named with stealing a quantity of bricks and sold on May 20, and the latter with stealing a quantity of bricks and flags on April 30 and May Ist. Mr. J. 0. Swift, who appeared for the prosecution, briefly stated the facts of the case, and asked for a remand till Monday. The ni, n had been apprehended on a charge of stealing a large quantity of bricks and ether material from property in Garden-street, Greenbank, belonging to the executors of the late J. W. Glover. John Moore stated that on Thursday last he saw Masterson and Callaghan wheeling barrowsfel of material away from the property in Garden-street. On April 30th he saw Keerabam take a quantity of bricks and flags away from one o'clock till 5 30. He must havi taken away between 4,000 and 5,000 bricks, and next morning he W.lB engaged from early in the morning in taking away bricks and flees in Master- son's cart. Mr. Thomas, who appeared on behalf of the prisoner!, asked that the men might be admitted ont on bail. He suggested that they might be admitted out on their own recognisances. Mr. Swift objected. He submitted that it was a serious matter, and that substantial bail ought to be given. The damage lately done to the property amounted g6o6„—Keerahan said he had permission to take away "...iree months ago.—Mr. Kitchen, who said he the materfai i. was agent for the ,-operty or what was left of it, denied having given Keeriiall izrmiesion to take away the nee. SlTurtmv STmelle."—The fourth Brinsmead Concert was gic en on Saturday night to a large audience. Berlioz's Sym- phonic Fantastique, "Episode de la Tie (fun Artiste." was the piece de resistance of the first part, and was most ably per- formed. The other day one of our representatives calied upon Mr. Brinsmead to ask him a few questions about these concerts, which have proved a wonderful success. " "fon see," be said. "at this time of the year there are few opportunities given to the musicloving public for hearing classical masters in con- junction with modern compossrs. The mush:sal publie has reached a high steward of cultivation; the love of music has never been greater than in the present decade ; and I may may, without any egotism. that I am proud of the success which has attended my new effort for the advancement of the art to which I have devoted my life." Mr Brinsmead gave a sigh of ratisfaction as he ran his supple fingers over the enamelled keys of one of his grand pianos, enrapturing inv• ueeducated ear by w at is cal!ed in reusicsl circles toe " tone colouring nuances," showing all the grada- tions between the faiptest whisper and the grandest fortiseirno crash. Like all realiy great men, Mr. Brine - mead is an enthusiast, and his tongue trips lightly from one subject to another. He enlarged upon the ap- plication of electricity to pianos, and told me how one day he hoped to produce a sustained piano note such as is now ob- tained oniy on the organ. "I admit that my pianos are some- what expensive, but they are the best. I have lived for the per- fect{ in of the piano, and when ideal perfection is reached I shall retire frem the business." (This with a sly smile.) "I will not trouble you with the technicalities of my art. but I have taken out numberless patents for every part of the in. strument. The last is themes"' tuning pin by which a child can adjust the toms." And Mr. Brinsmead Eliscucses the evo- lution of the piano and its parts with an infinite gust'. Mr. Brinamead is a large employer of labour, having an army of four hundred men in his employ In the two tine factories, in in which sixty pianos a week are carted away te all parts of the world. It is computed hat one plano per hour is made during the working year—a vast output of harmony. No wonder that Mr. Brimmed is an enthusiast as he talks of his magni• cent factories—the result of a lifetime's laborious energy. Some day I hope to pay a visit to the factories, when a description of this remarkable industry may be of interest.—Fail Mail

Gazette. PRESICSTATION TO Mn. A. C. MCCORQUODALE, J.P. —The forthcoming marriage of Mr. A. C. hicCorquodale, J.P., Son of the late Liberal candidate for the Newton Divi- sion, Colonel George McCorquedale, will form the occasion of a very handsome presentation from the Liberals of the Division. During recent years, and especially at the time of the General Election, Mr. A. C. McCorquodale has worked earnestly and subscribed liberally in promotion of the Liberal cause, and the local Liberals have decided to accord him a tangible mark of their appreciation of his services, and of the respect in which lie is held throughout the district. A smoking cabinet of a costly and elaborate character has been subscribed for, and the follow- ing inscription placed noon a silver plate :—" Presented to A. C. McCorquodale, Esq., J.P., on his marriage, by the Earlestown Liberal (ilula. June Ist, 1886. With best wishes." The cabinet is of polished walnut, with silver mountings, and contains handsomely cut glass jars— for tobacco, spirits, cigars, &c., while there is every con- venience for the arrangement of smoking requisites. The article is of an attractive design, and in order to secure this no expense or pains were spared. It has been conveyed to London, where, prior to the "happy event," it will be banded over to the recipient. I NEWS. The Bank of Bombay has increased its minimum rate ut interest and discount from 7 to 8 per cent. The Lord Lieutenant and Laciy Aberdeen on Wednesday paid a visit to Coils, and were enthusiastically received. The Deputy Master of the Royal Mint reports that £8.999,942 worth of silver has been coined in England since 1873. Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes was presented to the Prince of Wales at .rlarlborough House, on Weduesday, morning by the United States Minister.

A woman named Britlard has been apprehended at Ashton-under-Lyne on suspTc!on of having poisoned young married woman named Dixon. The Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice and Princess Louis of Battenberg, left Windsor for Balmoral at twenty minutes past eight o'clock on Wednesday night. The :Police Enfranchisement Bill is endorsed by Mr. Tottenham. Sir W. Hart Dyke, Sir Julian Goldsmid, Vis- count Grimston, Mr. Biddulph, Col. King-Harman, and Mr. Ryland s. Captain George Symonds, of Penzance, and his twin eons, aged thirteen, war. upeet while fishing in a punt off Penzance on Wednesday morning. One of the lads was drowned, while his father and brother had narrow escapes,

THE DERBY.—The race for the Derby Stakes came off on Wednesday at Epzom. and resulted in an easy victory for the Duke ef I'Vestminqtei's Ormond,., the winner of the Two Thousand Gaineas, Mr. Peck's Bard second, and " Mr. Manton's " bt. Mirip ran a bad third.

On Monday, sear Blackwatertown, a few miles from Armagh, Hugh Daly, a small farmer, murdered his wife by kicking her, and afterward. gave himself up to the police. who found the woman's body at the place indicated, the brains being scattered about. THE MURDER AT PooLa.—At Poole, on Wednesday, John Jerrald King, pilot, was committed for trial charged with the murder of Alderman Hamilton. In answer to the charge, the prisoner said if he bad done anything wrong he was prepared to suffer the full penalty of the Englishi law.

Berlin corresponient says the Emperor William is in such a state of weakness that it ectrcely seems possittle that he can survive many days. He has failed with amazing rapidity during the last fortnight, and his manifest debility excitd a most painful impression at the parade on Friday last.

It is stated by a continental journal that the betrothal of Prince Oscar of Sweden to Princess Louise, eldest daughter of the I'rince of Wales, will soon take place, and that the oflicial betroth tl has only been delayed by the re- fusal of the Swedish Ittichstag to grant the necessary ap- panage for Prince Oscar. A CRUBL Lurostriosr.—At Liverpool As,ivs on Satur- day, James Kelly, formerly a warder in an Irish gaol, was sentenced to five years' penal servitthie for forging re- quests for payment of money, he having represented to the wives of various men under remand that he could, if paid, provide better prison accommodation for their has. bands.

The Royal Commission oplia the depression in trade and industry resumed its meetings on Wednesday morning, at Richmond Terrace, after an adjournment of a month, Lord ladesleigh presiding. There was a good attendance, and the currency quastien was taken into consideration. Three members of the raper Manufactuters' Association were also examined.

FATAL RAILWAY ACCIMINT.—On Thuslay morning, at Camp Hill, Birmingham, some labourers were repairing the parapet of a bridge on the Midland railway when, owing to the default of the look-out man, a train dashed op and knocked three of them down. One was killed on the spot, and another r2cAvad the concussion of the brain, Tl 4 third was only slightly hurt. Mtt. BURT'S SALIRY.—At the annual delemafe meeting of the Northumb,rland Miners' Union, in Newcastle, on Monday, Mr. T. Butt, M.P.. was re-elected secrAary. A proposal wet made to reduce his salary from £5OO to £350, chiefly on the ground that the latter amount is more in keeping with the salaries of other labour representativett than the former. The motion was lost.

ExTRAoRDINARY cri.nt,—Toe ;!.ctior or Deaner Mur- gatroyd against the Ble.ckburn Tramway Co. for damages was conc!uded at Liverpool Assizes on Weduesday. Mrs. Murgatroyd was dragged off an overcrowded car by a drunken pass,ngr,r. Her infant child, whom she had in her arms at the time, was killed, and she herself sustained severe injuries. The jury awanied £2OO. _

ICS FLOES IN THE ATLANTIC. —I he steamer Nova Sco- tia, which has ai aived at t. John's, Newfoundland, from Liverpool, reports that an Arctic ic- floe nearly 200 miles wide is floating to the eaetward of Newfoundland, including many icebergs. The steamer Plover, com;ng from the ex- treme north of Newfoundland, reports that a heavy ice floe is moving southwards across the track of Transatlantic steamers.

ALLEGED POISONING.—At the Askton•under-Lyne Polite Court, on Wednesday, . Mary Ann Brit land was again ex- amined in connection with the charge of having caused the death of Mary Dix-m by administering to hr vermin kil- ler. Prisoner was rernauded. A application is to be made to the Horne Secr,:tary for an order to exhume the body of the prisoner's husband, who, it is believed, also died from poisoning.

A. RIVAL TO SUGAR.—" Saccharin" is the name given to a new sweet substance extracted (rem coal:ar, and which is estimated to be 230 times sweeter than cane sugar. One part sweetens 10,000 parts of water. Unlike cane sugar, it is harmless in diabetic diseases, and it is now used in certain Berlin hospitals for sweetening foods and medicines. At present it is extremely expensive as compared with sugar, it being some 404 per pound.

SERIOUS CII.II2GiS AGAINST A POLICEMAN.—At Birming• ham, on Monday, P.C. Wingate charged Ellen Budge with disorderly conduct on Stturday night. The woman told the magistrate that the officer, who was in piaib clothes, had a stick with him, and thrashed her till her body was black and blue. Two witnesses supported this statement. The bench discharged the woman, and ordered the attention of the Watch Committee to be called to the case.

SHOP Hones.—A conference on the subject of the shop hours' movement was held at the Grand Hotel, Manchester, on Wednesday, the Dean of Manchester presiding. A reso- lution was passed approving 'the principle of legislation as applied to shop huts, this decision being consequent upon the demonstrated failure of voluntary effort to produce the desired result." It was also decided to bold a public meet- ing in the city in furtherace of the movement.

bEBAT LO,SES THROUGH THE RECENT STO'IMS.—Now that the snow has nearly disappeared from the fells and dales of Westmoreland and Cumberland, it is possible to estimate the great losses sustained by the farmers and gar- deners. Sheep are still being thawed out day by day, and the total number that perished is now put down at 5000. Many of them were lying feet uppermost, and a large num- ber were starved to death. Many paies also auccumbi!4 the cold.

PARLIAMENTARY Peocnbrun.—At a meeting of the Pro- cedure Committee, on Monday, the Chandelier of the Ex- chequer, in reply to a question from Sir Michael Hicks- Beach, as to what portion of the estimates the Govern- ment would propose should be referred to a StaLding Committee, said the Government would have no proposal to submit to the Committee. The Government desired it to be clearly understood that for the resolutions as they now stood they would take no responsibility, nor would they recommend them to the House of Commons. A resolution which aims at a reduction in the number of questions gave rise to an animated discussion, but eventually was agreed to as originally submitted. The next resolution provides that no motion for the adjournment of tbe House shall be made until questions have been disposed of and the or- ders of the day or notices of motion entered upon, ex- cept by general consent of the House. Some discussion arose on the interpretation of the term " general consent," and the Committee adjourned without coming to a final decision. _ _ .

OBANGIZtoneo.—A disgraceful off air occurred at Stewardstown, county Tyrone. on Saturday evening, when the Tullybogne Temperance Orange Band marched into the town. Having marched about and played their custo- mary tunes they got into collision outside the town with some Roman Catholics who had assembled to defend their chapel, from expected wrk eking by the Orangemen. The police with difficulty kept the two parties separate, and Mr. Chambre. an Orange leader and magistrate, got the band to move on. The police, knowing the intention of the Orangemen to march by and perhaps wreck the Catholic chapel, entreated them to go home by a different route, but they declined. The Catholic defenders bad in the meantime hastened to the chapel yard. Mr. Chambre and Mr. Woods, another local magisirate, accompanied the band, as well as the police. At the Catholic chapel the Catholics received the assailants with rolleys of stones, and the yard being higher than the road and surrounded with a wail the defen- ders had a certain advantage over their onemy. Mr. Cham- bre and part of the police hurried the Orangemen forward, while Mr. Woods and the rest of the police remained at the chapel gate to keep the Catholics from getting out. A por- tion if the Orangemen made a detour to get at the foe, some of whom were nothing loth and met them by a back way. The police again interfered, and with the assistance of Mr. Chatnbre got the Orangemen to move off. A small reinforcement of police came up at this time from another station. The Catholics were called upon to leave the chapel yard and disperse, but they refused and said they would stay all night. There were several melees, in one of which Mr. Woods got a blow on the head from a stone thrown by the Catholic defenders, and numerous other persons were also struck on both aides. At length the Catholics, forming into process;on, came out from the yard and marched four deep back to their first position. They then tried to march back, but were dispersed by the police. It was not nnt,l one o'clock en Sunday morning that order was completety restored in the streets. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 29, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 29, 1886.

THE House of Lords, with a persistency I worthy of a better cause, has again rejected I the bill to legalise marriage with a deceased Wife's sister. It was thought that their lord- ships had been brought at last to see the error of their ways ; it is not long since they Passed the second reading of the bill by a narrow majority; but on Monday evening- it was thrown out by a majority of 22—the numbers being 127 for, and 147 against the i bill. The House of Commons s distinctly at issue with the House of Lords on this question, for the measure has again and again been approved by the Lower House. Their lordships block the way in this, as in Many other matters, and they are sorely trying t„11 patience of the people. It is galling to ;milk our fellow-subjects in the colonies have legal rights in the matter of choice of a part- ll.,.„er.which are denied to residents within the united Kingdom. The DUKE Off ARGYLL, W.ho has shown himself less and less liberal slnce he parted from MR. GLADSTOI4E, led ti.ie opposition to the bill; but he was per- tinently reminded that in taking this course he . did not occupy an enviable position, seeing that he was a member of the-Govern- ulent which advised the Royal assent being given to legalise marriage with a deceased Wife's sister in South Australia, Victoria, and Tasmania. His Grace, by way of reply, said "these things were done without the slightest reference to personal feeling ;" but surely if the Divine Voice," which he appealed to, requires that this country should "stand firm O n the ancient ways," it is not less needful that the "Divine Voice" should be obeyed by our brethren in the colonies. The DUKE 4111 ARGYLL ought not to play fast and loose with what he professes to regard as sacred ties; it may lead some to conclude that tue. re is nothing sacred about them. When n 15 remembered that the law, as it stands, as passed half a century ago, as a sop to 'lle Bishops who would otherwise have "posed a special Act to legalise the mar- rl,ge of a certain Duke with his deceased Wife's sister, people may be pardoned if they think there is something of cant in talking about "ancient ways" and the "Divine 'Voice." The Archbishop of Canterbury, as the spokesman ot the priesthood, resorted, In the absence of solid "argument, to vague talk about England not being "the place i Which should break n upon the sanctity of the family." The breakers in upon sanctity are, as it seems to us, those who uphold a tYrannical law which. aas no sanction in either reason or Scripture, and which brands as illegitimate unions which would be re- garded as sacred in other portions of Her zilajesty's dominions. It is computed. that that from 800 to 1,000 of these marriages take place every year, and such is the state °,..! the law, owing to the stupidity of the u se of Lords—backed as it is by the 'bishops—that the children of these unions are treated in the matter of 'succession to Property as though they were bastards. This Is a grave scandal—a scandal not to those Who contract marriages of this class, but tea Legislature which is not abreast of civil's- -4tion. What can be more natural for a Workingman who loses his wife, and is left With several children, than for him to conclude, in certain cas s, that the sister of the deceased parent will make a good wife And a good mother to the children? To sug- st this as equivalent to proposing to marry ins own sister is the veriest nonsense: for there can be no more blood relationship in the lecond marriage than there was in the first. t is true that tiir Bishops have made a good seal of use of CHRIST'S expression—" they tWain shall be one flesh "—but no one save a 4PeCial pleader would think for a moment of

putting a' literal interpretation upon the phrase. It is a metaphor, an excellent meta- phor ;.and to regard it in any other light is to make it ridiculous, not to say r that it shuts out the possibility of divorce. CHRIST spoke of himself as a door, but he must be indeed wooden-headed who would argue that the "Divine Voice" meant a conversion into so many square feet of timber. Nor does the Scriptural argument gain strength by the reference which the Bishops make to the Levitical Law. The passage upon which they chiefly rely is the riith verse of the ath chapter of Leviticus, namely, "Neither shalt thou take a wife to her sistet to vex her, to uncover her nakedness, besides the other in her lifetime." The best authorities are agreed —and by this we mean the majority of Hebrew and Greek professors— that this means what is apparent on the face of it, that under the Levitical code a man was not per- mitted to marry his wife's sister so long as his wife was alive. Modern law preserves this prohibition, and it goes further—it puts a man in prison for having more than one wife. The Jews were not so particular—for Solomon was not to a hundred or two in the way of wives. The Jews as a race were polygamists, but they had some little notion of decency; they thought it didn't look well to "take a wife to her sister to vex her, beside the other in her lifetime ;" and so they laid it down that there should be no marriage with a wife's sister whilst the wife was alive. "This necessarily implies," to quote Professor FORBES, " the Permission that a man may, after the decease of his wife, marry her sisti,r." In Deu- teronomy it is given as law that the widow who is without children shall have the right to demand that the brother of her deceased husband be given to her in marriage; but how could that be if the Jews held the idea of prohibition because of degrees of affinity ? The relationship is the same in the one case as the other. The fact is, the less the clergy say about the Levitical marriage code the better. Nineteenth century civisilation is be- yond it, and it is beyond the miserable huggermuggering of the House of Lords. But let the lords for the present go their way; they will have to go another way as soon as the Home Rule question is settled. There is some satisfaction in thinking that the time is rapidly approaching when the House of Lords will be mended or ended.
RUNT ABA.TRIEENT.—We understand that at Col. Blackburne's rent audit, held at The Childe of Hale on Thursday .week, 10 per cent. was returned to the whole of the tenantry.

THUNDERSTORM.—On Thursday night a thunder- storm broke over Cheshire. While the storm was raging a flash of lightning struck a house at Broxton, ran down ,the chimney, and set fire to it. The mantel-piece was destroyed. The storm lasted an hour, and as accompanied by a heavy fall of hail.

BEA-USTED HOUSE.—This is an institution for the training and education of weak-minded boys, with reference to which a doctor writes to the "Lancet —" A better place for weak-minded boys there cannot possibly be. The house is commodious, the grounds are extensive, fruit is plentiful, the management is characterised by great liberality and kindness, and the terms are moderate. A personal visit has convinced me that many parents with afflicted children would be rejoiced to hear of such a home for them.

THE QUEEN AND FIVE LITTLE CREWE GIRLS. —On her Majesty's birthday the following telegram was despatched in the name of Miss Connie Speak- man, daughter of Mr. Speakman, solicitor, from a child's p:rty at Crewe to the Queen :—" Five little Crewe girls we, Send birthday wishes unto thee." In a very short time the following gratifying reply was received :—" The Queen thanks Miss Connie Speakman and her little friends for their kind wishes." The Queen, on Monday completed her 67th year. On June 29 her Majesty will have reigned 49 years. SANGER'S CIRCUS. The numberless persons who delight in the varied amusements of the circus will have the opportunity of a treat afforded them by the visit of the great circus of Mr. G. Sangers to Warrington on Monday and to R,uncorn on Tuesday. This is stated to be the first appear- ance of this famous establishment—reputed to be something like the best of its kind—in the pro- vinces for twelve years. The proceedings at both Warrington and Runcorn will be in- augurated by a grand procession in which no doubt the great resources of the es- tablishment will be strikingly displayed. In ad- dition to what is probably a unique staff of male and female performers, Mr. Sanger is the possessor of an unequalled stud of performing animals, ' including a group of elephants. A SHEEP IN THE PULPIT.—Not long ago, says a correspondent in a contemporary, an amusing inci- dent occurred in a country school-chapel not a hun- dred miles from Warrington. It was Sunday after- noon, and there wanted a good half-hour before commencing school, and only a few scholars were present, when, through the sclopol door, two of the school lads were seen bringing with them an un- willing sheep. With much difficulty they succeeded in getting the sheep up the pulpit steps and into the pulpit itself. There, panting and quiet, it re- mained until the school assembled and the superin- tendent opened by giving out the usual hymn. The boys in the secret had been told to say nothing when the teachers came, and nothing was said until the. poor sheep itself began to bleat, and in a sort of frightened treble sung out baa-ba-a! "Who is doing that?" inquired the Worthy super, supposing some of the lads were mis- chievously imitating the tremulous tones of a sheep. There was no reply. " Let us pray," and all knbeled while the good man prayed, but while he did so another bleat was heard, and another. Was it a plaintive response to a petition? or a sincere " Amen " that he heard? No it sounded like none of these, so the prayer ended, the super, somewhat per- plexed and annoyed, proceeded to box, the ears of some of the youngsters whose behaviour was.very suspicious. In fact he promised a book to anyl scholar who would tell him who the delinquent was who dared to conduct himself so rudely. Receiving no reply, he was about to administer a universal castigation, when one little urchin shouted out to save himself from punishment, "Teacher, there's a sheep inside th' pulpit," and in the pulpit sure enough he found the timid and unconscious cause of all his trouble, which he speedily liberated to wander in green pastures and more congenial cora- pany, with the queer reflection—" Its not the first time by any means that a sheep has got inside a pulpit.' THE BIGAMIST BAILIFF. At the Liverpool Assizes on Friday week George William Hardwick, alias George Robert, 51 years of age. county court bailiff, pleaded guilty to having at Widnes, on the I 22nd 'November, 1875, feloniously married Agnes; Gregson, his former wife, Mary Jane Bracewell, be- I ing then alive. Mr. Shand was for the prosecution and Mr. Swift appeared for the defence. Mr. Swift on behalf of the prisoner said that Hardwick married his first wife in January, 1860, and lived with her until 1868. At the end of that time dif- ferences arose between them, for which the pri- soner took the blame, and at the request of his wife • he left her. He saw her several times afterwards, and in January, 1869, as the differences could not be made up, he acceded to a proposal of her father and brother to keep away from her on condition that they would look after and see she had all she wonted. He left the neighbourhood in 1871,- and got employment at Wigan and afterwards at St. Helens, where he had acted for several years as a bailiff of the County Court. In the summer of 1875, while lodging at a beerhouse in St. Helens, he be- came acquainted with a domestic servant there, and the result was that he went through the form of , marriage with her in November of that year. He I lived with her down to October, 1885, and in that month he had occasion to go to Leeds, where his ' first wife was living, for the purpose of drawing a sum of £3O which was owing to him out of an estate. His first wife heard he was getting the , money and thought she should have some of it.' He gave her'.Es and a further sum afterwards, and also forwarded 50s to his second wife. When his first wife was again brought face to face with him -;cmplications arose which prevented him returning to St. Helens, and the end of it was that the second wife and her children became chargeable to the parish. The guardians took out a warrant against the prisoner, and on his arrest his whole history came out, whereupon the police commenced the present prosecution. He (Mr. Swift) submitted the case was one which might be leniently dealt with, considering the offence was committed eleven years ago. His lordship said there were very little extenuating circumstances in the case, and sen- tenced the prisoner to eighteen months' imprison- ment.

-- It was kindly of the Mayor of Warrington to invite the members of the local Dramatic Society to meet Mr. Edward Terry at break- fast. But if it was intended that the pro- ceedings should be pubUc, how comes it that the press were not invited ? And if, the breakfast was a private matter between his Worship and his friends, how comes it that a report appears in one paper? Has some- body been eavesdropping ? These are ques- tions which are being asked. It is not to be supposed that anyone would wait outside un- til the breakfast was over, and then beg per- mission to pick up the crumbs of speech; of course not.

Nothing strikes a stranger more, after being struck with Runcorn Bridge as a triumph of engin- eering, than to find that, if be wants to get from Widnes to Runcorn, by rail, he must go first to Dit• ton Junction—a long way wide of Widnes. Direct railway communication between Widnes and Runcorn is imperatively needed; and the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority have done right to petition the London and North. Western Railway Company for a ,station on the Widnes side of the bridge. The people of Widnes must follow this up ; there must be peti- tion on petition—"line on line," until they get Burla a line as they certainly require.

Mr. John Crosfield, the Liberal candidate for Warrington, attended the Liberal meetirl at E tries- town on Saturday as a Newton elector, and made a stirring speech. There is no beating the bush with him; he goes straight to the point. He was just a little hard on Mr. Peter Rylands, who seems to be "catching it" all round. The audience was out-and- out for "Gladstone and Home Rule," and as this is Mr. Crosfield's cry there was perfect accord.

Liberal members of Parliament—Ar. Rylands in- cluded—are disposed to complain of the pressure, at this crisis, which is sought to be put upon them by their constituents. But why should they complain? The electors are acting within their right in making their views known; and members are not compelled to vote as they are requested. They can vote, if they like, against Home Rule. And what if they do lose their seats? They surely do not want to be representatives of people they do not represent.

He denies having urged or contemplated resistance to the Home Rule Bill other than constitutional resistance; but contends that if the Bill pass, and a l'arnellite Parliament be set up in Dublin, Ulster will be justified in resisting, its authority. The PRIME MINISTER has pinned the ranter of Belfast down in such a way that there is no possibility of escape. There is no wriggling out of the words "Ulster will fight; Ulster will be right." They are dis- loyal; they are treasonable whether spoken by a lord or a labourer. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON sought, the other day, to en- force the duty of loyalty; let him pray now for Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL.

At the meeting of Liberal members of Parlia- ment, held at the Foreign Office, on Thursday, Mr. Gladstone opened wide the door for the outsiders who wish to return to the fold. Without committing himself to any scheme, the Prime Minister leaves the way clear for some plan "for securing the presence of the Irish representatives in the House of Commons at Westminster during the consideration of Imperial and general matters, as well as on questions of taxa- tion in which Ireland was particuarly interested." What more, it may be asked, does anybody want who is in favour of Home Rule Englishmen, whatever Mr. Chamberlain may think, would never consent to Irishmen having the power to settle their own affairs at Dublin, and the affairs of the English, Scotch, and Welsh at Westminster.
LOCAL NEWS.

ROUNDERS.— Widnes v. Olympic (Liverpool).— This match was played at Widnes on Saturday, and ended in a victory for the home team by 28 runs. The home team went in to bat first, but only made a poor show, their score at the end of the first innings only amounting to 28 runs. Tke visitors' team then went in to bat, but, like the home team, they only made a poor stand against their opponents' ' bowling, seven of their men not rn4king a single run. Their first innings only amounted to 13 runs, thus leaving the home team with a lead of 15 runs on the first innings. In I the second innings both teams showed up a little better with the bat, the home team totalling 39 at the second attempt, of which Ileyes made 15 in good style; the visi- tors' second attempt amounting to 26 runs. After the match the home team entertained the visitors to a good tea, and afterwards enjoyed themselves with a little har- mony. Score : WIDNES. OLYMPIC.
