The House of Lords has thrown out the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, and the Durham Sunday Closing Bill. When are the people going to direct themselves to the task of throwing out the House of Lords? The letting of the refreshment bars in con- nection with the Newton Races was fixed to take place by auction on Monday. The reserve prices were not reached ; but nobody need weep. It is not a bad sign when "John Barleycorn" is not first favourite.

Total A RUNCORN NEWSAGENT SENT TO GAOL.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Moniay, John Cliffe, newsagent, Ash- ridge-street, Runcoro, was charged with stealing six newe- papers, the property of the London and North-Western Rail way Company. Mr. Ferrand, of the solicitors depart- ment, Lime-street, prosecuted. Evidence was given by Mr. Cupis, publishing manager of the " Mercury " office, Liver- pool; David,,Mushit, a packer in that office; Detective- Sergeint Person; Arthur Fletcher and Alfred Humphreys, boys. It appeared that for some time parcels of the" Liver- Pool Mercury " had been missed from the railway station, , and on Saturday a test parcel, containing half a dozen copies of that journal, was made up at the publishing office and despatched by the 6 35 train from Lime-street. The parcel was adlressed "Mr. Newton, Runcorn," and was ac- companied by Detective-Sergeant Pearson. When the par- cel was thrown out on the platform at Runcorn, the prisoner was observed to turn it over with his foot. read the address, and then, when the newsboys had departed, he picked up the parcel and walked away. Immediately on leaving the I , premises he tore the label off the parcel, and threw it on the I ground, aril Sergeant Pearson who followed him picked it up. The prisoner deposited a'• Mercury at the she!) of Mr. MeQuinn in High-street, and also left a newspaper at the House of Mr. Tonks. Sergeant Pearson thereupon took the prisoner into custody. The prisoner in answer to the charge said he had bought three " Mercurvs " at tho rail- way bookstall, but Ate hur Fletcher proved that he only pur- chased a "Sporting Chronicle." The prisoner pleaded euilty and was fined £2 and costs, £2 lie 01, or in default a month's hard labour. He went to gaol. A GoLo 'NIFDAL —The Ho YAL and lISPE4IAL Crncoto FREN• TIN° of LA/unto have elected dr. John B insrnead a Fellow of that Society and have awarded the Gold Medal to him.

Lord Salisbury, Lord R. Churchill, and Sir Richard Cross are 'expected to attend" a Tory demonstration at Haydock Park to be held shortly. " I can call spirits from the vasty deep, but will they come ? " Still there is no harm in expecting. Sir Richard will come of course; but that is not tempting he is a very hard Cross to bear.

The fighting on the Greek frontier was a species of maaness, seeing that everything was tending to a peaceful settlement. It is said that the officers on both sides wanted to "distinguish themselves by being first in the field." Some of them now lie in undistin- guished graves, having paid the highest penalty for their rashness.
MR. SHAW LEFEVRE intends to ask the House of Commons to stop any further ex- penditure on the Nile and Trafalgar, which are, he says, certain to cost together con-

RUNCORN GYMNASIUM was closed for the season on Thursday evening. WIDNES BATHS.—These excellently conducted baths will be opened for the summer season to-day., The building has undergone all necessary renovation, and cleanliness and attention may be relied upon. NEW CEMETERY AT HALTON.—Ttie contractors for the new cemetery at Halton have nearly completed their work, and the Vicar is making arrangements with the Lord Bishop of Chester for the consecration of the ground. MR. JAMES FOLEY. WIDNES.—This gentleman conducted a religious service in Malin'. Temperance Hall, on Sunday evening. There WAS a fairly good congregation, and Mr. Foley preached a sermon front the Bth verse of the 16th Psalm. NELSON-STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The Rev. R Yeatman preached in the above place of worship on Sun- day, the subject of his address in the morning being " Strength in weakness," and that in the. evening, "Unbelief and its results." EIALTON SCHOOL SERMONS.—The annual services in aid of the Haltou Parochial Schools were held on Sunday. In the morning and evening the Rev. H. P. Ramsden, M.A., Diocesan Inspector of Schools, occupied the pulpit, and in the afternoon the Rev. J. Lockwood, Vicar, was the preacher. The collections amounted to £lO 4s. ANNIVERSARY SERMONS AT RUNCORN.—The anniversary service,: of the Mill Brow Wesleyan Sunday School were held on Sunday, in Helton-road Chapel. The Rev. E. J. Hope, of Dudley, was the preacher. Special hymns were sung by the choir and scholars, Mr. J. A. Frith being at the organ. At the evening service the National Anthem was sung in honour of the Cleeen's birthday. Upwards of 25 was collected in aid of the School Fund. Tier, StamEN DEATH OF A BOY AT WIDNES.—The ad- journed inquiry into the cause of the death of Patrick Batten, aged 10 years. the son of a labourer, who lives at 19, Caroline-street, was held at Whines Police Court, on Mon- day, before Mr. S. Brighouse. The boy died suddenly on the 11th inst. Dr. Neil, who had made a post-mortem ex- amination, was of opinion that death had resulted from compression of the brain, caused by convulsions, and a ver- dict accordingly was returned. A COUNTY COURT FOR. WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, solicitor, has eeceived a communication from Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, MP., in which that gentleman states he has again called at the fiord Chancellor's officer to further the petition for a county court for Widnes. He adds that he ascertained that the matter is practic illy settled, and that even if a change of Government were to take place the future Lord Chancellor would be informed that to all in- tents the prayer of the petitioners had been granted. FUNERAL OF A SUNDAY SCHOOL SCHOLAR AT RUN. CORN.—Thei funeral .of Mr. Wm. Powell Williams, eldest son of the Rw. Evan Williams pastor of St. John's Pres- byterian Chapel, Runcorn, took place at Runcorn ceme- tery on Tuesday afternoon. The deceased, who was 18 years Of age, died on Saturday morning after a lingering illness. The funeral was attended by many members of the church with which the deceased was connected, and the body was borne by several members of his Sundae, school class. A number of wreaths were placed on the coffin, The Rev. E Jones conducted the service. ACCIDENT TO THE RUNCORN MAIL CART.—.4II accident, fortunately unattended by serious results, occurred to the mail cart belonging to Mr. S. Yarwood, on Thursday morn- ing. When at Halton Brook, Co the return journey, and travelling at a high rate of speed, the arm of the axle (Collin's patent) broke. and the wheel came off. The dri- ver, Samuel Hopley, was pitched into the road, and luckily escaped without injury. The horse, a speedy animal, con- tinued its course and did not stop until it had dragged the cart to the post office, the usual terminating point. The cart was an almost complete wreck, and the horse suffered from several bruises. RESCUE FROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN. —John Dyson, a boy eight years of age, who lives in Jackson's-lane, had a narrow escape from drowning on Wednesday night. He fell into the Bridgewater qmal near Green Tern, and his struggle took him to the middle of the canal. Two men who stood near and the mother of the boy were tenable to render any assistance, but fortunately Mr John Guy, of Eaton-street, arrived on the spot, and without hesitation plunged into the water and brought the drowning lad to the side. This is the second rescue Mr Guy has made, and his gallant action deserves some acknowledgement. His clothes and watch were injured. PROMOTION OF SUPERINTENDENT LEAH, OF RUNCORN —The people of Runcorn will learn with regret of the im- minent removal of Superintendent Leah from their midst. Mr. Leah has been promoted to the charge of the more im- portant division of Nantwich, vacant through the death of Superintendent Mayo. During his two years residence in Runcorn, Mr. f.eah has won the coOdence and respect of all classes, by the kindness, courtesy, and tact he has dis- played in the discharge of his duties, and whilst sorry to lose his services. his promotion will be hailed with satisfac- tion. Mr. Leah will be succeeled by Superintendent Hol- lingeworth, of the Broxton Division, and who was formerly stationed at Runcorn. WINDFALL FOR WIDNES RESIDENTS.—At the Stockport churchyard on Saturday, the remains of Mr. Henry W r- rall, of Old Lam, were interred, and there is to be another proof of the old adage that its an ill wind that blows no- body good. The deceased gentleman, who was of a very eccentric disposition, and led a life of celibacy, was reputed to be enormously rich. Re has, however, left behind him no intimation as to how his property has to he disposed of, and his hoardings will consequently be divided amongst the next of kin. Five cousins, it is said, will be entitled to a fair division, and amongst the lucky number are William Abbott. of 8, Timperley-street. Simms Cross, Widoes, and Mrs Groeme, a widow, who lives at Ditton. To the latter especially, who has two children dependent upon her will the windfall be acceptable. DESERTION OF FAMlLY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell junior, and Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Joseph Stanley, a labourer, was claargect with deserting his wife and four children. On the fifth inst. the prisoner's wife applied for relief, and Mr. Scannell visited the house where the family vele living in Dock-street. There was neither food nor It. edure, and Mr. Scannell described the place as more like tuo fair of a wild beast than the habita- tion of human beings. At this time, it was stated the pri- soner was drinking in a neighbouring puhlic-houce, and hearing his wife had applied for relief he decamped. There was due to the Prescot Guardians the snm of £7 4s. The prisoner, who had been previously convicted of assaulting and deserting his wife, was sentenced to two months hard labour. LAWN Tgrails.—Croxteth v. Runcorn: This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, and resulted In favour of Croxteth by 4 events to 4, 10 sets to 9, and 83 games to 79. Score :

I " LOOKED IS WELL AS EVER."—During the hearing of the Widnes wounding case at Liverpool Assizes on Monday, on the conclusion of Dr. McDonald's evidence, the judge remarked that be was proud to see that tbe chemical gas of Widnes agreed with him. He looked as well as ever he did. Oa Police-Constable Cummins getting into the witness box, the judge carefully seamed him over from head to foot, evidently looking if the chemical gas agreed with him also. A ItiroutoteN SCALDED AT WIDNES.—At the works of Messrs. Muspratt and Sons, at Widnes, on Saturday, Thomas Gilhooley, of Moon-street, and a number of other men were engaged "drawing "a salting-down pan. One of the boards of the platform raised above the drainer that carries away the liquor gave, way and Gilhoeley was pre- cipitated into the hot liquor in the drawer and was severely scalded on the back, legs, and shoulders. He was taken home and attended by Mr. „Richards, assistant to Dr. Mc- Donnell.

WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES.—A public tea meeting and entertainment was held in this place of worship on Thursday evening. About 150 persons partook of the tea provided. The subsequent proceedings were pre- sided over by the Rev. R. Yeatman. A programme con- sisting of sacred and secular vocal selections, and a perfor- mance by hand bell ringers was gone through in capital style. Several friends from Runcorn assieted successfully. Miss Travis ably officiated as accompanist. The proceeds of the entertainment are to be devoted to the bazaar fund. SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.-1 he anniver- sary services in connection with Farnworth Wesleyan Sun- day School were held on Sunday, when sermons were preached, morning and evening, by the Rev. J. McTurk, of Warrington. In the afternoon an address to scholars, teachers and friends was given by Mr. Robert Garnett, of Penketh. During the day special hymns were sung by the choir and Sunday school scholars, assisted by a few friends. The collections amounted to over £l3. On Monday evening a service of sacred song, entitled "Little Dot," was given by the scholars, choir, and friends in the chapel, Derby- road. Mr. J. Brock presided, and there was an excellent audience. The Revs. R. Burdon and J. Hothersall read the beautiful and touching narrative. The singers were under the able conductorship of Mr. S. Lamb. WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.—The annual sports of Widnes Athletic Club will be held on Friday and Saturday next, the 4th and sth June. Entries close to-day. There is every prospect of a successful fixture in every way. The annual report of the club has just been issued, and, referring to the fact that the Widnes Cricket and Football Chiba in- tend holding an athletic festival late in the season, said it was generally admitted that there was room for two athletic festivals in Widnes, and the committee therefore appealed once more to their friends and the outside public to assist them in maintaining the position of the Widnes Athletic Club. Mr. F. H. Gossage had presented for competition in the quarter mile district race at the ensuing sports a silver goblet; Mr J. M. Gibson, silver mounted meat and fowl carvers for 120 yards district race ; Messrs. Elkington and Co., shield for -half mile open handicap. The balance sheet shows that the receipts had amounted to £5OB 12s 9d, in- cluding a balance of £47 Ils 10d limn the previous year. &Oise:lotions amounted to £72 19e 6s, competitors' en- trance fees £55 12s 61. sale of tickets £B6 Os 61, admission to field £213 18s 11d. The expenditure reached a total of £425 4e, the principal items being prizes £192 103 and general field expenses £136 2a 10d. There was a balance in hand of £B3 8s 91.
SINGLES. T. W. Soeakman (R) beat L J. ICNour (0). 6-3, 6-1. H. Coeltson (C) beat Thomas Glover (R). 6-4. 2-6, 8-6.

CHESTER REGIMENTAL DISTRICT.—The Queen has approved of the following appointments made by the War Office :—Colonel Patton to the command of the 32nd Regimental district at Chester. vice Lieutenant-Colonel J. P. Glyn; Colonel E. Leach, C. 8., to be assistant-adjutant and quartermaster- general on the stiff. THE HOME RULE MEETING AT EA.RLESTOWN.,— At the enthusiastic meeting in support of the Home Rule proposals of Mr. Gladstone, held in the Via- duct Institute, Earlestown, last Saturday night, and a report of which appears elsewhere, the chairman (Mr. G. W. Rawlins, of Rainhill) was requested to foward a copy of the resolution to the Prime Min- ister. On Thursday Mr. Rawlins received the fol- lowing acknowledgement : —lO, Downing-street, Whitehall, 26th May, 1886.—Sir,—I am directed by Mr. Gladstone to acknowledge with his best thanks the receipt of your letter, forwarding to him the resolution passed at a meeting of the Liberals of the Newton Division.—l am, sir, your obedient ser- vant, G. W. SPENCER LYTTLETON.—G. W. Rawlins, Esq." CO-OPERATIVE FARMING IN CHESHIRE. The movement among Cheshire Agriculturists for the establishment of an association for the direct sup- ply of dead meat, cheese, butter, Sze., from the pro- ducer to the consumer, has now assumed a practi- cal form. The Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture tavoured the principle, and there is no doubt it will be carried out to some extent in donnection with the new Dairy Institute, at Aston Hall, Worleston, but the promoters of the Direct Supply Association have decided to embrace all kinds of agricultural produce, and have already registered a company for this object. Only English produce will be dealt with. The scheme, as now started, differs some- what from that originally brought forward, being founded on strict co-operative principles. Depots are to be formed in the principal market towns of Cheshire, with abattoirs at some central place for the slaughter of cattle. THE BOOTHS AND BARS AT NEWTON RACES.—The annual letting of the grand stand, the brick bars, and booth spaces for the annual races at Newton Common, on Tuesday and Wednesday next occa- sioned some interest on Monday, when a large num- ber of persons gathered in the vicinity of the Com- mon. The letting should have been by auction, and Councillor T. Sutton, of Warrington attended for that purpose. The restriction of the races to two days, however, appeared to have had a depressing effect upon publicans, for it is stated that not one of the offers reached the reserve prices. Many of the booths, &c., were afterwards let by private treaty, Mrs. Clough, of Manchester, securing the grand stand, with its bars. Mrs. Smith, of Manchester, and Mrs. Prescott, of Manchester,•took several of the bars and booth spaces. The remainder will be taken up, it is expected, before the races.

DEATH OF Mn. PETER WHITLEY. A well- known gentleman, Mr. Peter Whitley, of the firm of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., of the Wilders- pool and St. Helens breweries, died on Saturday evening in London. Mr. Whitley, who had had a long illness, and had not been able to leave his bed- room for some months past, died somewhat sud- denly. He was nephew to Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., and a brother of Mr. Edward Whitley, M.P. for the Everton Division of Liverpool. his father being Mr. John Whitley, a well-known and respected solicitor, of Liverpool. His brother, Mr. John Whitley, died a few years ago. Mr. Peter Whit- ley married Miss Cobb, of Exeter, but leaves no issue. His loss will be felt by the firm in the breweries, in the management of which be had always displayed great tact. One of his last acts was to send a cheque last week to Mr. Beamont for the proposed schools in Battersby-lane. On Sunday morning the Vicar of St. Thomas's, Stockton Heath (the Bev. T. S. Tofts), in his sermon referred, in touching terms, to the loss the parish had sustained by Mr. Whit- ley's death; and the flag at the Conservative Club, Sankey-street, Warrington, was hoisted half-mast high as a mark of respect towards the deceased gentleman.

Whitson (0) beat A. R. Norman and J. B. Hons., d (R), 6-0, 6-1 F. S. Joule and A. 1 fmming (R) beat A. Phelps and W. Lowndes (0), 6-2. 6-3. POISONED BY LAUDANUM AT WIDNES.—Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner. on Monday, held an inquest at the Widnes Police Court on the body of Robert Roberts, a labouter, who lived at 9, Thomas-street. Roberts had been ill for about ten months. Daring a portion of that time he had been an inmate of the southern Hospital. Liverpool, and the remainder at home under the care of Dr. McCam- bridge. As he was troubled with sleeplessness he sent a girl named Emily Speakman for 11 worth of laudanum on Wednesday evening. The girl told the deceased that Mr. Bennett, the chemist, said he was only to take 15 to 20 drops, and he replied that he knew how much to take. He added "15 drops is not enough."—Mr. Bennett was called, and stated that about 40 drops of laudanum had been taken from the bottle. That quantity would not kill a man in good health.— The Coroner: How much do you think I could take ?—Witness: From 180 to 200 drops. (Laugh- ter.) The deceased died on Thursday morning without re- gaining conscimusness.—& verdict to the effect that the de- ceased met his death by misadventure through drinking an overdose of 1 .udanum was returned.

CONCERT AT ST. EDWARDS RC. SCHOOLS RUNCORN.— On Monday evening a miscellaneous entertainment and concert was given to a very crowded audience in the above schools by the children of the school assisted by a few few friends. 'The programme was commenced .by the children appearing in a body on the stage all dressed in white and carrying bouptets and singing "The sister's birth- day" in a very tasteful manner. Next followed Mr. Quinn, who created much laughter by the song "An awful little scrub." A. laughable farce followed in which Miss Burke and F. Cross were the principal actors. and they they sus- tained their parts with admirable effect. Miss Oakden, Widnes, contributed to the success of the concert by singing "Our Mark." Mr. Daken gave an amusing reading. Mr. T. Williamson sang two songs with taste and he secured much applause. The entertainment concluded with a comic bagatelle styled "Matrimonial contracts," in which all filled their respective parts with credit. The capital manner in which Mrs. Byrne and Mr. Coleman acted in their respective capacities of a strong-minded woman and a self-willed husband was very noticeable. Altogether the entertain- ment was a most enjoyable one and reflected great credit on Mrs. Byrne for the assiduous care she had taken in training the children, and also on the other members for attaining such a standard of perfection in the short time they had in which to rehearse their parts. The proceeds were in aid of the school fund.

- THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME.—PAYMENT OF IN- TEREST OUT OF CAPITAL—The report of the com- mittee appointed by the House of Lords to consider the Standing Order affecting the payment of inter- est out of capital, which was drawn up last week, was made public on Wednesday. It is pointed out that down to 1883 Standing Order 167 of the Com- mons was practically similar to Standing Order 128 of the Lords, which required the insertion of a clause in all railway bills prohibiting the payment 'of interest out of capital. In 1883, upon the re- commendation of a Select Committee of the House o. f Commons, an alteration was made by that House in this Order allowing upon certain conditions the insertion of a clause permitting the payment , of interest out of capital. The Lords' Com- ' inittee report that they have carefully con- ' sidered the evidence submitted to the Com- mons' Select Committee, and they had determined to ascertain from some person of large financial ex- perience whether the existing prohibition main- tained by the Lords would be likely to act as an ob- stacle to the raising of capital for the purpose of sound and legitimate enterprises. They have ob- tained upon this point the evidence of Lord Roths- child, and upon a consideration of-the whole of the i evidence they have arrived at the conclusion that t is expedient to alter the present Standing Order,i and that this may safely be done if due provision s made that the public shall be informed that the i interest paid during the construction of the works s being paid out of capital. They therefore recom- mend that the presen Standing Order of the House of Commons should in substance be substituted for the exigting Standing Order 128, but they recom- mend certain verbal alterations rendering more clear the obligation to give fall information to the public. div.head: WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.

The annual meeting of Widnes Football Club was held on Wednesday night, at the Norton Arms, Lugsdele, Dr. MeCambridge presiding, and amongst the large nuint,sr of members present were Dr. Mcoonn•ll, Meier& W. Ireland, H. 0. Richards. J. E. Farrell, W. Kiddie, H. Stirrnp, T. Hineley, J.. 1. Letbatn, J. Bingham, A. Hutton, A. Brown (secretary). and J. Ashell (treasurer).—The Chairmati ex- pressed his pleasure at presiding over that gathering, as he took great interest in football, and especially in the gl'idnes Football Club. Great success bad attended the efforts of the club during the past year, especially the secend team, and next year it was proposed to have a third team, wkich it was thought would materi,lly add to the success of the club. He was sorry he could not congratulate the club on being the winners of the West Lancashire Cup, but there was a "trood time coming," and he was sure that next year, should they play together all the season, they wou'd be vety near winning the trophy, even if they did not do so outright. (Applause.) The Sec,tary then read the annual report, as follows t-- " The committee beg to submit their annual report for the season 1885-1886. The result of the matches played is— First team :—Played 27, won 14, drawn 6, lost 7. Second team :—Played 20, won 14, drawn 3, lost 3. The first team have secured altogether 14 goals, 30 tries, and 83 minor points, against their opponents' 5 goals, 13 tries. and 57 minor points; while the second team have scored 10 goals, 39 tries, and 78 minor points, against their opponents' 3 goals, 4 tries, and 24 miner points. These results taken on the whole may be considered satisfactory, although very little improvement has been made in the number of matches , won. The committee have again to cill ;attention to the large number of defeats experienced away from home. This ' is unaccountable, as the teams this year have been tolerably representative. The secend team haYe again sustained their reputation, having only been defeated three time. The total score for the season shows their great superiority over their opponents. It may be noted fleet tney have twice this season lowered the celows of the Salford ' A ' team. At the commencement of the season Mr. T. R. Sutton kindly brought down a st-ong tea,n from Manches- ter, hut we regret to a ate that owing to the miserable weather the match was a failure financially. We have to thank the peblicaus and shop- keepers for the interest which they have manifested in the club by playing a match on Good Friday, the proceeds of which, at their expressed wish, are to be devoted to provid- ing the players with suitable outfi's. This item, amount- ing to £l2 Os 61, does not appear in the balances sheet, but is held over for the purpose specified. In electing the new committee, the present Executive desire to point out the advisability of haying as few members as possible elected, and are of opinion that this will effect great improvement in the selection of thoroughly representative teams. The committee beg to report that since the last meetine arrange- ments have been made to hold athletic sports on aueust 21st, jointly with the Widnes Cricket Club. Tne preceeds will be expended in improving the ground, Sic. We ly,g again to think our president, member., and general sup• porters for their continued help." (Applause ) The Treasurer then submitted his financial statement,

from which it appeared tbat the receipts had amounted to £261 2s 11d, and included a balance from the previous year of £4 5s 3d; Border Towns' Union remuneration, £10; subscriptions, £3l 12s 6d Widnes Alkali and Gossage's Workmen's match, £3 5s 6d; charity match, £6 33 ; first team gate money, £155 l 9 9d ; second team gate money, £3O is 7P. The payments amountea to £252 Os 114 i, and included £63 us 10d for ground expenses; printing and posting account, £23 12s 4d; less of time to players. £9 4s 10d ; remuneration to W. Kiddie for injury to arm, £ll Os first team fares, £24 16s 10d; second team fares, £l5 8s 3d ; estimated cost of drainage, &c., £35. There was a balance in hand of £9 Is 11P. On the proposition of Mr. Oakden, seconued by Mr. Richards, who remarked thst he thought they ought to heartily thank Mr. Ireland, through whose instrumen- tality chiefly they had obtained the £lO from the Border Towns' Union, the report was unanimously adopted. Mr. H. Wade Deacon was unanimously re-appointed pee- aided, on the motion of Mr. Brown, seconded by Mr. Ire- land.

The Chairman was compelled to leave at this point, and Mr. Ireland took his place. The following were elected vice-presidents :—The Revs: G. Bond and S. A. Spooner, Captain Williams, Drs. J. Mc- Donnell and J. McCambridge, and Messrs. T. T. Mathiesop, C. E. Barlow, L. Pilkington, Allen Leac,in, T. Gerrard. J. L. Muspratt, E. K. Muspratt, T. Bolton, T. Cottingham, Edwards-Moss, M.P., H. S. Tlmmis, and W. W. Gossage. The election of officers by ballot resulted :—Captain of the Ist team, Mr. W. Kiddie; sub-captain, Mr. J. H. Smith; captain of the 2nd team, Mr, H. Stirrup; sub-captain, Mr. J. Wright. Mr. Farrell, the late captain, refused to be nominated. Mr. A. Brown and Mr. F. Wright were unani- mously re-elected secretary and assistant secretary respec- tively, as was also Mr. Ashall treasurer. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Hem- ingway, it was decided that the committee includes no playing members except the captains of the first and second teams, the two secretaries and the treasurer.
The committee was then constituted as follows: Messrs. J. J. Latham, W. Ireland, T. Hingley, H. 0. Rich- ards, A. Hufton, S. Price, F. Smith, J. Howarth, and C. Hemingway.
It WA—S re-solved to leave the committee to decide upon the new these for the corning setson.
The annual dinner Was fixed for Whit-Monday fort- night. _

-On the proposition of Mr. J. J. Latham, seconded by Mr. Hutton, the committee were empowered to offer medals for competition to the employes of the works in the district. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the committee and officials on the motion of Mr. Oakden, seconded by Mr. F. Smith. Mr. Brown, secretary, and Mr. Ashall, trea- surer, responded. A similar compliment was paid to the late captains and sub-captains et the first aud second teams. The Chairman was also heartily thanked for presiding. It may be stated that an excellent list of fixtures has been arranged by the secretaries for next season, and some interesting and excitisg struggles may be anticipated.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present, the Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Bradshaw. Deacon, 'raison. Robinson, Glover, Brock, and ‘3r. 11. Danhy (clerk).
WIDNES CHILDREN IN INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS.

The District Education Committee reported that there bad been 199 applications for payment of fees, and 196 per- sons appeared for contravention of Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 192 cases. Thirty-one per- sons were convizted by the magistrates, and one boy was sent to an industrial school.—ln moving the adoption of the minutes, Mr. Deacon said he and the clerk had visited the various industrial schools in Liverpool, and had seen the children sent by the School Board. The children all ap- peared well and happy. They went to the schools without notice, of course, and in each case saw the children alone, , and allowed them to ask questions. The result of the I visit was satisfactory in all ways. There were about 140 children from Widnes in the industrial schools now.— The minutes were passed.

div.head: PRIZES FOR_TRACRERS.
div.p: PRIZES FOR_TRACRERS.

The School Management Committee reported that Mr. R. Holden Davies having expressed his williogness to give prizes to those pupil teAchers who had distinguished them- selves in the annual scriptural examination, they begged to recommend that the best thanks of the Board be given to Mr. Davies and that his offer be accepted.—The minute was passed.

div.head: THZ DETENTION OF CHILDREN.
div.p: THZ DETENTION OF CHILDREN.

The Management Committee repotted that they bad sent the following instructions to all the head teachers tee' That all school rooms must be vacated at half-past four, sect that the caretaker may enter any school at half-past four (except one room, at the discretion of the head teacher of each de- partment, which must be clear at five o'clock, excepting Friday, when it must be cleared at half-past five). '—Mr. Imison moved the confirmation of the minute, and ex- plained that it had been thought necessary in consequence of a caretaker having cotnpleined that he could not get into the semol in time to clean it.—Father Clarke agreed with the minute, because it would prevent the child'en being kept in too long. over time, of which there were numerous complaints.—Mr. Glower was very much obliged to the committee for taking this step, as the children had been kept beyond time. As, however, the Board prohibited corporal punishment discipline had to be administered in some way, and it could be done better by "keeping in " than by the cane—Mr. Deacon said as a matter of fact chil- dren were kept in school in the morning, and there were constant complaints. He should have been glad if some- thing had been done with regard to the morning 5ch001..., The Chairman said the letter written to the teachers covered the morning school. If it did not effect its object the com- mittee should draft a more drastic resolution.—The motion was carried.

div.head: REPAIRS TO SCHOOLS.
div.p: REPAIRS TO SCHOOLS.

On th 3 proposition of Mr. Brock, the recommendation of the Sites and Building Committee, that the tender of Messrs Phillips and Reav be accepted for the repairs, colouring, cleaning, and painting required at Simms Cross schools, and that of Messy Lea and Son be accepted for the repairs, colouring, cleaning, and painting required at the Warring- ton-road and West Bank st:hools, was adopted.

div.head: F 1 NANCE .
div.p: F 1 NANCE .
Tbe Finance Committee recommended payment of ac- counts amounting to £551 6i 9d. and reported that the re- ceipts for the month were £165 9s 51—Passed.
MIL It. H. DAVIS.

The Clerk read a letter addressed to the Chairman from Mr R H Davies, who said he was sorry he should be unable to attend to his duties on the School Board for same time, as his health made it necessary that he shduld take a voyage. He regretted extremely that he should have to leave just now, and he should he very pleased to hear that some other member bad volunteered to fill his place on the School Management Committee.—The Chair- man raid Mr. Davie had been extremely ill from paralysis, but he was now much better, and had been recommended to take a sea voyage. He was now on his way to Australia in a sailing ship, and he would be absent five or six months, and they had every reason to hope that he would come back fully restored to health and strength. He saw Mr Davis a week before he sailed, and Mr Davis then thought of resign- ing, but he (the chairman) dissuaded [him from sucn a course. Mr Davis had been a member many , years, took great interest in the work, was extremely active sod useful, ' and it would have been a great pity if he had severed hie connection with the Board. He hoped the Board would ap- prove of the course he (the chairman) took.—Mr Glover suggested that Mr Robinson should volunteer to take Mr Davis's position.—The Chairman, however, thought it would not be courteous to Father Finegan, chairman of the committee, to appoint anyone on the committee without consultiug him, and the matter was referred to the next meeting. _ _
Theo. =s no other business of public interest.

Council lor J. Greening. DRUNIERNNESS.— For having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on Saturday night Mary Hulse, a straeger, was fined 5s and costs; John Lawriuson, for a similar offence in Napier-street, on Saturday night, was dismissed ; Michael Mellor, who bad been before the court 26 times since 1868, was fined 58 arid costs; Edward Crosby, a young man, whe h 1 been drunk and fighting in Market-street on Saturday, was fined 5: including costs; Annie McQaire, a young woman, who had been seven times before the court previously, was fined 51 and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in W nwink-street on Saturday night ;Edward Murray and Ann Murray, husband and wife, were charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Gee-street on the 15h last, and were fined 53 and costs each; beth Leyland, for having been found lying drunk on a market-stall on 13th inst. was fined 103 and costs. BEGGING.—Cieorgo White, an chi man, was charged with begging in Church-street and ream-street on Saturday ntbr, and was sent to gaol for seven days. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—Ann Reynelds, for having allowed the chimney of her dwelling-house to be on fire was fined is. OFFENDING LODGING-Mt:NI KEEPHRS.— Joseph Davies was charged with having on the 9th inst, kept lodgers without his house being registered. It was stated by two constables that at helf-nast four on the morning ef the day cession, they found a woman of had character and a man in a room of defendant's house. The man said he had paid sixpence for the uee of the room. A fine of 103 and costs was imposed, or 14 days' imprisorement.—Eliaabeth White was charged with having allowed nine perscns to INe in a lodging house licensed for seven only. The case was dismissed. TrEstyine.—Before Messrs. C. Broadbent and E. J. Guest. BREACH OF THE PEADA —Ralph Taylor and dames Lee, two young men, were charged with having committed a breach of the peace on the 23rd April in Buckley-street, and were each ordered to pay costs, 8s 64. DuuNiserreuss —John Barrett was charged with having been drunk and diso,derly at the police station on Monday night. Prisoner went to the police station for a ticket for the workhouse, hut having, lost it, be returued, and com- menced to curse and swear. Ho was discharged on pre- mising that he would leave the town. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Mr. Fairclough. DRTlNK.—Jenathan Hislam, an old Warringtonian, hut not resident in the tosn for the last ten months, was fined 5s including C 0519 for being drunk and begging in Bewsey- street on the previous night. FarDAY —Before Mr. J. White and Dr. Gornall. SLEEPING 017 T.—For sleeping out in Berry's-yard, Tan- ners-lane, Catherine Connolly, a young woman who lead been 23 times before the court, was sent to gaol fcr 14 days; James Dillon and Thomas Flaherty, two young man, were charged with a similar offence at Monks, Hall, and Co's. works. Prisoners said they had come from 4inerica in the Glasgow, and not having menev to pay their fare to Manchester they were on their way there by road. They were discharged. He was ordered to pay it in a month or go to gaol for a fortnight; Michael Birmingham was ordered to pay Is a week towards his son's maintenance in a reormatory school ; a similar order Was made on Wm. Farrington, THREATS. Mary Ann Goedchild, an elderly woman, was charged with using threats towards Richard Tinkle. The case was dismissed.

DARES BURY PETTY SESSIONS. .TUESDAY.—Before Mr. Edward Greenell (in the chair), and Messrs. 'James Masson, C. Broedbent, and El. Neiid. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. Thomas Robinson wee charged with being drunk and disorderly on the 16th inst., and wee fined lOs end costs, or 14 days.—James Boetock was charged with a like offence at Appleton, on the 5,h Inst., fined 2,6 cl and costs, or seven days in default.—Jos. Miller was fined 10s and costs for drunkenness on licensed premises. CHARGE AGAINST A PuBLICAN.WaIter James Potter, I the Stag Inn, Walton Itsferion was charged with having opened his premises dazing prohibited hours on Sunday the 16th inst, and a man named Heesom was charged with be- ing found on the premisee.—Mr. A. Browne 'defended.— P.C. Bennett said that about ten minutes to eight on the morning of the 16th lost, he was in the company of P.C. Dutton watching the premises at Walton Inferior. They saw a man named Tyer go in by the back door and come out in about five minutee wiping his month with his band. Heesom came up about to or three minutes afterwards, looked round, and then ertered the house Witness and P.C, Merton went in about five minutes afterwards and found Heesom in the bar with a pint jug of beer in his -"hand drinking. Mrs Potter was in the ban and wets in the --act of pulling something from under her apron, and seeing them she nut it back. He heard it jingle, and he thought It was money. ehe said Heesom paid for it on Saturday night and came in to drink it on Sunday morning. He asked for Mr. Potter, and she said he had gone away ; but she afterwards called him from upstairs. Witness inked round and found a glass with some freshly drawn beer in it Hee- som lived next door but one. Mr. Potter said he was very sorry, and hoped he (witness) would overlook it.—P.C. Dutton, Moore, corroborated the last witness's statement. He added that Mrs Potter said Tyer had brought something from Warrington, but he (the constable) never saw him bring anything. Sergeant Booth, s.tationed at Stockton Heath, said that about twelve o'clock Mr. Potter came to his house. lie said, "1 suppose you have had a report from your men this morning about my house," and he (witnesel replied thet he bad. He told the defendant it was no good coming to him about it. Potter seid be hoped he would overlook it, and added, " be as lenient as you pos- sibly can."—Mr. Browne said that this pint of beer was a gift. On Sanday morning Heesom went to the pump oppo- site the back door to fill a kettle of water for breakfast. While he was there he saw Mrs Potter at the window, and went in. He came out and went into his own hence. He again reterned to the public. house and went in. The floor was open, as there were no conveniences in the house. Mrs. Potter then gave him a jug of beer, which WM not measured, and no money peesed. The jug of beer was a gift from Mrs. Potter, unknown to the defendant himself. Potter had kept the house for over two years, and another in Warrington for 13 menthe, and there bad been no conviction aeainst him. There was no complaint even against him by the police.—J. Heesem gave corroborative evidence and slid he was prepared to swear that no money passed between him and Mrs. Potter. She gave the beer to him, and she bad often given him been—Potter was fined 20s and costs, and the Chairman added that the license would be endersed next time. Heesone was deed lOs and costs. NOTES BY THE WAY. At Kennington Oval on Saturd Ay Surrey beat the Au- stralians by three wickets, after a well fought out m.atch. At the conclusion of the previous day's play, the Austra- lians, with nine wickets down in their second innings, were only 82 runs to the good. A thunderstorm, accouipanied by rain, early on Saturday rnJrning, rendered the wicket slow, and the 84 runs Surrey had to get to win proved no easy task. As it was, Mr. Shuter, Driver, and Mr. Walter

div.head: TTTE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MA Y 20, 1886
div.p: TTTE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MA Y 20, 1886

Road were all out for 19 runs, but some careful cricket by l' Abel and Maurice Read raised the hopes of the Surrey sup. porters. At lunch time four wickets were down for 33 runs, and Abel—who had betted well far an hour and three-quar- ters—being out soon after the resumption, the possibility of the Australians winning became apparent to every one. The Colonists bowled and fielded splendidly; but some cool and plucky batting by Mr. Roller, Wood, and Lohmann turned the scale, and at twenty minutes to four Surrey had gained the victory. There was a great deal of enthus- iasm at the finish. Although the match was so far advan- ced, over 4,000 people visited the ground. The game between Yorkshire County and 18 of Barnsley and District was resumed on Saturday, Hall and Peel, the not-outs of Friday, going to the wicket. Hall soon brought , up his score to 31, when he was clught by Wilkinson, his score including three 4's, a 6, a 3, and singles. Bowden in little time put together A score of 20, consisting of four 3's, a4,a 2, and singles. The top scorer, however, was Hun- ter, who, by careful play and and fine hitting, made a total of 35 before he was caught by Wilkinson. His score in- cluded a 6, two 4's, four 3's, and singles. Ihe Barnsley , team began the second innings by sending Nicholson and Watson to meet the bowling of Emmett and Peate. The chief features of the game were Nicholson's finely played , 24, Harris's 21, and Elayley's 17. All these played well for their scores. Score :—Yorkshire. 64 and 136 ; Barnsley and Dietrict. 37 and 97.

Cambridge University resumed their 'rata with England on Saturday, when England, who had lost Crossland, and were deprived of Mr. Studd's services through an accident to one of his knees. required 237 to win. Some good cricket was witnessed. They stood till nearly half-past three, when the University were left the victors by 103 runs. Mr. Thornton hit Mr. Mirehouse to square leg clean into the ad- jacent field for six, and likewise made five fours. Mr. Burls was at the wicket whilst a hundred were made. Ulyett was, however, quickly disposed of, and Mr. Walker played on. Mr. Vernon gave trouble, and was last to leave. A fine catch at long on by the University captain dismissed him.

The match between Lord Sheffield's team and the Parsecs took place at Sheffield Park, on Tuesday. Rain fell heavily, notwithstan ling which the visitors, who were giver choice of innings, elected to field. The wickets were shifted to a moderately dry spot, and at 11-30 play commenced. At the luncheon interval the home team bad lost nine wickets for 105 runs, of which W. Payne had contributed 29 in good form. The innings closed at 3-50 for 142. Mr. Wyatt played a good not-out innings of 35, notwithstanding the wet state of the wickets and the incessant rain. The Parsees fielded very well. M. Framjee bowled in good form, obtain- ing four wickets at a cost of 47 runs, and Mr. lihambatt4 took three wickets for 27. In their first inninFes the visiters were disposed of for 4. Although showing good ability, the wet wickets completely disorganised them. In their second essay they were more successful, obtaining 53 runs for the loss of four wickets at the call of time. Mr. Daater and Mr. Dania showed good batting qualities. At lienninr.,,ton Oval, on Wednesday, Surrey defeated Yorkshire by 27 runs.

Tyrer moved that the salary of Mr. 0. M. Barton, relieving officer, be increased from £lOO to £l2O per annum. He stated that was the recommendation of the Finance Com- mittee, and said when Mr. Barton was appointed 2 years ago he was led to believe that his salary would be increased if he performed his duties satisfactorily. The other re- lieving officers had received increased salaries after serving similar periods, and he thought if they now refused to give Mr. Barton an increase it would be an injustice.—Mr. W. Birch*ll seconded the motion, and said Mr. Barton had at- tended to his duties in a very efficient manner, and be was entitled to the advance in order to put him on the same footing as the other officers.—Mr. William Middlehnrst opposed the proposed increase, and said the present bad times 'were not suitable for an increase of salary.—Mr. Matthews said Mr. Barton bad proved laimself to be a very good and efficient officer, and he thought Mr. Barton was fully entitled to the increstee.—Mr. Kenwright was ageinst the tnotion.—Mr. Johnson moved an amend- ment that the consideration of the advance to Mr. Barton 'be postponed for 12 months.—Mr. Leatherbarrow said be l thought it was distinctly understood that any relieving offi- cer who served two years should have an increase.—Mr. PlDaine and others continued the discussion, after fehich the ' amendment was carried by 12 votes te 11.—Mr. Jackson : It is a great injustice.—Mr. Tyrer : I should consider it a i great injustice.

Mr. Whitbread, who was loudly cheercd,.said that apprehension had been expressed that those who objected to certain portions of the bill would be powerless to make amendments in Committee, but as there were so , many Tories in the House he thought they need be under no fear that they would have sufficient help in bringing about the altera- tions they desired. Mr. Dillwyn, on behalf of Welsh members, expressed the full belief that the concessions the Prime Minister had thrown out would be satisfactory to them, and that the Prime Minister might rest vssured of the hearty support of the Welsh members. Mr. Illingworth congratulated the Government on the change which had been made, and thought Mr. Gladstone's proposals would secure the unity of the party and ensure the second reading by a large majority. Among the other members who took part in; the diacussion were Mr. Joseph Arch, Mr. Bradlaugh, Mr. Brinton, Mr. Beith, Mr. Rushton, and Mr. Rathbune: The meeting was of a very harmonious character; and it was freely expressed at the close that the second reading was sure to be passed.—Mr. Brun- ner at the close called for three cheers for Mr: Gladstone. which were heartily given.—Mr. Glad-- stone during his speech passed a high eulogium upon Lord Hartington, but did not refer to Mr. Chamberlain and those who wereacting with him. —Mr. Gladstone, at the close of the meeting, walked over from the Foreign Office at 1-40,, He carried a red despatch box under his arm, whilst Mrs. Glad- stone leant on the other. A large crowd cheered him on arriving at his residence, Mr: Gladstone re- peatedly bowing.—Sir William Harcourt and Mr. Morley were the last to leave. They 'stood for some time conversing before Mr. Gladstone's •house.—The meeting lasted one hour.

The Clerk read the following letter:--"2lst May, 1888, lam directed by the Local Government Board to acknow- ledge the receipt of your letter of the Bth inst., and to in- form you that they are not aware of any objection to the appointment of Mr. Elijah Baxter as assistant overseer for the Woolton district of the Precot Union. div.head: RESIGNATIONS.
div.p: THE RESIGNATIONS.

The Local Government Board wrote under date 25th inst with reference to the resignations by Mr. Ralph Leigh and Mr. William INliddlehurst, for the township of Speko and the Urban Ward of the townshio of Windle, respective- lv,and statiog that from the reasons assigned by those gentle- men the Board had accepted their resignations. The Board would shortly issue an order authorising th,- special election of a guardian for each of the two. townships mentioned., The Boa.td also forwarded for the information of the Guar- dians copy of correenendence with Messrs. Rowe, Pember- ton, and L'iort.n with reference to the nomination of Mr. R. A. Graves for Speke at the recent election, and whose nomination was declared invalid.—The Clerk observed that the Lecal Government Board did not ask for any observa- tions upon the letter and he did not think they were neces- sary.

div.head: GUARDIANS AND PAUPER CASES OF INFECTIOUS
div.p: THE GUARDIANS AND PAUPER CASES OF INFECTIOUS
DISRASE.

The Clerk stated that since the het meeting of the Guar- dians the Corporation of St. Helens had sent a bill asking ; the Guardians to nay the survi of £lB for the maimtenance of Ellen Kay and Samuel Latham, alleged by the Corpora- tion to be paupers. On the receipt of the letter he wrote to the Corporation. The letter was considered ley the Health Committee of the Corporation on the previous day (Wednesday), and he saw from the papers that the town clerk had advised that the Corporation could not recover the amount of that account. It would be an advantage if the Guardians arid the Corporation could arrange upon a fair sum which the Guardians might pay the Corporation to receive peeper cases.—ln reply to Mr. Dine, the Clerk said the cases in gumption were of an infectious character, which the Guardians could not with propriety receive int* the Workhouse. The Guardians held, and they were con- firmed by the Local Government Board, that it formed no part of their duty to protect the public health. The removal of any person to a place where infectious disease was likely to be stamped out fell upon the Corporation. or the local authority, and there was no obligation upon the Guardians to provide accommodation in the Workhouse. Since the last meeting of the Gaardiane, a Case of smallpox had made its appearance in Widnes. The relieving officer sent for the fever van, but he sent word that the case could not be received into the Workhouse, whereupon the reliev- ing ()Meer did the best thing he could. He secured an empty house, furnished it with the necessary furniture, and the poor fellow was removed thereto. The relieving officer. informed him that the man was now in a fair way te re- covery. The local atMerity made an offer to take the man and pat kim in a canvas tent, but after consulting with the- medical ether, it was thought that the provision proposed by the local authority was not such as they could properly. make use of—The' Rev. T. Chambers slid that case had' been before the Widnes Relief Committee that morning, and the ratepayers had already been taxed to the amount of £3 Iss, with his maintenance, and it was still going on. He thought it was important the ratepayers should consider the advisability of providing other accommodation.—The Bev, Father Finegan thought there was something very unsatis- factory about the case reported from Widnes, and be as a Widnes Guardian did not approve of it. He be- lieved it was the duty of the Board to pro- vide for pauper infectious cases, and he thought it was not the duty of the local authority to remove every pauper case. In regard to the case in question, the house had been selected in the worst place in Widnes, and he should not be doing his duty if he did not protest against taking a house for smallpox patients within what he might call a stone's throw of a large Catholic school containing 600 or 700 childreneand a large Catholic Church, where nearly 8,000 worshippers attended on Sundays. He thought Widnes was wideanoneh in area to provide accommodation for isolated cases. The tent bad done good work in the past, and might: do again.—Mr. Matthews said oases for- merly came into that hospital, and he did not know how they could come now.—Mr. Waring thought it was no part of the duty of the Widnes local authority to provide an in- fectious hospital for pauper casee.—The Clerk said the Pub- lic Health Act provided that local authorities should pro- vide accommodation for the inhabitants of their district. The Act stated further that local authorities might make ar- raugements with Guardians to ply a reasonable sum for the maintenance of pauper cases, but the Local Government Board's opini,on was that the providing of accommodation for rthe inhabitants of a district included paupers and non- paupers The Rev. T. Finegan observed that the case in question was that of a tramp, and the doors of the Workhouse were closed against ,him. 'Rethought it was the duty of the Union to receive a tramp suffering from Infectious disease.—The Government Inspector explained that the relieving officer and Guardians were bound to re- lieve cams of destitution only. If the relieving officer's attention was drawn to such a case as that mentioned that day, and be found the man destitute, he was bound to do his utmost in the best way he could until the next meeting of the Guardians, when it was for the Guardians to say whether or not he bad dealt properly with the case. If a man was found lying by the side of a road abeolately destitute and suffering from smallpox, and a place could not be found for him, he should be given an order for ad- mission to the Workhouse. He suggested the advisability of the Guardians making arrangements with local authori- ties in regard to infectious cases, and said there could be no difficulty in the way of Guardians paying reasonable sums for the maintenance of pauper oases. In order to meet all cases, he thought it was of the utmost importance that sanitary authorities should erect buildings for isolation, and that Guardians should come to an understanding with them so as to be able to send their cases there.—The matter then dropped.

THE LIBERAL PARTY AND THE HOME RULE BILL. IMPORTANT MEETING. The following is a copy-of the letter which Mr: eladstone addressed to his supporters 10, Downing-street, May 25. "Dear sir,—lt is proposed to hold a meeting at the Foreign Office on Thursday, May 27, at noon, of all members of the Liberal party who are desirous, while retaining full freedom on all particulars of , the Irish Government Bill, to vote in favour of the ! establishment of a legislative body in Dublin for the management of affairs specially and exclu- sively Irish. I earnestly request the attendance at ' the meeting of all such members of the party.— Yours faithfully, "W. E. GLA.DSTONE. I The Press Association says :—The meeting of those Liberal members who will "vote in favour of the establishment of a legislative body in Dublin for the management of the affairs specifically and exclusively Irish," was held at the ForeigneOffice at • noon on Thursday, by invitation of Mr. Gladstone. The gathering appeared to excite much interest, and a crowd assembled in Downing-street to watch the arrival of members. Among the first of these to put in appearance were Sir George Balfour, Mr. Cyril Flower, and Mr. T. B. Potter. These were , rapidly followed by Mr. Marjoribanks, Mr..Carbutt. ! Sir Mathew Wilson, Messrs. Shirley. Theodore ; Fry, O. V. Morgan, Thomas Blake,. 11. 11. I Fowler, T. 11. Bolton, A. Jones, Dilwyn, Mather, Leake, M‘lnnes, Dodds, and MsArthur, ' Sir Frederick Milburn, Sir Lyon Playfair, Dr. Hunter, Messrs. Arch, Macfarlane, Waugh, Essel- mont, and Picton, Dr. Cameron. Sir If. Kay-Shuttle- worth, Messrs. -E. R. Cook. Hibbert, Illingworth, Duff, Isaac Holden, and A. Holden, Sir Joseph Pease, i Messrs. T. Shaw, Cowen, S. Mason, Dr. Farquharson, Professor Stuart, Messrs. J. Leicester, C, Acland, j and Hayne, Sir William Harcourt, Sir George Camp- bell, Messrs. Ince, Moulton, Montague, and Roe, Professor Rogers, the Lord Advocate, Messrs. Watt. Pickersgill, Strong, Coleridge, Pickard, H. J.Wilson, Howell, W. Crawford, Spencer, Osborne, Morgan, John Morley, Campbell-Bannerman, Quilter„ Newnee, Broadhurst, Carvell Williams, Whitbread, Jacks, ! Herbert Gladstone, Fletcher, Ruston, Clark, 11. IRichard, E. R. Russell, and Agnew, Sir Charles Russell, Messrs. Childers, Lawson. Burt, and Buxton. At ten minutes to twelve Mr. John Morley called at ! the Premier's official residence, and had an inter- view with Mr. Gladstone, proceeding then imme- diately to the Foreign Office with Mr. Campbell- Bannerman, Mr. Herbert Gladstone following them from the official residence a few minutes later. It was ten minutes after twelve before Mr. Gladstone crossed over, which he did amid cheering and clap- ping of hands from the crowd. As he entered the reception-room, he was loudly cheered. Among the other members present were Sir John Swinburne, Messrs. A. Morley, Conybeare, Bradlaug,h, Allison, ' and Shaw Lefevre, Sir Chas. Dilke, Messrs. Brinton, . Gibb, Gourley, Cohen, Durant, Ingram, Ashton, Col- man, Maclver, and John Wilson (Houghton-le- Spring), and Sir Charles Forster. Mr. Gladstone commenced his speech almost im- mediately upon entering the room, and; as he pro- ceeded, the large crowd assembled outside could hear frequent outbursts of applause from. the Liberal members within. He intimated that be would in- troduce some important modifications into the clauses affecting the presence of the Irish members at Westminster, and that if the bill passed the se- cond reading it would not come on for the commit- tee stage until the autumn, when a special session would be held for the purpose of dealing with it. . In the interval the measure would be so remodelled as to introduce the new arrangements proposed with regard to the retention of the Irish members. Some of the Liberal members presenteat the meeting consider that, although the promised concessions to the dissentient Liberals are very great,.they will not be successful in meeting the views..of Mr. Chamber- lain, who, in consequence of theeterms in which the, circular of invitation was drawn, was not pre- sent at the gathering. Mr. Gladstone, the Central News says, stated that no, one would be committed by listening without protest or objection to what he had to say, as it was desired that the fullest freedom of opinion should prevail. Lord Salisbury:sepeech had decided the condition of the contreversyeand had intensi- fied the importance of bringing ,about a settlement , of this question. An abstract resolution had been suggested, but the same object, might be obtained by its being clearly understood' that the second reading of the bill would. do namore than estab- lish the principle of autonomy for Irelance, The responsibility of proposing such a principle was enormous, and had been duly appreciated lay ' the Government. Endeavours, had been made to , emasculate that principle,, and convert the bill into a delusion and a snare. He contended that it had been usual to take seegond readings of important measures without attaching to the act any more significance than that for which he now contended. As to the union of the two measures, the Laruleßill , was a matter wholly- within the power of Parlia- ment, and those whalloted !Or the second reading of the Government of Ireland Bill would be in no degree committed to • the Land Purchase Billaand their vote would only be regarded as a sort of Platonic adoption of the, principle of the bill. It was easy to imagine all kinds of difficulties, but those difficulties would disappear when there was a genuine desire to meet the case. Man:h- persona, who approved a. the main object of the bill felt a strong objection, to, the exclusion of Ireland from the consideration of Imperial affairs. With re- spect to this matter, the Government now felt that there would be no difficulty in framing and sub- mitting a plan for securing the presence of the Irish representatives in the House of Commons at Westminster during the consideration. of Imperial and general matters as well as on questions of tax- ation in which Ireland was specially interested. It would, the right hon. gentleman thought, be impos- sible at this time of the year to secure adequate time for the sufficient discussion of the clauses of the bill in its Committee stage. It was, however, desirable to get a clear and sufficient issue before the country, and the issue could well be formulated • after the second reading. After the second reading the Government would not seek to take any further steps during the present session. It was, however, highly desirable that the question should be settled as speedily as possible, and therefore he proposed to hold an autumn session for the reintroduction and consideration of a bill dealing with the Irish bill, to contain amendments QII the subjects already in- dicated. (Applause.)

div.p: SHOCKING BRUFAI,IIY TO A WIFE
AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Mr. J.. greet and Mr. H. Gaekell, jun., a labourer narne(t Daniel I Gilmore was charred with being drunk and disorderly in Walnislepwreet on the 15th May. He was also charged with •Ssatilting Patrick Roberts. On the eveoleg of the 15th lost Robert, who is a greengrocer living in Caroline- street, went to the house of a man named Hyatt for a half- crown owing, to him. The prisoner advised Ryan riot to pay the money, as he could net afford it ; but Ryan did so.. The prisoner said. " Are you paid ?" and upon receiv- ing a reply i the effirrnative, tilled Roberts a glees with beer from a half gallon jug and said " Here's a glees of ' beer in the bargain." Roberts refused the beer, and the prisoner trbeeatened that he would have to fill the jug before he went. hoberts declined and the prisoner pudeed him to the ground, and as he was leaving toe house ;sicked him.— Ryan and his wife were called and swore there was U 0 tnrhance in; the house whatever,—The prisoner, who was in 1884' committed for trial for unlawful wounding and ordered to pay compensation, was fined 7* 6.1 and costs, Ts 6d, for being drunk and disorderly, and 103 and costs, 91 6c1,. for the assault.--The prisoner was then charged, with assaulting his wife Mary. The pro- secutor said on Saturday afternoon the prisoner went home the worse for drink, And as he threatened to I takeher life she left the house. She lied to leave the house nearly every Seturday. because she dare not stay. She did not return home until Sunday morning, the 23rd inst. She Itold the prisoner where she had been during the nieht. and " it was all right "until' opening time," when the prisons', got some drink. He shut the doors, and abutted her in a fearful fashion He seized her by the neck, and knocked her head violently against the wail many times, and then struck her on the top of the head with the poker. Afterwards he dragged her upstairs, and matte her mince bleed very much. .She opened the bedroom windew, and screamed " murder, murder," and a constable came. The prisoner threatened to cut her throat And the throats of her children, and she was in fear of her life. He had acted to her in this way before, and she asked for a separation order.. In answer te the prisoner, witness said he gave her 320 on Saturday for a fortnight, hat she had to spend 25e in getting clothes out of piewn.—P.U. Pitt deposed that on hearing the screams of mwder he went to the house. Mies. Gi,mnre was bleeding at 'he nose and month ; and appeared to have received great illueage. She fainted when teen, into a neighbour's house.--The prisoner made a long statement about his wife's shortcomings, alleg- ing that throureh her making had acquaintance he had had to remove to half-e-dozen different parts of the town. He expressed sorrow for the assault, but he was chastising her for her own gocd.—P.O. Pitt recalled, said he knew Mr. Gilmore two years and she had always kept herself respec- table. She was-not a drunken woman.—The Bench sen- tenced the prisoner to two months' hard labour.

Mr, Henley, the Government Inspector. gave a lengthy address with regard to his inspection of the Workhouse, and said he thought the present accommodation was not suffi- cient to meet the requirements. It bad been ever-crowded during the winter, and at the present moment was practi- cally full. If the scheme for the erection of an additional hospital upon the Adjoining ground had been Abandoned, it was for the Gunn/line to consider what other scheme they could adopt so as to meet their requirements._ He thought some of the present arrangements were inconvenient for the °Meer', and sAid it was clear if they did not make m.bre accommodation in the house they must make accommoda- tion outside—lt was decided to refer the recommendations to the Visiting and Building Committees.

div.p: TUN NNW 11815TANT OTBRSHER FOR WOOLTOIIG

The Rev. T. Chambers antl Mr. Neilson, J.P., raised the question of the amount of the bond proposed to be entered into by the new assistant overseer for the township of Woolton, and suggested the advisability of increasing the bend so as to cover am amount equal to the sant of money he could have in his possession at one time. Mr. Neilson said they had suffered a great deal in the past and they wished protection for the future.—A long discussion ensued, during which the Clerk said the consideration of the bonds of all the officers of the Union had been referred to the Finance Cosnmittee, and their suggestions upon that matter would shortly came before the Board.—The Chairman said the Board wished to do what was perfectly right, but a good deal depended upon the overseers of the different townships In looking Atter the assistant overseers and the amounts they collected.—The question was ultimately left over ustil the report of the Finance Committee was received.

RULE. MEETING AT EA.RLE3TOWN. SPErA..,'I3 BY MR. JOHN CROSFIELD, J.P. A public Rome Rule meetinv. ()ailed by the Liberal Council and " 300 " of the Newton Division, wag held in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown, on Satur- day night. There was a large attendance, many Irishmen being among those present. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. W. Rawlins, of Rainhlll, and he was supported by Mr. RD. Holt, J.P. ( Liverpool), Mr. George Melley, J.P. (Liverpool), Mr. R. C. Richards (Manchester, secretary tSo the National Reform I -Union), Mr. John Crogfield, J. P., the a4opted Liberal candidate for Warrington ;: Mr. C. M. Percy, the Liberal Labour candidate toff the Ince Division at tho last election ; Messrs. r: A. R. Neill (Bold),,. Birkhead (Earlestown). W.. Mitchell (Golborne), Kelsall (Rainhill), W. Urquhart (Newton), J. Pres- cott. L. F. Foulkes, B. Harrison, G. Ratcliffe, le. M. Campbell (registration agent;), T. Morris (secretary, Earlestown and District Liberal Club), and others. The CMAIRMAN, who was will received, said he bad letters of apology from several gentlemen. Mr. Charlre- Bioadisent, of Warrington, said he eras- sorry he would not be able to come, but he wished thew every success, He had adetter frorn Mr. William Summers, lets member for Otaleybridge, who said—" I trust that you will have a suc- cessful meeting, but I much regret that my engagements in London will not permit me attendingthe demonstration favourable to Home Rule." (Applausw.)' He had a letter from Mr. Jacob Bright—(applause)—ho wrote.—" I regret not to be able to attend your meeting, wishing yon success." Mr. E. R. Resell, M.P., wrote be was sorry lie had an engagement in London, otherwise it would have given him great pleasare to attend the meeting, and Mr. W. Mather tele- graphed that a definite engagement prevented his presence at the meeting.- A telegram from Mr. Herbert • aladstone— (applanse)—stated that it was with great regrehhe must re- fuse the invitation. He had a letter from Colonel alcCor- nuoaale--(leud applaase)—who said he was sorry absence from home made it impossible for him to come, 1-,u;he ven- tured to hope some scheme would be adopted whereby the ills of Ireland would cease. (Applause.) A letter from Mr. Charles rilkington steted that he had engaged to go- abroad but wee prevented by the sevdre illness of his brother, Mr. Richard Pilkington. He was very sorry he was enable to , attend, but he aontinued " I hope you will have a nuecees- ful meeting.. I think nearly all Liberals wish to give Home Rule to Ireland." The Chairmae proceeded to state that that meeting had originated with the Liberal " 300," which represented the Liiaeralistn of the division. A short time ago they had x meeting of the " 300," and a resolution in favour of the policy of Mr. Gladstone with regard to Ire- land was ;permed without a sinnle hand being held up against it. But it was felt at that meeting that that was not enough—that the electors of Earlestown should heve an opportunity of meeting together and join in discussion upon that subject, That they should have an opportunity of raising their voices in support of their grand old leader in his effort to send a message of peace to Ireland. (Applaurre.) They all knew this was a crisis of no ordinary kind; It was a crisis of fir greater importance than any within his own recollection, and he doubted if tiers had been a crittie of such importance any time duriag the present century. It was very Important that wherever Liberals were stauncla they should meet together and do their best to support her Majesty's Government. They had a very strong oppoeition against them. They had the 'Tories, who were traditionally operated to them and had never yet dorm anything and who would never do anything for Ireland—(applause and a voice : " Nor for England.")--as long as they could help ie They unfortunately had those of their own political faith who were not now helping them. He thounat they were making a mistake, which they would shortly have to regret and very bitterly regret. (Hear, hear.) It W 39 all the more important therefore that those who were staunch and true to Mr. Gladstone elioutel let the country know it. He briefly comrnenteshupon a late Tory meeting in that hell and said they would flora that the resolution to be placed belore them was not of eueh a doubtful character an that introduced at Sir Richard Croes's meeting. The Tories claimed that they wished to maintain the union between Great Britain and Ireland. They (the Liberele), 100,. wanted to do it—(hear, hear)— but they wished the union to be brined upon the affections et the two people, ‘ttpon the common love they ought to bear between one and another, a coinmen national interest, and a common patriotism. (Applause.) They did not want a paper union, based upon the hatred of people, or a union supported by Britieh bayonets by which the people were thwarted in their just and reasonable aspirations for toed autonomy. It was for that holy union Mr. Gladstone was spending perhaps the last months of his wonderful political life, and to create a lasting political union. He hoped they would support their grand old leader in that m:sornficent effort. (Applause.) 1 Mr. GEORGE MELLY, .P.P: (Liverpool) proposed "That this meeting, believing the time has come for a permanent settlement of the Irish question, reeognises in Mr. Glad- stone's bills for the government of Ireland a just and wise solution, and it therefore expresses its unabated confidence in Her taajesty's Government, and offers them its hearty support in the present crisis" (Applause.) He spoke at some length of tree grievances which existed among the Irish people in regard to their non-representation in the House of Lords, the militia, and the Arms Act, and said the Nationalist parte were represented at Dublin Castle. not by Irishmen, bat by Scotch noblemen or English peers, anhl the whole government of beland in the House of Com- mons had been, whichever' party was in power, and would continue while the present system existed, to be in the heeds of English and Scotch statesmen. What they wished for was a union beeed upon fair play and upon good government, and while they could not accept the advice of the moderate Literate, they could say by the measures of Mr. Gladstone they ensured union to a disunited nation, sod added to the power and preolge- of a common empire (Applause.) • Mr. H. C. RICZARD3s seconded the resolution. He seid they were toad that they were simply blindly surrendering their judgment to their leader, Mr. Gladstone; but he was anxious of setting. forth the main, principles of the bill to show that they would not be surrendering their judgments blindly. He referred at considerable length to the measeres, and urged that ever since the Act of Union was passed the Irish people had never ceased to agitate for its repeal. (Ap- plause.) He said the opponents' of Mr. Gladetone had no alternative scheme to suggest, and the position of Mr. Glad- stone in regard to that matter reminded him forcibly of the position of the late Sit Robert Peet in regard to the great Free Trade controversy. It was written of Sir Robert Peel that he gave the people bread, but it would be written of Mr. Gladstone that he had given the people peace. (Ap- plause.) Mr. C. M. Purim who, was received with cheers, sup- ported the resolution. He said he hoped there would be an appeal to the country. soon, ae-they were told the people had not been asked theiropinione The sooner it was taken the better, and there was one divirsion of this county which would tell a different story at the next election to that it did befere—(hear, hear)—end then, was one distinguished member of the Tory Cabinet, if he could not find his way to the House of Lords—(laughter)—bad bettsr become a candidlate for an hush constituency, because amongst those contendang elements Mr. Gladstone referred to there was sure to be. room for a man of Sir Ric- hard Cross's dispositioneand he might find himself at home In Debbie, but he must change Kis residence from the New- ton Division. (Applense.), sal'e- only hoped at the next election they migbt get to good a candidate to fight their battle as these had on the last occasion. (Aaplanse.) No mate fought better or more bravely than Colonel McCor- quodale. (Applause.): He (Mr. Percy) supported Mr. Gladstone's bills pure and simple, and was quite prepared to support it with exch amendratents as be thonaht neces- sary. They were told it was simply hero worship—this worship of Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone, to him, was the greatest hero that ever breathed—(applause)—aad he was net ashamed to say that ranch as he appreciated the bill '.upon its own merits he appreciated it much more in con- ,!equence of the dietinctione the eminence, and the truth of its author. (Applause.) Lord Salisbury had told them his plan for Ireland was, to exile one million of its people and Ito give it 20 years of coercion—(" Shame");—but the day for exile had gone. They did not want to banish men from their native soile but they wished it to he a nation happy and prosperous so that hisemen would be inclined to return to it and settle, in it in their declining years. (Applause.) He had not one wort/ to say against Lorch Hartington, who had done good', work for the Liberal party, but he hoped he would find the error of his ways e'er long. Of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain he had no hesitation in saving his conduct with regard to the measure had almost placed him outside of Liberal circle,. He could believe in honest opposition, but be believed Chamberlain was troubled with an overween- ing ambition which inithat case had overleaped itself. (Ap- plause.) He believed the heart of the people were with Mr. Gladstone, and that if an appeal to,the country was made he would be returned to power with such a majority as would make Tory opposition vanish like mists before the .sun. (Applarse.) The Irish nation had suffered under lEteeslish, rule 700 Years of injustice. The very iron of in- :justice had entered their souls, and wherever Irishmen had settled in all parts of the world there was a feeling of bitter- ness at the injustice of English rule. He believed that last saws made a mistake with the American Colonists and lost the greatest colony a nation ever possessed so bad 1.74 by misgovernment and injustice caused a feeling of bitter- ness to arise in millions of the people. So far as the in- tegrity of the Empire was concerned, amongst the most eloquent of our Senators had been Irishmen, in the battle. fields upon which victory had been won, Irish blood had been spi led. (Applause.); Oar Empire was their Empire, our traditions were their traditions, our history was their (history, by wiping ont the sense of tyranny and injustice Ithey would make the Irish a loyal, prosperous, and conten- ted people, and he believed the result of Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy would be that the English and the Irish com- bined would go on iu terms of amity and good will. still further strengthening the foundations and the walls of the Empire of which they were all so propd. (Applause.) The resolution was then passed amid cheers, without a single dissentient,
