Con. for young ladies fond of pastry.—When is an orange not an orange? Why, when it's a little tart, to be sure "11l make you dance!' cried an irate mother pursuing her erring son' slipper in hand. "Then," remarked the juvenik, " we shall have a bawl." IN THB MERRY MONTH OF May.—First artist: "How are things looking, Jim, since I saw you last?" Second artist: "Looking up—decidedly looking up. Last year I was floored; now I'm 'skied." "When a woman goes horseback-riding," says an Ameri- can paper, " she wears a silk plug hat. She does that so that the horse may believe she's a man, and not be frigh- tened at her. She couldn't fool a Kentucky mule that way." Said a four-year-old, on being told the story of Little Red Riding Hood," I don't see what the wolf wanted to eat up the little girl for. I should think the grandmother would have been enough for it. She would if she was as large as mine."

REAL CHICKEN Soup.—Customer in New York testae- rant : " Waiter, this chicken soup has feathers in it." Waiter : "Yes sah. If yo' want soup made oaten chickens old 'cough to be bald, sah, yo'll have to go to some odder 'stablishment." _ _ _ _ _ _

--Charitable parson, to ragged and shivering tramp, daring ' a spell of cold weather: Well, my man, I object to giving , money; but, if you come home with me, I will give you an overcoat that will last you through the winter.—Tramp: Overcoat, is it, sure? And it's for raining my business yer after ! CILITHLTY TO CHILDRBL—The conversation of two little girls amused me. Said one: "When I grow up I'm going to be a school teacher." "Well, I'm going to be a mamma, and have six children." "Well, when they come to school to me, I'm going to whip 'em, whip 'em, whip 'em" (with crescendo intonation). "You mean thing!" (with horror) what have they ever done to you!" The choir was sadly out of tune on a certain Sabbath morning, and, after rendering an opening anthem most execrably, everybody seemed to take it for granted, and looked upon it as exactly the proper thing to do, when the pastor aLnounced for the morning lesson the twentieth chapter of Acts, beginning, "And after the uproar was ceased."

HOW SHE MANAGED.—Young wife: Tell me' dearest, isn't this milk nice and rich ?—Young husband: Yes, it is much better than we have had. How did you manage ? Young wife, enthusiastically : I engaged a new milkman who guarantees his milk, and I have bought enough to last a week! There—wasn't that fine?

"I say," said the smart little son of a country printer who had just started a local paper, as he entered a shop in the town, "do you keep knives ?" "Oh, yes," responded the shopkeeper—" we've kept them for years!" " Well," remarked the boy, starting for the door, "you ought to advertise, and then you wouldn't keep 'em so long !" Ethelborta : "I want a pair of slippers for pa. Number tens, please, and—squeaky." Genial shoemaker: "Squeaky', mise ? I'm afraid we haven't any of that kind." Ethei- berta :"lam so sorry! Couldn't you make him a equzaky pair? There is a certain young gentleman who visits me Irequ2ntly, and—and it would be very convenient for him to know just when pa is coming." WARM MINISTRATIONS.—A minister in the North was taking to task one of his hearers who was a frequent de- faulter, and was reproaching him as an habitual absentee from public worship. The accused vindicated himself on the plea of a dislike to long sermons. "'Deed, man," said his reverend monitor, a little nettled at the insinuation thrown out against himself, "if ye dinna mind, ye may land yerael' whaur ye'll no be troubled wi' sermons either lang or short !' " Weel, maybe," retorted John; "but it'll no be for want o' ministers, at ony rate l" Some prospectors in West Virginia found signs of natural gas on a farm belonging to an old man, and they went to his house and asked permission to bore and try farther de- velopment. "What's the gas good for?" he asked. "To take the place of fuel." " Will it take the place of wood ?" "Oh, yes "Then yon can't bore a darn bore around here I've got five *tapping bg Bons who are too infernal lazy to do anythings more'n cut nuff wood to warm their shins; and, if we had nateral gas to barn, I'd have to hire a nigger to help the boys draw their breath !" "Why, Mary Ann, I haven't seen you in an age. You must come home and stay with me." "I can't do it, I've got married since I saw you last." "You, married! Why you always said that you never would get married." "I know that, but I got married as a matter of accomri,oda- lion." "To accommodate your husband, I suppose." " Oh, no! not at all. You see almost every day before I was mauled a por,r unfortunate wretch of a tramp would come to my house, and beg for a pair of my husband's cast-off pants or an. old pair of boots, and I hated to send him away empty handed, particularly as he really needed clothes, so I got married just to accommodate that tramp with my hus- band's old clothes. _ _ _

Some time ago Mr. Will Carleton visited one of the lowa towns in his capacity as lecturer, and was duly placarded on the walls, "Will Carleton October 5." The next lecturer in the coarse was Hon. Will Cumback of Indiana. In view of this event posters were printed, "Will Cumback December 11." The bill-poster was instructed to pat theee bills in the place of the Carleton ones. His paste must have been better than his orthography, for, having heard that Mr. Carleton was re-engaged for an evening later in the season, he supposed this to be a typographical statement of the fact' • and so he posted the new bills directly under his name; and the unique announcement then read as follows, "Will Carle- ton Will Cumback December 11," and remained on the walls of the town for several days, till rectified by somebody who knew how to spell. Two young ladies were overheard talking glibly and con- fidentially in a suburban train. "Now, Mary," said one, "tell me why Charlie and you quarrelled." "Because he's a ninny; that's the reason. You know he's been coming to see rue for two years, and I could tell as plainly as anybody else that he was overhead and ears in love with me. But he didn't seem to have any go in him, and I got impatient, just as any girl would have done. A •few nights before Christ- mas he called to see me, and, before he went away, I said, "Charlie, I want to make you a Christmas present, but I want to be sure it will suit yoa. It is something nice, warm, useful, ornamental, and will always stay with you.' 'A scarf?' he said. No, not a scarf,' I said, 'though it might embrace you. It weighs aboat one handfed pounds, and I've I heard you say you thought it very precious."ob, I know,' he said—' a bicycle r By this time I was nearly mad; bat I made one more effort. 'Not a bicycle,' I said; but it can walk, has a mouth, eyes, pretty hair, and is very affec- tionate.'Now I know! he said; and what do you think the ninny guessed that time? A big Newfoundland dog! I was never so disgusted in my life, and have not seen Charlie since. He has treated me shabbily; and low leap. year has gone, and I hate him." " SIIGGIESTIONS."—" The invitations lent of late to naval officers requesting them to furnish suggestions for a change Of uniform remind me," says a writer in the Boston Journal, "of s similar invitation issued by Jefferson Davis when he was secretary of war under General Frank Pierce. One of these invitations was sent to Lieutenant Derby, a good draughtsman and a merry wag, who sent in response a pro- position for having a twe-inch iron ring appended to the seat of each enlisted man's trousers. Long and formal specifications demonstrated the utility of this ring. Each officer was to carry, instead of a sword, a long white-ash pole with a hook on one end. By hooking this into the ring of a private he could be kept in line of battle if he were dis- posed to hang back, or caught if he attempted to run away. The ring would also be useful in the artillery services for draught-parpoees, while the caval?'e• men could he locked to , rings in their saddles, and so kept from falling off. The illustrations which accompanied the specifications repre- sented officers catching infantry stragglers and forcing them Into the ranks, dragoons padlocked to their saddles, and , artillerymen, with gun-prolongs hitched to their ringe, hauling heavy pieces of artillery up steep heights. It was very funny, and the clerks in the War Department enjoyed some hearty laughs over it ; but, when it reached the secre- tary, he became indignant land regarded it as an insult. He ordered charges and specifications to be drawn up, and a court-martial was actually ordered, when it came to the ears of Governor Marcy, the secretary of state, who was level-headed, and who advised Davis to let the matter drop. He might convict Derby and have him dismissed from the service; but he would be laughed at from one end of the country to the other. Davis took the advice, and Derby's 'suggestions' are still to be found on the files of the War Department."

SUPPLYING FALSR NEws.—At the Mansion House Police Court, London, on Monday, Charles Fowler was charged with endeavouring to obtain money by false pretences from the Press Association. Limited. The solicitor for the pro- secution said he would be able to establish not only the particular charge, but several others of a similar nature. The supplying of false news had been going on for some time. The Press Association had used every effort to nis- cover the authors, and had employed detectives for the pm-- pose. Mr. E. Bobbins, manager of the Press Association, proved the receipt of the news of an attempt to murder a sweetheart at Milton on the 28th November, 1885. It pur- ported to come from "J. B. Harrison," and was in the pri- soner's handwriting. Some years Ago the prisoner, in his own name, supplied accounts of fires, but they were found to be bogus fires, and orders were gives that no more of his copy should be used. The cashier of the Press Association proved that in December last prisoner applied for payment of an amount due to " Harrison " or " Martin3or."—The prisoner, who admitted that the copy was in his handwri- ting, was remanded, the presiding alderman stating that he would accept bail in two sureties of £lOO each. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, t MAY 29g 1886 • LITEMPOOL INTERNATIONAL EX- HIBITION. • LOCAL EXHIBITS.—No. 2. Wiredrawing, one of the staple industries of War- rington, is well represented at the Exhibition, and amongst the exhibitors the manufacturers of this town hold a prominent place. This class of exhibits are 'hen one is passing from the principal entrance towards the Liverpool trophy displayed on the right hand side of the main avenue. It might be sup- posed that there would be little of interest about this department of the great "worlds fair" except to the expert, but if this opinion be entertained by any one we may safely augur that they will be agreeably undeceived When they come to witness the amazing variety of uses to which wire is put in these days. They will see compounded of strands of wire ropes of great thickness and immense strength wherewith to tow ocean-going vessels, in close con- nection with slender cords designed to hang pictures or form the meshes of fine netting; wire for ttle- graphic purposes, and wire shaped into spring mat- tresses of singular strength and flexibility, and the same material designed to subserve numberless other ; useful purposes. Conspicuous amongst the exhibitors are Messrs. Rylands Brothers, Limited, of Warrington, who have a handsome show case standing about 9 feet high. Be- hind the glasses of this case may be seen samples of every kind of wire for manufacturing purposes, an- nealed steel wire for fencing, bright and galvanised wire for wire workers, coppered wire for spring workers, charcoal wire, and various other sorts. There are also specimens of probably every kind of steel copper and iron ropes to be used in connection with the rigging of ships and the working of mines, inclines, collieries, &c., and there is likewise galvanised sash cord, and cord to be used for the pur- poses of communication and picture hanging. One of the exhibits which will attract the eye is a tall pyramid of coiled wire rope, graduating in size from considerable thickness to extreme fineness. These ropes, as may be sepposed, are put to many uses, as it includes the best galvanised rope for ships rig- ging, charcoal flexible ropes for hoists, fine cords for picture hanging, sash cords, &c. In another part of the case are to be seen coils of galvanised wire for telegraphic purposes, fine galvanised steel strands as supplied to various railway companies, and simi- lar material which has been supplied by Messrs. Rylands to the Indian and other governments. It is needless to enumerate the various other objects of interest to be seen at this stand, unless it be the. patent galvanized flexible crucible steel hawser on a neat and very strong reel, a class of hawser which has been supplied to the Admiralty and various shipbuilders. The exhibits of the Whitecross Wire and Iron uompany, Limited, cannot fail to command atten- tion, and will very forcibly impress upon the spec- tators the magnitude of the work done by this firm and the completeness of their processes. The foun- dations of a massive pyramid are formed of rough ! lumps of raw pig iron, and upon this there rests 1 samples of the manufactured material varying from I rough round wire-rod about a quarter of an inch in I diameter to the smallest size of wire. There are other two pyramids which are built up with large coils of wire ropes suitable for a variety of purposes, the more massive being much used for the standing rigging of ships, and the light and flexible for working the sails. There are likewise samples of rope admirably adapted for hauling and winding in connection with collieries, inclines, &c. Of special interest will be the samples of telegraph wire which this firm turns out in such large quantities; and amongst the other items to be seen there is a powerful wire hawser, one of a kind much used on vessels, and wire nails in the several stages of manu- facture. In short, no one can view these well- arranged exhibits without having a better concep- tion of the various processes in connection with the important industry of wiredrawing. The Longford Wire Company, Limited, furnish many interesting exhibits, and these are ingeni- ously and attractively displayed. In addition to several products of the wire industry which they have in common with the firms already men- tioned, they evidently make a speciality of their admirably designed Woods' patent galvanised mat- tresses. These are displayed in great variety. To give ocular testimony of the singular strength and flexibility of these mattresses there is exhibited an ordinary hospital bedstead and mattress combined, and on the mattress are placed forty 561 b. weights, or in other words one ton weight, and over it is placed the announcement, "This mattress is guaranteed to resume its original position when the weights are removed. These weights are re- moved and replaced every day during the time of the exhibition." Another test of the quality of the galvanised materials used :in making these mattresses is applied by placing a piece of the material together with a piece of tinned wire be- neath dropping water. The result is that the gal- Tanised material remains quite clean and unaffected whilst the tinned wire shows unmistakeable signs of corrosion. To still further attest the su- perior qualities of the wire of which Wood's patent mattresses are formed, there is a sample of it with two sGlb and two 2.81 b weights suspended by it, and in connection with this there is placed the intimation "Sample of galvanized wire No. 19 gauge used by us; breaking strain 2181bs. No other mattress manufacturer can use ,this strength of wire." Objects of general interest on this stand will be found in the sleeping saloons designed and fitted with the firm's mattresses for use on board ship. , One of these is of iron and brass, nicely decorated and finished, and furnished with two mattresses, while the other is a frame of wood fitted with two berths, upper and lower, a fea- ture of this frame being that the upper berth ia fixed to the back of the frame with hinges, and may be dropped when not in use and made to act as a cushion to rest against, and the lower berth may be used as a couch. There are likewise two ordinary domestic bedsteads provided with Woods' patent mattresses and patent locked socket. The stand of this firm, it may be safely asserted, will well repay a careful examination. A further notice of local exhibits will be given next week.

THE WORLD GONE MAD.-Mr. Justice Wills, trying A case under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, at Leeds Assizes, on Monday, said he l.,gan to think that part of the world had gone mad on this subject. At the assizes a year ago there were two or three cases of this kind ; this time there were 35. Unless they exercised caution there was a danger of seeing a state of things which would be a terror te a great number of innocent people as well as to the guilty. THE JERSEY BANK FRAIIDS.—EXTRLORDINARY ALLIGA- TIONS.—At the trial of Charles Sorel, sub-manager of the Jersey Bank. at Jersey, on Tuesday, evidence was given that, during the last tive years, the reports presented to the shareholders were regularly falsified. The liabilities in 1879 were understated by £70,000, and increased to over £243 000 in 1883. Interest had been charged on outstand- ing accounts and creeited as profit. out of which dividends were declared, though neither principal nor interest was paid.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER
LONDON, THURSDAY.

It seems to men of this generation that never be- fore, except perhaps at the time of the repeal of the Corn Laws, has political feeling been excited to the height at which it stands to-day. But it is, when we come to think of it, a ratter of much more modern occurrence. When Mr. Gladstone intro- duced his first proposals to free the Irish land and disestablish the Irish Church, faction ran as high and political parties were as widely divided. As the Attorney-General reminded the* House by a quotation from a speech delivered some sixteen or seventeen years ago by Mr. Plunket, Irish Tories were as willing then, as now, to die in opposition to the iniquitous courses of Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Plunket is not a man of the Johnston or Saunderson type, much less does he resemble that man of (militia) war, Mr. Ashmeacl-Bartlett. When we find Mr. Plunket declaring in the year 1869 that he and his friends are prepared to die in defence of the state quo in Ireland we realise in a moment how bitter must have been the passion aroused at that epoch, and how futile are these explosions of burlesque agony from shocked Tories. Mr. Plunket, every on is glad to know, is alive and well to-day, and so six- teen years hence will be Mr.lohnston, of Ballykil- beg, Major Saunderson, and Captain (or is it Colonel?) Ashmead-Bartlett, of the militia force. There has not yet been time to ascertain the , effects of the meeting at the Foreign Office to-day, when Mr. Gladstone took counsel with his friends upon the political situation. The general impres- sion is that it will have a favourable effect upon the waverers. One thing is quite certain. It will tend to fix the hour fcr the settlement of the question in the division lobby. There is nothing more to be done now except to vote. The utmost limits of• con- cession have been reached and announced, and if members cannot now make up their minds as to how they shall vote, they will never do so. The British public may therefore expect to wake up on Wednesday morning and find themselves either face to face with a dissolution or riding at comparative ease in smooth political waters, with the settlement of the Government of Ireland Bill relegated to an autumn session. _

These are, I believe, the two alternatives. If the second reading be passed the Committee stage will be postponed to an autumn session. This is a sheer necessity apart from political exigencies. The Irish Bill has been the lean Eine that has swallowed up the rest of the flock of measures submitted this session. The estimates are in a very backward state, necessitating the taking of a vote on account. With the second reading passed, supply would be forth- with dealt with, and the other ordinary business of the session wound up as rapidly as possible. The House would adjourn about the middle of July to meet again in Oct. for the great battle. On the other side, assuming the defeat of the Government on the second reading, there is immediate dissolution, and there will follow one of the most hotly-fought general elections since that of 1868. The issue is looked forward to with great confidence in Minis- terial circles. There is no doubt that, unless the Conservatives help them, nine out of ten of the followers of Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain will be bundled out of their seats. The question is whether the vacancies will be filled up by Liberals or Conservatives? _ _ _

_ Very little is heard just now of Lord Granville. He appears with great regularity in his seat in the House of Lords, and he conducts the affairs of the colonies. But interest in Parliamentary affairs is just now centred upon the licuse of Commons, and the duties of Secretary of State for the Colonie are for the moment confined to entertaining the repre- _ _ _

_ sentative colonists.who are being feted-in Lonaon. ! Popular opinion about Lord Granville is that he is ; an amiable,- and accommodating nobleman, who ! does not concern himself very deeply about any phase of political affairs. It is a little surprising to hear, as I do upon the authority of one of his ! colleagues, that in Cabinet Council Lord Granville! takes a most deciled Dart in discussion of the ! Irish question. He is one of the boldest and most ; consistent supporters of Mr. Gladstone in his policy of trusting Ireland, and will listen to no suggestion ! tending towards the emasculation of the bill. This is pleasant news, considering that Lord Granville is I generally accredited with a disposition towards ; Whiggism, and is popularly regarded as being rather ' a drag on the chariot wheels of Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy. The departure of the Queen for Balmoral in the very midst of the political crisis has effectually re- moved the good impression made by her Majesty's recent partial emergence from retirement. The end will come within a week. Before next week closes it will be known whether the second reading of the Government of Ireland Bill has been passed in the House of Commons, or whether it has been defeated, and Mr. Gladstone has appealed to the country. It surely could not have been a matter of Irreparable inconvenience had the Queen's holiday journey northward been postponed for that time. The event would have been of the less importance were it not for the insistence of her Majesty upon the carrying out of the slightest details of formali- ties, whether she be at Windsor or at Balmoral. We have learned from her published works. and have gathered from statements in the biographies of others, how jealously her Majesty preserves the simulacrum of personal rule. Practically, the na- tion is ruled by Parliament, and the Royal veto, which is retained in the written constitution, is a _ _ _

dead letter. But it pleases her Majesty to proceed on the assumption that she is the actual and auto- cratic ruler, and no step is taken, or, at least, none formally legalised without her consent. This position is maintained with reference to the minutest points. Ministerial offices are at the dis- position of the Prime Minister of the day, who re- presents the will of the majority of the people. In making an appointment, from the Chancellor of the Exchequer down to the Parliamentary groom- in-waiting, Mr. Gladstone would be actuated solely by considerations of the fitness of the person de- signated. The fiction is, and it is daily set forth in due form in the" Gazette," that the fortunate ob- ject of the Prime Minister's choice is appointed by her Majesty, and woe unto somebody if, by any chance, a newspaper chronicles the appointment before it has been submitted to the Queen. A gen- tleman closely concerned once told me that when an appointment had been arranged all Ministers in the secret lived in a state of trepidation till the appointment had been submitted to her Majesty, fearing that it would prematm ely get into the newspapers, with the inevitable result of someone

receiving a severe wigging. This is all very well ; but it creates exigencies very difficult to deal with when her Majesty is making holiday at Balmoral, and Westminster is in the fierce heat of a political and Ministerial crisis. Last night Dover House was thrown open for the first time by the hospitality of the newly-created Minister for Scotland. Dover House is situated at Whitehall, with an entrance from St. James's Park. It is a splendid mansion, and was at one time spoken of as the home of the First Lord of the Treasury. It would have been a pleasant change from dingy Downing-street. But somehow the arrangement never came off, and when the Secre- tary of State for Scotland was created Dover House was made the official residence of the Minister. Extraordinary efforts were made by Lord and Lady Dalhousie to make the reception worthy of what is, in a sense, a historical occasiou, and they were wholly successful. The staircases and rooms were lavishly, and with perhaps unusual taste, decorated with flowers and foliage. But the speciality of the decoration was the clusters of arms which shone upon the walls. The full band of the Scots Guards were stationed in the vestibule, supplemented by six pipers, who, on the stroke of midnight marched, through the brilliant throng, with pipes in full swing. Most of the Foreign Ministers were there, and Mr. Gladstone looked in for half an hour, hav- ling put on in honour of the occasion one of his biggest collars. He has of late rather laid aside this peculiar mark of supremacy, and its revival last night was much noted. Mrs. Gladstone was also present, and stayed long after the Premier had disappeared. The Derby week is always important at the theatres. There is generally a change of programme. All the good managers "go up one." This year it commences the American season. We used not to have an American season. Now it seems established that once June sets in American troupes come over and the Londoners go to the provinces. Also we have had our first week of Italian opera. Notwith- standing all that has been said to the contrary it has been an opera of stars, or rather of one star. Patti comes for concerts. The costly Prima Donna is to get £2OO for singing for a few minutes at the Albert Hall. We can't afford her as a star at Covent Gardens and have need to take up with a tenor. Spaniard Gayarre has come to the front in the most extraordinary manner. The French have adopted him as a favourite. The Paris opera being in difficulties its director sent for Gayarre, who came , from Spain, sang a certain number of nights with feverish success and went home to Spain with a bundle of bank notes in a sealed parcel which he was not to open till he had crossed the frontier. I forget how much it was, but it was certainly more than he expected. His success was superb. Here he has sung, but the English are colder. It was as Gennaro he made his debut. The Royal party were in their box. Gayarre has plenty of fire, but the purity of Neario and the sweetness of Ginglini remain still unreplaced. At the Avenue they have been giving an old opera of Offenbach's at morning performances. It is delightful to hear this tuneful music and sad to see what opera bouffe has descended to. The Creole, now called the Com- modore, has an articulated plot, a story with action and progress in it, and is set to music. It is not a mere case of music-hall airs added to a bewildering skeleton of a play which no one takes the trouble to attempt to understand.

div.head: IMPROVEMENT.
div.p: IMPROVEMENT.
FREE LIBRARY.

Sir,—l would like, with your permission, as a working- man, to say a word or two upon the above question. as I consider it conc-rns us more than any other class. There we those who seem to think that when we have the use of the reading-room and the books there, we have all we need. But, whilst it may suit the requirements of a few (And I am sure all will acknowledge its great value), the great major- ity are left out in the cold. The average workman, it at all fond of home, does not have too much time to spend with his wife and family, and I would ask what share he is to have in bringing up his children if be is only to eat and sleep at home, as would be the case,nearly, if he was to de- vote a few nights to the reading-room. Many working- men, besides working hard all day, have to walk a long way to and from work, and mar live a considerable distance from the reading-room. His going there means farther labour, and the pleasure would be turned into a toil,whereas if be had his book at home he might take it up as leisure presented itself to him. Nor would a thoughtful man care to have his children to go and select their own reading, and read away from home. I for one wish to know what my children read, and to have a say upon it, and I know I am not alone in this respect. The question of ways and mane seems really to be the great obstacle in the way; but surely this cannot stand in face of the fact that many towns of ii-(33 note than War- rington have their Free Libraries, and have had to get them without having, as we have, a Library to commence with. Some, if not all, of the suggestions made in the " Guar- dian " might be practically adopted; and I am sure the article in the "Examiner " last week dealt very ably and fairly with the obstacles in the way ; and I hops that once the public get to know that it can be done without further ! burdening the rates, the difficulties will all vanish, and that such will soon come to pass is the wish of
A WORKINGMAN.
THE ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRADE DEPRES- SION.

Sir,—Your readers will remember that previous to the General Election a good stroke of business was effected by the Tory party by the help of the Fair Trade cry. It was put to the working classes, as being the party most in- terested, that no one ought to object to an inquiry into the cause of the depression, and a great amount of apparent con- fidence was shown that such an inquiry would result in an unanimous verdict in favour of a return to Protection ; this same Protection to be clothed in a garment as varied in colours as Joseph's coat. The party epposed to the inquiry based their opposition on the grounds that Koval Commie- lions are expensive and their work very protracted, and, what is of more importance, that all possible information was already in hand an could be at once acted upon, in the event of a Parliament sufficiently Radical being elec- ted. If working-men fancy that by calling themselves Tories and voting for rich landowneis they are protecting British interests then they are making a mutt egregious mistake, and nothing brines this out so well as the reports just isened. It is possible that the leedere of the Tory party may find that they have made a whip for the Radical party to use, and that before long it will he used withoat stint. How can the working-man elector expect the rich MAR with his thousands invested in railways to vote foe a bill in- tended to reduce railway charges ? Sir Lowthien Bell in his evidence states—" For the last two or three wane for every shilling a ton which iron falls in price they (the nil wave) grant a rebate in GermiliV, I think, of one per cent off their usual rates, wed at the present moment the Ninth for all iron-making eriaterials carried in larger qu rothiee amounts, I think, to about from 13 to 15 per cent." It is thus seen that national enterprise is encouraged, and that wages, although lower in Germany, are not the all importerat factor in the competitive race. The same witness on this point states that although labour is cheaper in Germany than with us, ours is more efficient in such operations as those met with in the manufacture of iron." When we further consider the immense distances over which ore and finished goods hive to be taxen be rail from 200 to 300 miles, and that they only barely succeed in sup- planting us in the markets, we are led to ask, what would be the result supposing we had the railway rates and the low royalty rents of Germany ? As it is', the British maker is enabled to deliver an article like railway rails fully as cheaply. if not more so, than those in Germany on board a ship for exportation." The evidence given by Mr. Smith, manager of the Bar- row Steel Company, is especially interesting as an answer to those who quer,toionniythsiex weeks superiority w of e Englishhad an order srdteeerl rails. He Bays for 10,000 tons of steel rails at £2 10s a ton higher than the price that was current in the States, and I presume that £2 108 was supposed to represent the difference in value between the American and the English rails. We have since then obtained another order, and we have two or three more neeotiating." When it is understood that these orders have been obtained in spite of a pretective duty of 19 dollars a ton, we may reasonably hope that when the burdens now weighing on hnainess operations are cleared away, briehter days may be in store for us. This witnese, speaking of royalties, puts them at, OR the west coast, Os eld a ton. Ore is imported from Spain, the royalties on which are Si per ton. Added to the difficulties of our manufacturers are rates and taxes of such a character as do not affect the foreign makers. It is clear from reading over the evidence that there is a desire on the part of witnesses not to say anything orejudiciel to either the interests of Rrilway Companies or landowners. Those who in Warrington remember that at the outset of the Ship Canal scheme several gentlemen in- tereeted themselves to a laudable extent in its promotion. and then suddenly collapsed, will understand hew vested interests can be brought to bear upon private companies. This question of Royalties and railway rates is one that will have to be fought out at the ballot box, and no candi- date calling himself Whig or Toty if not safe on these ques- tions should be supported by workmen. DEATH OP M. LLOYD JONES.-Mr. Lloyd Jones died at his residence, Stockwell. London, on Saturday night, aged 75. He bad been ill for several months. The deceased, who was born at Bandon, county Cork, served his appren- ticeship in a Lancashire linen factory. Early in life he became imbued with advanced political ideas, and far many years was an able missionary and follower of Robert Owen. He was an active promoter of the co-operative movement;and was a well-known writer on political sub- jects.

div.head: RUNCORi•I BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORi•I BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The ordinary fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon, under the pre- sidency of Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton. There were also present—Mr. John Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood, and Messis. Mclntyre' Had- field, Wallington, Lewis, Aaron, Farrell, Brandreth, Speak- man, Stokes, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). VISIT TO Tun WOREHOUsE.—The following letter had been received by the Clerk:—" Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to tender to you for the informa- tion of the Guardians of the Runcorn Union the accompany- ing copy of a report which the Board have received from the CommitsiAners of Lunacy of a visit made to the work- house on the 19th ult. by Dr. Williams, one of the Visiting Commissioners. (Signed) COURTENAY BOYLE."—[Copy. " Four males and eleven females in this workhouse are classed as of unsound mind, and have to-day been seen by me. I can report favourably of their general care and treatment. Three of the males were in bed. Nearly all of the females are usefully employel The dietary is good. CHFSTBR ASYLUM—The following letter was also read from the County Asylum, Chester:—" May 20th, 1858. Dear sir,—Charge for Maintenance of Patients.—At a meet- ing of the committee of visiting justices of this asylum, held on the 18th inst., it was ordered that the charge for maintenance be reduced to 7s 7cl per head per week, com- mencing from the let April last.—l remain, dear sir, yours fat hfully, J. E. EDwARDs, clerk to the visiting justices.— To the Clerk to the Runcorn Union." THE CLERICS REMUNERATION.—There was another letter from the Local Government Board as follows :—" White- hall, S.W., 24th May, 18811.—Sir,—I am dirccted by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the let inst., and to state that they sanction the payment to you by the Guardians of the Runcorn Union of the sum of £B5 for your services as clerk to the Union Assessment Committee during the past year, and of the sum of £3O in consideration of the extra cervices rendered by you under circumstances mentioned in your letter.-1 am, sir, your obedient servant, ALFRED D. ADRIA.IT, assist- 'ant secretary.—To Mr. H. Linaker, clerk to the Runcorn Board of Guardians."

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The ordinary fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Lieut. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present :—Mr. John Weir (vice•chairman), the Revs. J. W. N, Tanner and J. Lockwood, and Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Hadfield, Wal- lington, Lewis, Sthkes, Brandreth, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances).

div.head: PROPOSED NEW RAILWAY STATION.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW RAILWAY STATION.

The seal of the Board was attached to the fcrilowing peti- tion :—" To the Chairman and Directors of the London and North-Western Railway Company. The humble petition of the Guardians of the Poor of the Runcorn Union, in the county of Chester, acting as a Rural Sanitary Authority, sheweth :-1, That a railway station on the Widnes side of Runcorn Bridge is not only desirable, but hai become an absolute necessity; 2, That many gentlemen of position employed in Widaes reside at Runcorn, Frodsham, and Helsby, and have no means of getting home except 11 Walking across Runcorn Bridge in all weathers, or the equally objectionable alternative of walking (many of them some distance) to Widnea station, and taking the tedious and expensive journey by rail via Ditton Junction; 3, That such exceptionally defective communication is depriving a large population from living in the districts of Runcorn, Frodsham, and Helsby, many of them now residing at Dit- ton, Hunt's Cross, Halewood, Garston, and Sankey, on the Cheshire Line 4 Railway; 4, The exorbitant railway fares for crossing the bridge should also be considerably reduced, especially to contractors going further than Runcorn, and should net much exceed, if any, the present contracts for walking the bridge; 5. Your petitioners assure you ths many persons are most desirous to build houses and take residences in Cheshire. but are entirely prevented through this want of railway accommodation, and we are convinced the, a station en the Widnes side would develop a large passenger traffic and add considerably to your company's receipts. Your Petitioners therefore pray that immediate steps be taken to place a station on the Widnes shie of Runcorn Bridge, which will be of the greatest convenience to the public, and will at once encourage and ensure an im- mense increase in passenger traffic. And your petitioners will ever pray. (Signed) JOHN ASHTON, Chairman."

div.head: OUTBREAK. OF . _DIPHTHERIA..
div.p: OUTBREAK. OF . _DIPHTHERIA..

Dr. Adams, medical officer of health, submitted his annual report on the sanitary condition of the Rural Sanitary dis- trict of the Runcorn Union during the year 1895, and also the following special report :—" I have to report an out- break of diphtheria at Frodsham. Four cases have occurred. On my inspection of the house suspicion fell upon the drinking water, which consists of filtered rain water from a large underground tank. I examined the interior of the cistern, and discovered a large pipe at the top, probably meant for an overflow pipe, but through which foully offen- sive sewage was discharging into the cistern. The whole sanitary arrangements connected with the water supply and drainage here require inspection, and there are also detects connected with the water closet. I would suggest that this Authority instruct their inspector to make a complete report upon the sanitary arrangements upon these premises. And that the water be immediately analysed. All usual precau- tions are taken for preventing extension, and drinking the water prohibited."

DRAINAGE OF WESTON. The seal of the Board was attached to a mortgage for Westou drainage to secure £450, and farther debentures not exceeding therewith .£6l6.—Mr. Aaron moved that a vote of thanks be tendered to the engineer, clerk of works, and contractor for the excellent manner in which they had constructed the sewer at Weston. He spoke highly of the efficient, workmanlike, and practical way in which the work had been carried out, and said he thought the persona he had enamerated were deserving of the thanks of the

Board.---The Chairman thought it would not be *ise to set such a precedent.—Mr. Brandreth asked if tba work was being done for nothing. (Laughter.)—A desultory discus- sion then took place as to whether the Board should tender the vote or not, but Mr. Aaron's proposition not being Se- coned, it fell to the ground.

CORRESPONDENCE. The Chairman said the following letter bad been ad• dressed to him as Chairman of the Board :—" River View, Overton, May 24th. Dear Sir.—When can I see the minute you and the Clerk said on Friday evening was passed by the Guardians, when the Sanitary Committe was first formed, that before a person could sit at the same be must be rated at £25? Your answer will oblige —Yours truly, J. H. HARGRRATES. Mr. John Ashton, chairman of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority." There was a post- script to the letter saying that a copy ef the writer's letter would be sent to the Local Government Board if his appli• cation was not entertained.—Mr. Hadfield proposed that the ' letter be laid on the table.—Mr. Aaron seconded.—Mr. Lewis remarked that Mr. Hargreaves had been nominated, and he evidently thought he had a right to sit. He only wanted to see what prevented him.—The Chairman: I should have been quite satisfied if he had not added the postcript to his letter.—Mr. Hadfield : Mr. Hargreaves came• and used most offensive language at Friday's meeting, and yet he had no business there at all —Mr. Lewis asked if he was prevented by law or by a bye4aw passed by that Board. —The Chairman : It is by a bve•law which was passed when the Committee was first appointed.—Mr. Aaron : He says if we will not give him what he wants he will write to our masters.—The Rev. J. Lockwood thought that because Mr. Hargreaves had acted in a certain way they need not act in a certain way. They ought to be above it. He should suggest that a letter like the following should be sent to Mr. Hargreaves :—" Dear Sir,—By such an Act of Parliament no person can sit on the Committee not less rated than £2s:"—The Chairman said if the letter was laid on the table he should simply acknowledge it, and say that it bad been dealt with in that way.—The Clerk pointed out that the Act of Parliament stated that members of Parochial Committees should be qualified as the Guardians should decide. It did not say what the qualification should be. That was left entirely to the Guardians.—Mr.. Hadfield stated that all those things were explained to Mr. Har- greaves at the meeting on Friday.—The Chairman: Mr. Hargreaves has evidently got an idea in his bead that the qualification is made at this time purposely to exclude hire, and that £25 has not always been the qualification. Rut that is not so.—The proposition that the letter be laid on the table and no further notice taken of it, was then put, and carried.

div.head: LA'ls FST NEWS.
div.p: LA'ls FST NEWS.

, Mr. Jesse Collings will contest Lincoln at the general election. An important discovery of gold bas been made in the Kimberley district. Last night's " Gazette " is flooled with honours dis- tributed ill honour of the Queen's birthday. THE Gaze was run on Friday with the following result: Miss Jummv, 1; Argo Na.vis, 2; Braw Lass, 3; 12 ran. Richard Hadley, seagoing engineer, who is alleged te have been stabbed by his brother George, at Jarrow, on Saturday, died on Friday. The laiad agitation in Wales is now assuming very serious proportions. Several farmers have proposed to withhold their rents altogether unless their demands are granted. It is stated that the Government intend to bring in their promised Registration Bill at the earliest possible moment, so as to have it in operation next spring if a general elec-

tion should then be found necessary. John Butler, a self-actor minder, hanged himself in his house at Ashton-under-Lyne on Friday morning. He injured himself recently and had been unable to work. his wife had gone to the doctor's when he committed suicide. .

TRAGEDY AT 13 shacking discovery has been made at Hyde. A man named Knott, residing in Back _Ver- non-street. reached home late on Thursday night, and found his wife and child lying dead in bed. The child, which is aged seven months, appeared to have been strangled, and it is suspected that the mother destroyed herself by taking poison. A post mortena is to be held to discover the cause of death. TUB CONVICT TRAVIS.—The High Slseriff of Cheshire had not received any communication on Friday morning from the Home Office respecting Robert Travis, hotel keeper, lying under sentence of death in Cheshire County Gaol. The officials confidently anticipate a favourable reply to the influential petition whioh has been forwarded on Travis' behalf, supplemented as that is by the favourable opinion of the foreman of the jury which tried him. The execution is fixed for Tuesday. AL&RMING GAS EXPLOSIOg.—An alarming explosion of gas occurred at the shop of Charles Tyler, pork-pie manu- facturer, Nottingham, on Friday morning. Tyler used a large gas oven for baking purposes, and fifteen minutes after the gas had been lighted a terrific report startled the neigh- bouts, and the oven was found completely wrecked, while I the walls of the bakery were blown outwards and the roof removed. Some m isonry was blown a considerable dis- tance. Tyler, his wife, and daughter had remarkably nar- row escapes from serious injuries. THE .snne CANAL BILL. A London correspondent writes :—You may regard it as almost positive now that the Manchester Ship Canal Bill will pass the House of Lords and receive the Royal assent before many weeks have pas- sed. There was no opnosition on Thursday to the proposal to amend the standing orders of t)e Upper Chamber so as to permit the payment of interest out of capital, and the principle is now sanctioned by the orders of both Houses. The Interact Bill introduced by the promoters of the Ship Canal will be put down for second reading probably on Monday, and immediately after the Whitsuntide holidiys a select Committee will be appointed to consider it. This in- quiry will be very brief, and it is doubtful whether the London and North-Western Railway Company and the other interests who have all through opposed the project will deem it worth while to carry their hostility to the pre- sent bill further.

div.head: HOME RULE CRISIS.
div.p: THE HOME RULE CRISIS.

It is stated that a meeting of Mr. Chamberlain's suppor- ters wai held on Friday afternoon to consider the attitude to be taken in reference to the Home Rule Bill. It was agreed that the concessions proposed by Mr. Giadstone in his speech on Thursday were Rot acceptable. The position will therefore remain as before At a meeting of the Liberals in Trinity Ward, Burnley, on Thursday evening, a resolution was adopted, declaring that Mr. Rylands, M.P., by his recent action on the Irish question, had forfeited the confidence of the electors in that Ward. Whe resolution was passed by a perfectly un- animous vote.

The Wellington, Salop, Liberal Association, after an ani- mated debate, have carried a vote of confidence in Mr. Glad- stone, thotigh the member voted against it. Lord Randolph Churchill still believes that the bill will be rejected, and took an even bet with Mr. Labouchere on Thursday afternoon to that effect. The Duke of Westminster has placed at the disposal of the Liberal Union Cotnmittee the Derby Stakes which were won on Wednesday by his Grace's Ormomde. They amount to about £5,000, a good windfall for the committee.

div.head: BELGIAN SOCIALISTS.
div.p: BELGIAN SOCIALISTS.
BRUSSHLS, FRIDAY.—The Socialists threaten a great de- monstration In all provincial towns on the 2311 Jane. THE MOUNT ETNA ERUPTION. -

- ROME FIUDVI.—Tne streams of lava are now less vl- lent in the direction of Nicolosi. The country around, however, is still in danger. During the night the inhabi- tants of Nicolosi remain in the streets watching the course of the eruption. The prefect, bishop, and military authorities are os the spot ready to render assistance if necessary. MOVEMENTS OF DON CARLOS. The Central News Berne correspondent telegraphs :—The Spanish Embassy at Paris has sent to the Legation at Berne demanding information of the Federal Council rela- tive to the movements of Don Carlos. The Council, in reply, state that the Pretender appeared at Lucerne and then abruptly left for Austria, crossing from Switzerland by the Gotbard Bailway.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. ROUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. ROUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUs.—The Earl of WEMYSs gave notice of further amendment 3 on the third reading of the Crofters Bill.—The report of amendments on the Irish Labourers' Acts was agreed to.—Earl SPENCER moved the second read- ing of the Contagions Diseases ',Animals) Ball, which was agreed to.—The report of amendments ost the Infants Bill was also agreed to.—Earl GRANVILLE, replying to Earl Harrowbv, said arrangements were being made at the Colonial Office for a separate department having charge of all matters relating to colonisation. _
The House then—adjourned- HOUSE X4' COMMONS.

The House met at four o'clock. QUESTIONS —EXTRADITTOIC—Mr. BRYCer replying to Mr. Howard Vincent, said negotiations to place extradition on a more satisfactory footing were going on with the Gov- ernment of the United States.—Mr. Bryce, replying to another question, said intelligence had been received of the discovery of a plot for the assassination of Plince Alexander of Bulgaria, and his Prime Minister, but no facts had been elicited to implicate the Russians in the matter. THE HOME RULE BILL.

Sir M. BEACH said yesterday he believed the Prime Minister had stated that there were two courses that could he pursued with the Government of Ireland Bill—either to let the Bill bis kept alive,, after it had been read a second time, for an autumn session, or to let it lapse an 4 be remo- delled and re-introduced in a new session to be called in the autumn. He should like to know which course the Gov- ernment intended to adopt. Mr. GLADSTONE said he had so stated, and he had also stated that the Government preferred the latter course. He felt he was not at that moment called upon to make a more positive statement. Sir M. H. BEACH said the answer of the Prime Minister was so unsatisfactory that he moved the adjournment of the House. He thought they should know the exact course that was to be pursued regarding the bill, whether it was to be withdrawn or not, and, if withdrawn, why. He desired to know why the Government measure was to be put aside for six months. Such a course would paralyse the forces of law and order in Ireland. The course to be pursued would continue the present Government in power, but it would be an Administration not having the power to carry out the policy it advocated.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the course the Government thoeght would be best to adopt with regard to the bill was that which he had stated. It was obvious that the bill could not be passed through its ordinary stages in the present session to enable it to go to the House of Lords in time for its being dealt with there. The Government had raised an important issue, and it was their desire to keep the greatquestion clear The Government had entered on a conflict and they were prepared to go through it to the end. They were prepared to concede as far as possibls to friends, but he declined to take the ad- vice of the opponents of the bill. The second reading would be solemn pledge to Ireland that the House of Com- mons intended to proceed with and pass the bill, but he pointed out that could not be done in the remaining time of the session. He contended that the Government had ad- opted the best course under all the circumstances. Lord R. Canostu, accused the Prime Minister of speak- ing with two -micas on this subject. They had asked the right hon. gentleman a simple question, and to that question they could get no direct answer. There had heen great talk of going to the country, but the whole of the proceed- ings of the Government showed that they did not wish to do that, and the policy they were adopting was to prevent the people expressing their opinion on the bill. Tbe whole of the action of the Government was pure Parliamentary Inancevriitg. He could not conceive why the Government declined to state what course was to be pursued with the

bill after it was read a second time. He was determined he would elicit that information by moving adjournment after adjournment at a future stage; and, further, he would do his beet to prevent the Government hoccussiog the House of Commons.

• The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHWQIIER justifled the course the Government proposed to adopt, and expressed a hope that the Government would be able to withstand even the determined opposition of the noble lord.

Lord iIAUTINGTON said he was not surprised at the pre- sent motion. He thought it but reasonable that the House should know the exact course that was to be pursued with regard to the bill they were now asked to read a second time. They had been told there were two courses that could be adopted ; either to adjourn tbe House after reading the bill a second time, or to wind up the session, prorogue, and reintroduce the remodelled bill: He thought a distinct answer ought to be given to that question. The Chancellor of the Exchtquer, and after him Mr. Gladstone, said they had clearly stated the Government were in favour of the latter course and prorogation. Lord HARTINGTON said there was no precedent for that course. The House was to be asked to give its assent to the Mond reading of the bill, which could not under any circumstances pass into a law. The House had never until now been asked to read a bill a second time which was geed.

Mr. T. P. O'Comion condemned the present motion for the adjournment ,of the House, and denied that the bill was dead. On the contrary, be said it was too much alive for the noble lord and his friends. The motion of adjourn- ment was made, not for the purpose of getting information, but for disturbing and distracting the public mind, and preventing the union of the Liberal party. Mr. Itemns peinted out that the motion for adjournment was fully justified, as by it they had at least get it that the bill, after the second reading, was to be withdrawn, proro- gation was to follow, and a new bill introduced to an autumn session.

Lord J. Memisus said as the information sought bad been gained, there was no need for pressing the motion for the adjournment of the House to division. (Cries of "Oh " and "Nc.") Sir M. BEACH asked leave to witbdrAw his motion. The Irish members. with loud cry of "No," refused to assent to that course. The House divided : For the adjournment Against

The announcement of numbers was received with loud cheers and laughter by the Irish members. Tax ADJOIIRNSD DEBATE.—The adjourned debate on the motion for the second readirg of the Government of Ireland Bill and Lord Hartington's amendment to read the bill that day six months WAS resumed.—Mr. Blom said he supported the second reading and ha doing so denied that he was in the slightest way assenting to the disintegration of the empire.—Mr. E. BecxErr could not vote for the second reading of the bill, lubricated as it had been with jam. There was difficulty in every clause, danger in every sen- tence, and mischief in every line of the bill. This specimen of the constructive genius of the P.ime Minister bad been riddled to pieces by the arguments of its opponents, and he hoped before another week it would be entirely dead and the Government rid of fer ever.—Mr. ATHERLY.JODias sup- ported the second reading of the bill. [mgrr errrixe.]

div.head: NUISANCES.
div.p: NUISANCES.

The Inspector reported the I-xistmce of a nuisance at Whitley Superior, arising from foul privies; of which notice had been served for abatement. It had been of such a character as to necessitate another inspection, and arrange- ments would have to be made to prevent a recurrence. A nuisance was also reported as existing at Walton Inferior, arising from an accumulation of the deposit of objection- able refuse. Notice had been served for its removal, and he
(the inspector) bad no doubt but that it would b'e complied. with.
SERIOUS FAMILY DISPUTE AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesdly, before his Hon- our Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, William Bate, boatowner and merchant, Argyle-villa, Greunway-road, and his wife, Mar- garet, brought an action against Henry Jackson, proprietor of Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, to recover a gold watch and diamond ring, alleged tc be wrongfully detained. Mr. Jackson made a counter-claim of £l9 Ts 61, which was made up of charges for four days' board and lodging of the plaintiffs ad his family, £4 money lent, and LT paid to Annie Harrison by the defendant on behalf of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs were represented by Mr. Squarev, barrister, Livetpool (instructed by Mr. J. Burton), and Mr. F. A. Lake was for the defendant. The hearing of the case occu- pied five hours, and, as stated by Mr. Squarey, was to the effect that Mr. Bate and Mrs. Jackson were brother and sis- ter. In September of last year Mrs. Jackson told Mrs. Bate that her husband was in need uf money to meet: a heavy account, and the result of the interview was that Mrs. Bate lent Mrs. Jackson the gold watch and diamond ring upon which to raise money. Subsequently the jewellery was pawned with Mr. lmison, Church-street, for £l5. Efforts since made to obtain the return of the articles had been without avail, and it was not until these legal proceedings were threatened that the counter-claim was set up.— Mrs. Bate confirmed this statement, and in cross- examination by Mr. Lake, said in May, 1883, her husband was in difficulties, and the furniture of the house in Stanley Villas was seized by the sheriff's officer, and the furniture was subsequertly sold. Previous to thet'tinie Mrs Jackson and her husband had been unfriendly. She knew thetyackson's bad lost a con- siderable sum through her husband. On the Bth May, issa, she, her daughter, her son, the baby, and Aranie Har- rison went to Wilson's Hotel and stayed four days. Her busbanl only stayed one night. ,e be alleged that Mrs Jack- son invited them to go and that they thought it very kind of her and accepted her offer. She never said they would have to pay, and she (witness) never offered to pay. They lived with the Jackson family and were not treated as cus- tomers. She admitted having the use of the pony and cart to remove furniture one night, but nothing was said about pay. She denied having asked Mrs Jackson to pay Annie Harrison, her servant, £7 wages due.—Wm. Bate, husband of last witness examined, said in March, 1883; Mr. Jackson became surety for him for £4O in the Union Loan Company, and he deposited the watch and ring with him as security. Be paid off that loan and received the jewellery back. He borrowed £3 about April or May from Mrs Jack- son, and had repaid £2 ef that amount. He put the value of the watch and ring at £37 —By Mr. Lake :1. be defendant's pony and cart was used in removing furniture from his (witness's) house during the time the bailiffs were there. The landlord, however, interfered, and the removal was stopped. He gave £l5 for the watch 30 years ago, and £22 for the ring about 12 or 15 years ago. —Miss Bate gave evidence of a confirmatory character.— Mr. Lake said personally he regretted very mud) that there should be any necessity for this unfortunate family dispute to come into court, but they had been unable to settle it.— His Honour said these sort of actions were a perfect abuse of county courts.—Mr. Squares, also expressed regret that the case should come into court. His clients had offered to refer the case to the learned registrar, but the other side refused.—His Honour said tbese sort of things were demoralising to the country, and interfered greatly with family relationships. County courts were never intended for such actions.—Counsel endeavoured to come to some understanding, but Mr. Lake announced that they were un- able to settle the case. Ha called H. Jackson, the defen- dant, who said the plaintiff's family came to his house on the 9th May. Mrs. Bate said they would pay. He pro- duced his book and said the items were entm.ed at the time they were incurred. They promised to pay on numerous occasions.—Mr. Bete: Eh, what a lie !—His Honour : If you address such language as that in this open court I commit you.—Mr. Bats: I beg your honour's pardon.—His ' Honour: If you use such language as that I'will commit you, although yen are the plaintiff in the action. Your language is abominable. A man in your position ought to know better —Mr. Jackson, continuing his eviolence, said the plaintiff's family were treated as ordinary visitors to the house. Sometimes they had their meals in ;the commercial' room and sometimes in the front room. They never had their meals in the kitchen. The charges made were the usual reasosiable charges. Mrs. Bate asked his wife to pay Annie Harrison's wages, and said she would pay her hack. —Mrs. Jackson, called, said her husband had lost about £3'6o through the onaife plaintiff. When the bailiffh were in the plaintiff's houSe Mrs. Bate sent for her and asked her if they could come and stay at the betel. She said they would pay for their rooms and for what they had. She had lent Mr. Bate £4, and never received a half-penny back. She borrowed that sum from Mr. Prescot, as she did not like to ask her husband as Bates had had so much from them, and never Paid them beck She piid Annie Harrison £7, wages due at the request of Mrs. Bate, because Mr. Bohanna, the sheriff's officer would not do so. She had asked for the £lO 7s 6d many a time, end Mr. Bate always made some excuse. At one time he sad he had been buying an 80 guinea piano. In March Mrs. Bete asked for the jewellery, and she (wit- ness) told her she should have it when she bad paid their acceunt.—Cross-examined by Mr. Equarey : She had lost her husband and children scores of pounds through Bates. Her husband on one occasion had to pay £lOO for Weaver dues for Mr. Bate.—Annie Harrison gave corroborative evidence. —His Honour summed- up at great length, remaking that

there was a direct conflict of evidence between brother and sister and sister-in-law and brother-in-law, and be had to ray who was speaking the truth. He gave a verdict of £25 damages, to be reduced to £1 on the return of the articles to the plaintiffs. He disalleared the whole of the counter claim with the exception of £2, part of the money borrowed by the plaintiff. Costs to follow the verdict.

A 1 BOLTON.—Ann Berry, factory opera- married, but living apart from her husband, was on Thursday morning committed for trial by the Bolton magis- trates, charged with the wilful murder of her illegitimate male child. A. soap box was found by some boys in a mill lodge. It contained the body of a child. The prisoner practically admitted that this was hers, but the defence was that the child died a natural death. TEE EARLESTOWN DRAUGH'TS CLUB.—The first general meeting of the members of the newly-formed Draughts Club was held at the Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-place, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening, when Mr. S. Wightman occupied the chair. There was a good attendance. Arrangements were made for purchasing draughts and boards, and it was also decided that a contest should take place among the members. The question of providing rules for the management of the club was also considered, and a committee was appointed to draw up rules and submit them at a fnture meeting. In concluding this letter it may be well to point out that although a large amount of information is given by our foreign consuls to the Commission, yet these gentlemen do not seem to be especially active in the countries to which they are appointed, as the following evidence will show. Mr. Smith, the manager of the Barrow Steel Company, said "that German officials in foreign countries constantly report as to new railways and other undertakings, and that German merchants and manufacturers are on this account often trying to negotiate business before we are infornted of it in this country."—Yours, c. • H. FRODSHAM. FRODSHIM AND FRODSHAM LORDSHIP PAROCHIAL CommyrrEss.—The fortnightly meeting of the absve com- mittees was held in the Town Hall, Frodahava, on Friday evening, when Mr. John Ashton presided. The Clerk pro- duced accounts amounting to £325 us I.d for engineers', legal, and other expenses in connection with the water scheme, but the account of solicitor to trustees of the late Major Ilitehen had not been received. The accounts were parsed subject to taxation. There was no other business of public interest. CHURCH MISSIONARY SOCIRTY.—On Sunday special set-- mons were preached in the Frodsham Parish Church, by the Rev. W. J Ball, M.A., late missionary in the Punjaub, in aid of the fueds of the Church Missionary Society, and on Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, when the Rev. FL B. Blogg. M.A., vicar, presided, and there were also on the platform the Rev. W. J. Ball, M.A., Rev. E. Marsden, and Rev. A. P. Reynolds. The Chairman said that during the year ended the 31st December last the Fredsham branch of the Church Missionary Society had contribute-i £5O 7s 10d, and he thought that about the same amount would be received for the current year. The Rev. W. J. Ball, who attended as the deputation, then gave a deply interesting Account of his labours as missionary at Lucknow and other places. and made a strong appeal for increased efforts in the missionary work. The Rev. A. P. Reynolds moved a vote of thanks to the deputation, which was carried, and the meeting terminated.
